title: Penn State wrestling reveals lineup for season opener against Bloomsburg
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
After revealing minimal details in the preseason, Cael Sanderson has released Penn State's first lineup for the 2026-27 campaign.

Here's how the Nittany Lions will shape up against Bloomsburg.

125 pounds: No. 1 Luke Lilledahl vs Justin Jones

Coming off a national championship last season, Lilledahl will get his junior season underway against Jones, a redshirt freshman.

The Orange County, Virginia, native is 5-1 this year after going 11-11 last season. He's racked up a pair of technical falls and a major decision along the way.

133 pounds: Masanosuke Ono vs Austin Pollard

Ono will make his highly anticipated college debut after failing to appear for the Nittany Lions last season.

It'll also be his folkstyle debut. Ono is a decorated freestyle wrestler and claimed a gold medal at the 2024 World Championships, also having a U20 World Championship under his belt from the same year.

Pollard is in his fifth year as a college wrestler, having totaled a 20-17 career record to this point. He's gone 5-4 in two seasons at Bloomsburg after transferring from Lock Haven.

141 pounds: Hayden Cunningham vs. Scotty Johnson

While Marcus Blaze made the jump to 141 pounds this season, Sanderson has opted to give Cunningham the slot in the season opener. He compiled a 12-10 record in open tournaments last season as a sophomore after redshirting in his first year as a Nittany Lion.

Johnson is in his first year at Bloomsburg after spending three seasons at Clarion, and is 4-2 in his limited time as a Husky.

149 pounds: No. 4 Shayne Van Ness vs. Jay Chase

Van Ness is likely to be out for blood this season after falling in the national title match last year.

He'll start on the road to retribution against Chase, a redshirt freshman who's worked to a 19-11 record in two seasons with Bloomsburg.

157 pounds: No. 2 Tyler Kasak vs. Michael Turi

Kasak is back in the lineup after redshirting last season. Turi is still undefeated in the early stages of his freshman campaign, sporting a 3-0 record as a Husky.

165 pounds: No. 1 PJ Duke vs. Morgan Schwarz

Duke was an All-American at 157 pounds last season and has jumped up a weight class to 165. He'll debut at the new weight against Schwarz, another Bloomsburg freshman with an unblemished 3-0 collegiate record.

174 pounds: No. 1 Mitchell Mesenbrink vs. Mohamed Abdelhady

Mesenbrink is also up a weight class from last season and will debut at 174 pounds after back-to-back national titles and a Hodge Trophy at 165.

Abdelhady, an Alexandria, Egypt, native, went 44-7 in two seasons at Indian Hills Community College before transferring to Bloomsburg this season. He's 3-1 so far as a Husky.

184 pounds: No. 2 Rocco Welsh vs. Gavin Hannah

Welsh went 24-1 last season en route to a Big Ten title and a national runner-up finish. He'll face a relatively inexperienced foe in his senior season debut, as 8-12 in two seasons at Bloomsburg.

197 pounds: No. 1 Josh Barr vs. Wyatt Bush

After claiming his first national championship last season, Barr will look to start his title defense off strong against Bush, a redshirt freshman who has totaled a 9-5 record in two collegiate seasons.

285 pounds: Connor Mirasola vs. No. 28 Mason Rebuck

It's a new Mirasola in the lineup for Sanderson, as last season's starter, Cole, will not wrestle this season while completing a religious mission trip.

Mirasola, a two-time U23 Pan American Champion, will make his 2026-27 debut against Bloomsburg's lone ranked wrestler in Rebuck. He went 23-8 last season, qualified for the NCAA Championships and placed third in the MAC.

title: Schlow Centre Region Library’s poetry open mic event shows power of the spoken word
author: Noah Spitzen | For the Collegian
description:
The Schlow Centre Region Library hosted its second Poetry Open Mic event of the fall season Wednesday evening, where local poets, singers and comedians got to display their artistry.

From Penn State freshman to State College senior citizens, attendees took turns performing their emotionally-charged pieces.

The event kicked off with a word from the host, Carmin Wong, Penn State’s inaugural poet laureate. She was backed by soft guitar and drumming from performer Rolando Simon.

Wong has spent most of her life surrounded by writing and poetry, earning her masters in fine arts and creative writing before her time at Penn State.

“I have a lengthy background in poetry, performance and writing, having been a part of the youth poetry slam scene in New York City, and then eventually going on to perform elsewhere,” Wong said.

When Wong’s spoken piece ended, Simon began a poem in Spanish, and towards the end, switched to English, telling the audience how he is of nowhere and of no color besides happiness.

Among the evening's performers was Isaac McHenry, 18, of Pittsburgh, with his original piece, titled “Another Piece of S— About Love.”

“I really like you, but what if our polls aren't aligned?” McHenry, a first-year studying mechanical engineering, said. “...So when you ask to kiss me, I think that because I really like you, I have to say yes. But as our lips meet, I feel again that familiar pit form, the one that only comes when I lie.”

McHenry said that he had little to no experience when it came to creative writing prior to a few months ago, after his arrival at Penn State.

“I saw the words ‘Slam Poetry Club’ at the club fair, and I was like, ‘That sounds cool,’ McHenry said. "So I just joined that and then started writing some poetry."

By taking inspiration from his own college experiences, McHenry was able to turn his struggles into poetry.

“I was recently in and out of a situationship with a guy that I met here,” McHenry said. “I won't go into too much detail, but it didn't work out, and it made me sad, so I wrote about that.”

Another performance came from Nyah Cubbison, 22, of Aurora, Colorado, who wrote about fighting for a loved one’s life when they are going through a hard time.

“We can fix it,” Cubbison, a first-year doctoral student, said. “We can fix anything. I will come and I will sort the glass out from your skin. I'll put feeling back into your burned nerves until you can feel again.”

Poetry has always been a part of Cubbison’s life, going back to her early childhood when she attended open mic events in Denver that gave her the inspiration to begin performing herself.

She said her poem was about the pressure that society puts on people struggling with their mental health to stay alive.

“I have a cousin who is my favorite person on the planet … she's had some mental health struggles since forever, and recently she attempted suicide … it’s kind of an ode to her, that we can fix anything but death,” Cubbison said.

Christian Mackey, 20, of Sharon Hill, Pennsylvania, had the audience hooked with his passionate delivery of his poem. On top of poetry, he is also a music producer, under the name Bandit.

“I started writing, like poetry and rapping, when I was like five, maybe, and I just thought it was cool, so I just started doing it, and then I realized that I may be possibly a little good at it, so I kind of took it and ran,” Mackey, a third-year studying psychology and music technology, said. “Started making music in eighth grade…it became a place to vent.”

Mackey said his inspiration stems from various genres, like old school gospel music, as well as artists like Earl Sweatshirt, Paramore, Nirvana and Foo Fighters.

“Why on God's green earth are we not inspired by God's green earth?” Mackey said. “Where the hell is our reflection of heaven? If you imagine streets of gold, then why do we paint our own gray or black with white and yellow boundaries, keeping us from being too innovative and by way of virtue, sinning.”

title: Preview | No. 7 Penn State women's hockey faces Mercyhurst amid win streak
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returns to action this weekend to take on Mercyhurst.

The Nittany Lions are currently on a seven-game winning streak coming off of their bye week. The blue and white will look to extend the streak to nine with another sweep, but this Mercyhurst team is not to be slept on.

The Lakers are currently having a very solid season, with the team being 5-1 in AHA conference play and 9-4-1 overall heading into this weekend's matchup; the team has also beaten a Syracuse squad that Penn State dropped a game to in early October.

The Lakers' main strength is the penalty kill; they have a 98% penalty kill rate, conceding only 1 of 50 attempts, and are one of the nation's best units.

The kill is led by senior defenseman Sofia Ljung and junior defenseman Abby Poitras; the tandem has combined for four goals, five assists and 52 blocked shots.

Djung was also named AHA Defender of the Week on Nov. 2 after a stellar series against Assumption University.

Mercyhurst's attack has produced 37 total goals and 61 assists so far this season on 524 shots. The Lakers average 2.31 goals per game while firing 37.4 shots per game. Three underclassmen lead the Lakers' attack, as the top three points leaders are freshmen.

Mariia Polozkova leads the pack with six goals and eight assists for 14 points on 58 shots.

Forward Duchenne Halle follows with four goals and eight assists for 12 points on 38 shots. To round out the freshman attacking line is Berlin Lolacher, who has totaled five goals and six assists for 11 points.

The goaltending unit has been the backbone of the Lakers’ solid start this season, with their three goalkeepers, Lexington Secreto, Grace Kipfer, and Magdalena Luggin, combining for a .948 save percentage with 327 saves, holding opposing teams to 1.28 goals per game with five shutouts. All three netminders have at least one shutout.

Since Penn State women’s hockey became a Division 1 program in 2012, Mercyhurst has held a slight advantage in the all-time series, leading the matchup 27-26-9 across 62 meetings. Mercyhurst dominated the early years, winning the first eight meetings, sweeping Penn State every season in their first three. Outscoring the Nittany Lions 44-5.

The blue and white earned its first victories in the 2014 season, winning 2-1 and 5-3. Since then, the series has become much more competitive. In postseason play, Penn State leads 3-2. All three victories came in conference championship games. The teams have met in the last four AHA Conference Championship games from 2023-2026

The key for the Nittany Lions will be to get a flurry of shots on Mercyhurst's netminders, to be cautious with the puck and also to break through the Lakers’ strong penalty kill. Players like Sofia Ismael, Grace Outwater and Mikah Keller will have to keep up the offensive production.

It will be interesting to see who gets the first start in net this weekend for the blue and white after a good stretch of performances from Morgan Stickney and Maddy Campbell. Coach Kampersal said the team runs three-on-three games in practice to work the goaltenders for the upcoming games.

title: Penn State moves forward with sale of Penn State York
author: Taylor Gottfredson | For the Collegian
description:
The Finance and Investment Committee of the Penn State Board of Trustees (BOT) voted in support of the decision to sell the Penn State York campus property to York College of Pennsylvania for $7.4 million on Thursday. The proposal is now seeking approval by the full board, which will meet on Friday.

York College, which is located two miles from the Penn State York campus, will collaborate with WellSpan Health to develop health sciences-focused opportunities on the 51-acre campus, according to a release from the college. York College will also work alongside the York County Economic Alliance, who spearheaded the collaboration.

"York College is uniquely equipped to preserve this campus as a central educational hub. We are excited about what this next chapter represents for the students who will benefit from expanded facilities and opportunities, and for the continued growth and vitality of York County as a whole,” Thomas Burns, president of York College of Pennsylvania, said in the release from the college.

Following Penn State's decision in May 2025 to close seven Commonwealth Campuses after the 2026-27 academic year, the BOT had previously approved the sales of Penn State Shenango and Penn State Wilkes-Barre on Sept. 18.

"This community planning process identified continued educational use as a priority," Renata Engel, vice president for Commonwealth Campuses and executive chancellor, said in the press release from Penn State. "This proposal would place the campus with an established local institution while also serving the university's financial interests."

The university ensured that Penn State York campus will still remain open through the spring 2027 semester, with continued support for students and employees. The campus currently has 262 undergraduate students enrolled.

"The York County Economic Alliance brought community voices together to think carefully about the future of this campus, and this proposal reflects the value of that work," Mike Stefan, vice president for Government and Community Relations at Penn State, said in the university's press release. "We're pleased that this proposal supports the community's priorities."

title: Column | Predicting Penn State wrestling’s 2026-27 lineup
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State wrestling is back, and the Nittany Lions are gearing up for their first match of the season in a home opener against Bloomsburg.

The team lost Levi Haines from the starting lineup last season as he graduated, but likely has a new look in many weight classes.

The updated roster dropped Wednesday morning. Here’s a look at which wrestlers could trot out on the mat for Cael Sanderson this season.

125 pounds: Luke Lilledahl (junior)

After a stellar true freshman season, Luke Lilledahl capped his sophomore year with a 25-0 unblemished record, and a national championship title under his belt.

His spot as a starter is one of certainty, as he earned All-American status two years in a row alongside his back-to-back Big Ten Championships since the start of his collegiate career.

133 pounds: Masanosuke Ono (senior)

With Marcus Blaze moving up to 141 pounds, a spot has opened up for a new 133-pound starter. Both Masanosuke Ono and Nate Desmond are contenders, but it is likely that Ono will earn the role.

Ono has had an interesting journey to folkstyle wrestling in the USA after his time in Japan as one of the most established freestyle wrestlers in the world. Ono is both a world and national Japanese gold medalist and has improved, continuously trying to master this new style, according to Sanderson.

141 pounds: Marcus Blaze (sophomore)

Marcus Blaze will move up after a fourth-place finish at 133 pounds, a decision made in the best interest of both Blaze and the program. As a true freshman, Blaze was declared an All-American, going 25-3 on the season and undefeated against conference competition.

He recently made his international debut, earning the 61-kilogram bronze medal at the Senior World Wrestling Championships. He was wrestling at 61 kilograms but is expected to jump to 65 kilograms for the Olympic Games, proving that this move is both for folkstyle and freestyle.

149 pounds: Shayne Van Ness (fifth-year)

Shayne Van Ness has the ability to be one of the standouts in Sanderson’s lineup this year, after his resilience on the mat over the course of his collegiate career.

Van Ness was able to come back from his medical redshirt season and fight his way onto the podium his first year back. He improved once again with a runner-up finish last season.

After failing to give up in the finals to Stanford’s Aden Valencia who notched a takedown in the first period, Van Ness has embodied what it means to have grit. There is no doubt he’ll be ready to come back and finish out his last year on top, and come out a national champion.

157 pounds: Tyler Kasak (senior)

After a redshirt season due to injury last year, Tyler Kasak will be back in his coveted starting spot, while PJ Duke will move up to 165 pounds.

Kasak is the No. 2-seed even after his time off the mat due to his standout sophomore season as a Big Ten champion and third place run at nationals.

Having Kasak back on the mat will be huge for Penn State, after he went 23-2 overall during the 2024-2025 season, and recently finished in sixth at the 2026 U.S. Open. The Doylestown, Pennsylvania native was leading in the semifinals, but had to drop out after a medical forfeit.

165 pounds: PJ Duke (sophomore)

Duke, a highly decorated underclassmen, was a key starter last season, going 24-2 overall. His only recorded losses were against Nebraska’s Antrell Taylor and current national champion Landon Robideau.

Duke has shown he can take on any competitor thrown at him, going on to redeem himself against Taylor in a major decision win to claim the Big Ten title. He moved up in weight class after having a strong first season at 157 pounds, so his biggest challenge this season will be taking on brand new competitors.

174 pounds: Mitchell Mesenbrink (fifth-year)

Mitchell Mesenbrink has had a historic run with the Nittany Lions, posting back-to-back Big Ten and national championship wins, being named the prestigious Dan Hodge trophy winner, and being a three-time All-American.

Even while moving up in weight classes, Mesenbrink is still the No-1-ranked wrestler ahead of the season, and is guaranteed to keep being a top contributor for the Nittany Lions.

184 pounds: Rocco Welsh (senior)

An Ohio State transfer, Rocco Welsh has the potential to be another national champion for the Nittany Lions this year, after claiming the Big Ten championships last year and finishing second overall.

Welsh earned four major decisions and six tech falls during the 2025-26 dual season, showing his offensive and defensive power on the mat and establishing himself as a force to reckon with.

He went 24-1 last season, losing only to Minnesota’s Max McNelly by a singular point in the finals last year, and missing out on a top of the podium finish by a 4-3 score.

197 pounds: Josh Barr (senior)

Barr is no stranger to the starting position, being one of the most recognizable names on Penn State’s roster.

The Davison, Michigan native is both a national and Big Ten champion, earning two-time All-American honors, and is ranked No. 1 ahead of his senior season debut.

Barr went undefeated last season with a perfect 24-0 record, and earned bonus points in all but one match. The points he scored during nationals were a key contribution to the success of the team once again in earning the national title.

285 pounds: Connor Mirasola (junior)

Connor Mirasola will take on the role of starter after it was announced that his twin and former starter Cole Mirasola will not be on the roster this season to serve in a religious mission year.

Connor Mirasola is not currently in the rankings, but has proven to be a strong athlete and is already weighing in higher than his brother, according to Cael Sanderson.

The new heavyweight starter has seen success on the mat, being both a back-to-back U23 and U20 Pan American Champion. He earned gold at the U23 Pan-American Championships at 125 kilograms, showing he can compete well at the heavyweight spot.

title: Preview | Penn State men’s hockey faces Big Ten battle with No. 2 Michigan
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s always fun when a rival is on the schedule when it means walking into the den of the No. 2 team in college hockey behind a notoriously unrelenting crowd. It’s a weekend that's likely been circled on Penn State’s calendar for months.

After the blue and white were swept by Notre Dame in its first conference series back home, the uphill battle continues as it hits the road again to face No. 2 Michigan, scheduled for a 7 p.m. puck drop on both Friday and Saturday at Yost Arena.

“(Yost Arena) is a very tough place to play. There’s a lot of things that you can be distracted by.” Guy Gadowsky said. “(Michigan) is extremely fast. We got to be on our horse…because if you’re playing tired against them, you’re going to be in trouble.”

Penn State

In the Nittany Lions’ Friday night loss, Gadowsky criticized his team’s performance, saying after the game that the team needed to “get on the same page in terms of what we believe this team should be.” Despite the 4-2 loss Saturday, the coaching staff was happier with the improvements the team had made.

“The areas that we really addressed that we have to get down first before moving on, they did an excellent job, and that’s the truth,” Gadowsky said.

Sophomore Jackson Smith continues to be a premier blue liner for Penn State, adding three points against Notre Dame for 10 total on the season, which has him tied with freshman forward Justin Poirier for the highest on the team.

The blue and white also continue to split time between goaltenders Josh Fleming and Ryder Fetterolf.

Fetterolf, a freshman, is 1-3 on the season after dropping Friday’s overtime match, but made a career-high 37 saves in the loss. In his second season with the Nittany Lions, Fleming has posted a .904 save percentage and stopped 25 of 29 shots faced on Saturday.

Michigan

Michigan is one of the blue-bloods of college hockey, and has seen some of the greatest successes of any collegiate program — including nine national championships and an NCAA-record 29 Frozen Four appearances.

This season, the Wolverines look poised yet again for a deep postseason run, starting the season at 8-1-0. A big factor in the early-season success is that Michigan boasts the nation’s top two point leaders, Michael Hage and Jayden Perron.

Hage, a junior forward, leads the nation in production, with 20 points through nine games. The 2024 first-round NHL Draft pick was the only unanimous selection to the Preseason First Team All-Big Ten, and has already added two weekly conference awards this season.

“(Hage) is a great player in many areas, but his speed is what stands out,” Gadowsky said. “You have to be ready as a defensive unit, not just the defenseman.”

Perron, a senior forward, is tied for the nation’s leading scorer with 10 goals, adding 19 assists to rank second behind his teammate in points. He was drafted in the third round of the 2023 NHL Draft and was recently named the Hockey Commissioner’s Association National Player of the Month for October.

The Wolverines also added to their arsenal this season by landing the projected No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NHL Draft in Landon Dupont.

Through eight games, the freshman defenseman has totaled eight assists and has continued to grow the conversation around his ability to be a future elite playmaker and franchise defenseman in the NHL.

title: Penn State wrestling to open season against Bloomsburg
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is set to host Bloomsburg for its first dual meet against the Huskies since 2011. The match takes place at Rec Hall at 7 p.m. on Thursday.

With many wrestlers jumping weight classes this season, the starting lineup will look drastically different in comparison to last season.

Here’s a look at each weight class preview ahead of the Nittany Lions’ first dual of the season.

125 Pounds: No. 1 Luke Lilledahl (PSU) vs. Justin Jones (BLO)

Lilledahl will start his season against last week’s MAC Wrestler of the Week. Lilledahl will look to continue his dominance at 125 after going undefeated last season and winning a national championship.

The matchup could be a competitive warmup to the season for Lilledahl, as Jones isn’t an opponent to overlook. Jones has had an impressive start to the season, going 5-0 and earning the title of tournament champion at the Journeymen Collegiate Classic.

133 Pounds: Masanosuke Ono (PSU) vs. Austin Pollard (BLO)

Ono could make his debut in folkstyle wrestling against Pollard. Ono, internationally a talented freestyle wrestler, has won gold at both the 2024 Senior World Championships and U20 World Championships.

While Ono’s transition hasn’t been smooth sailing, Thursday's match will be an opportunity for Ono to face competition outside of his teammates.

141 Pounds: Nate Desmond (PSU) vs. Scotty Johnson (BLO)

Desmond made an immediate impression during his redshirt freshman season. He finished with an 8-0 record, including a 5-3 win against Lilledahl at 125 pounds.

After going 4-0 at 141 pounds last season, Desmond will look to keep his streak alive against Johnson. The Husky transferred to Bloomsburg from Clarion after compiling a 18-16 record over three years.

A win over Desmond would be the biggest of Johnson’s career.

149 Pounds: No. 4 Shayne Van Ness (PSU) vs. Jay Chase (BLO)

Van Ness, who was named to the Big Ten 2026-27 Preseason Wrestlers to Watch List, will be seen facing Chase. The NCAA national runner-up will look to kick off his revenge tour with a win against an unranked opponent.

Chase, a redshirt freshman, will face by far his toughest opponent in his collegiate career so far. Van Ness could take advantage of Chase’s inexperience, to take a quick victory.

157 Pounds: No. 2 Tyler Kasak (PSU) vs. Eric Alderfer (BLO)

Kasak is returning from his redshirt season to face Alderfer after PJ Duke made his move to 165. During Kasak’s 2024-25 season, he notched a 23-2 record while earning a Big Ten Championship.

Alderfer will look to spoil Kasak’s return, who has his work cut out for him to begin the season, as Alderfer amassed a 21-7 for Bloomsburg last season.

165 Pounds: No. 1 PJ Duke (PSU) vs. Logan Baker (BLO)

Duke, one of Penn State’s several national championship contenders, opens his 2026-27 campaign against Baker. Duke finished third at the NCAA Championships as a freshman.

Duke decided to move up to 165, and his first opponent should be one of the easier matchups of the night. Baker has won twice in 11 career matches.

It’ll take a miracle for Baker to pull out a win Thursday.

174 Pounds: No. 1 Mitchell Mesenbrink (PSU) vs. Mohamed Abdelhady (BLO)

After dominating the 165-pound division for three years, Sanderson confirmed Mesenbrink's move to 174 pounds Tuesday. He’ll begin his path to a third consecutive national championship against Abdelhady.

Mesenbrink didn’t compete in any international freestyle competitions this year, so the match will be his first bout since his 20-4 win in the NCAA final against Iowa’s Mikey Caliendo.

184 Pounds: No. 2 Rocco Welsh (PSU) vs. Braidon Woodward (BLO)

The two-time NCAA national runner-up will look to finally add an individual championship to his resume this season. Welsh, who’s eager to return to competition this week, didn’t compete in any major international tournaments this summer.

The match will be his first since finishing sixth place at the US Open Wrestling Championships, where he won his first 3 contests before losing twice and medically forfeiting.

Woodward, who earned fifth place at the MAC Championships, will certainly have his hands full.

197 Pounds: No. 1 Josh Barr (PSU) vs. Wyatt Bush (BLO)

Barr, the reigning NCAA champion at 197 pounds, rejoins the lineup after an incredible 2025-26 regular season. Similar to Welsh, the Davison, Michigan, native spent a portion of his summer competing in the U.S. Open Wrestling Championships.

Barr competed as the No.1 seed at 92 kilograms, reaching the semifinals before losing in a 4-1 loss to Mike Macchiavello.

Bush performed well at the Journeymen Wrangle Mania, picking up a 4-2 decision over Duke’s Owen McGrory and a commanding 15-0 win over Sacred Heart’s Henry Downing. Bush will need to perform at his best to put up a fight against Barr.

285 Pounds: Connor Mirasola (PSU) vs Kyle Draina (BLO)

Following Sanderson’s announcement that Cole Mirasola will be taking a religious mission year and will be out of the lineup for the 2026-27 season, the starting spot at 285 pounds was handed to twin brother Connor.

Connor held an undefeated 8-0 record during his redshirt campaign while competing at 197. Over the summer, Connor added plenty of weight and won gold at the U23 Pan-American Championship at 125 kilograms, equivalent to 275.5 pounds this summer.

Connor will hope to keep the momentum rolling against Draina.

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State extend its winning streak to three games against Minnesota?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
The Governor’s Victory Bell trophy is on the line this weekend, as Minnesota heads to Happy Valley for the first time since 2022 for a primetime matchup at 7 p.m. Saturday.

Penn State is searching for its third straight win, while the Golden Gophers are looking to rebound after a loss to No. 4 UCLA. Both squads sit at 5-4 on the year.

Who will emerge from this cold-weather clash bowl-eligible?

Andrew Deal: Minnesota 28, Penn State 24

Penn State has its toughest game remaining on the schedule this Saturday against Minnesota, which could very well be the final loss of the season.

The Golden Gophers have played both Indiana and UCLA — top 10 teams in the College Football Playoff rankings — close in the past two weeks, and while they lost, they proved they can compete with the top teams in the conference.

However, they’ve also lost to Purdue in blowout fashion. On the other side, Penn State has looked like a better team in the past two games, despite not playing a complete football game against Washington.

I think those struggles to play a full football game continue. Minnesota now has the worst rushing offense in the Big Ten, dropping below Washington after last week. However, the Huskies ran relatively well against Penn State, something the Golden Gophers could do as well.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell continues his impressive season with another big game, but it’s ultimately not enough for the Nittany Lions to take down Minnesota. The Golden Gophers’ quarterback Drake Lindsey does what he needs to get them the win despite a low-rated passing offense.

Penn State will need to get a win in the last two weeks of the season after falling short against Minnesota to reach bowl eligibility. The Golden Gophers will solidify themselves as a team in the middle of the pack with the victory.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 28, Minnesota 24

Minnesota had a rough past two weeks, having to face Indiana and UCLA back-to-back, but the Golden Gophers held these games far closer than their record would predict, keeping the Hoosiers within a touchdown and dropping 20 points on the Bruins.

That said, Minnesota is a wild card team this season, and Penn State can be one of those teams who show how competitive the middle of the pack is this season in the Big Ten with a four-point win over the Golden Gophers.

Penn State has the top pass defense in the conference compared to Minnesota’s pass offense ranking No. 14. However, the Nittany Lions have the No. 6-ranked pass offense in the Big Ten compared to the Golden Gophers’ No. 8-ranked pass defense, so I’d wager it'll be a close game with Minnesota earning three touchdowns and a field goal.

I have two of Penn State’s touchdowns coming from Sowell and tight end Andrew Rappleyea, while running back Carson Hansen finds the end zone for the sixth straight game.

My bold prediction of the week is Penn State’s final touchdown will be scored on a pick six off Lindsey’s eighth interception of the season, and Audavion Collins will be the one to run it in.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 24, Minnesota 21

Minnesota is a hard team to figure out, but its results in the Big Ten are just slightly better than Penn State’s, as the Golden Gophers defeated Michigan and Iowa while losing to Indiana in overtime and keeping things close with UCLA for a while, even going into halftime tied 10-10.

But Minnesota was blown out by Purdue, a team that Penn State destroyed and has proven to be relatively bad after losing to Maryland last weekend.

What I do know about the Golden Gophers is that they usually play the Nittany Lions close. Penn State won by just one point on the road in 2024, and even lost to them in 2019 when the Nittany Lions were ranked No. 4.

Although Penn State has improved in recent weeks, there are still glaring issues, including the poor play in the second half. However, Minnesota is one of the worst offenses in the Big Ten statistically, ranking last in rushing yards per game and throwing for just 209 yards per game.

With the way the Nittany Lions’ secondary has played this year, the Golden Gophers need to run the ball Saturday to have a chance, but they’ve struggled to do that this year, which is why I’m giving Penn State the edge here.

Hansen will continue to build off his solid performances since the bye week, leading the Nittany Lions to a third straight Big Ten victory and clinching bowl eligibility.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 20, Minnesota 13

While Penn State nearly blew its lead to Washington last week, it showcased a dominant offense that scored four touchdowns in the first half.

The Nittany Lions will likely be without Koby Howard for the seventh straight game after Matt Campbell said his return is “in a pause state.” Meanwhile, Sowell is coming off another good game, with lineman Cooper Cousins saying Tuesday, “Chase Sowell’s a freak athlete.”

I think Sowell’s dominance will continue against a middle-of-the-pack Golden Gophers defense, while wide receiver Brett Eskildsen, tight end Benjamin Brahmer and Rappleyea also contribute.

As the passing game continues to grow, I think Penn State’s run game continues to produce at the level it has since the bye week. Hansen will have his second straight 100-yard game, while Cam Wallace also makes significant plays on the ground.

It will be a lower-scoring affair for Minnesota, which utilizes a pass-first offense. The Golden Gophers record the fewest rushing yards per game in the Big Ten, resulting in Lindsey taking the offense on his back.

I think Penn State’s elite secondary, which ranks third in the nation in passing yards allowed, will limit Lindsey’s production and result in the Nittany Lions’ third straight win to become bowl eligible.

title: Preview | Penn State men’s basketball set for bounce-back opportunities against Mercyhurst, New Haven
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
The first week of Penn State’s 2026-27 season has come and gone, leaving some answers and a whole lot of questions in its wake.

Mike Rhoades’ squad started as strong as ever with a season-opening 97-57 win over Canisius on Nov. 2 and looked strong early in its second game against Chattanooga on Nov. 5 before a second-half collapse nearly saw the Nittany Lions be upset by the Mocs.

Penn State pulled out a four-point win over Chattanooga and headed east for a neutral-site clash with Pitt at the Palestra, but looked less competitive in an 82-76 loss to the Panthers. The Nittany Lions will have a chance to get right against two mid-major opponents traveling to the Bryce Jordan Center this week.

Mercyhurst

Mercyhurst will travel from Erie to State College for a 6:30 p.m. tip off Thursday.

The Lakers hold a 1-2 record on the young season, but have played stiff competition. They opened the campaign with a trip to Milwaukee to play Marquette, where they fell to the Golden Eagles 78-43.

Mercyhurst continued the Midwest road trip with a journey to play Notre Dame in South Bend, Indiana. The Lakers lost 83-56 to a squad led by former Penn State head coach Micah Shrewsberry.

Mercyhurst picked up its first win of the season against a different iteration of the blue and white, hosting Penn State Shenango in Erie on Saturday. Deraje Agbaosi led the way with an 18-point performance to the Lakers’ 89-50 win at the Mercyhurst Athletic Center.

Jake Lemelman stands out as a player to watch for the Lakers, as he’s currently leading the squad with 15.7 points per game. Other potential names to know include Geoff Sprouse and Cameron Johnson, who are averaging 9.3 and 9 points per game, respectively.

An under-the-radar player on Mercyhurst’s bench is Or Faran, a 6-foot-5 guard out of Givatayim, Israel. He’s been quiet for the Lakers this season, but played a significant role for Team Israel at the 2025 FIBA U18 Eurobasket last summer.

It’ll be the first all-time meeting between the Nittany Lions and Lakers after Mercyhurst transitioned to the Division I level in 2024.

New Haven

Penn State will welcome New Haven into Happy Valley for a 4:30 p.m. clash Sunday.

The Chargers are also 1-2 this season. They opened the year with an away trip to Syracuse, falling 74-58 to the Orange in the JMA Wireless Dome. Then, New Haven traveled to Rutgers, where they suffered a more lopsided 81-54 defeat to the Scarlet Knights.

The Chargers hosted Army on Sunday and secured their first win of the year, a 63-55 victory fueled by 18 points from 6-foot-1 guard Danny Young Jr.

6-foot-7 forward Teshaun Steele is New Haven’s top scorer through three games, averaging 13.9 points per game on a 49.6% clip. He flashed in the Chargers’ loss to Rutgers with 15 points, eight rebounds and four blocks.

Zoumana Traore and Young follow close behind Steele, averaging 9.3 and 8.3 points per game, respectively.

Penn State and New Haven faced off for the first time last season in the first game of a home-and-home series. The Nittany Lions hit the road to play in front of 1,087 fans at The Hazell Center in West Haven, Connecticut, ultimately pulling out an 87-43 win behind an 18-point performance by Dominick Stewart.

title: Staff predictions | How many individual national champions will Penn State have?
author: The Daily Collegian wrestling staff
description:
Penn State had four individual national champions at the 2026 National Championships in Cleveland.

Three of those four are returning for another season and have begun the season as the No. 1 wrestler in their respective weight class. With multiple wrestlers changing weight classes, it could open up more opportunities to be favorites for the individual national championships.

While it’s still five months away, it’s never too early to predict how many national champions Penn State will have. Here’s our wrestling staff’s predictions.

Andrew Deal: 5 national champions

Penn State only lost one wrestler to eligibility in Levi Haines, and has a wrestler who could realistically be in the national title conversation in every weight class. Mitchell Mesenbrink, Luke Lilledahl and Josh Barr are all back, and I have all three of them returning to the top of the podium, even with Mesenbrink jumping up to 174 pounds.

I don’t see how either of the three wrestlers lose this season because of how dominant they were last year. Mesenbrink will face a whole new group of competition but I don’t think that really matters.

Outside of those three, I can see several others standing at the top of the podium. For this, I have Tyler Kasak at 157 pounds and PJ Duke at 165 pounds taking home titles, as well.

Duke was very open about how he needs to be more aggressive down the stretch after his loss to Oklahoma State’s Landon Robideau, and I think he shows that at a heavier weight. Kasak returns after initially being the favorite in his weight class last year, and I think he gets over the hump this year to bring gold back to Happy Valley.

Ava Aguiar: 5 national champions

With Mesenbrink earning back-to-back national titles, and Lilledahl and Barr coming off their No. 1 podium finishes, the odds are stacked in their favor to come out on top once again. However, we could see two new champions in Duke and Rocco Welsh this season.

Although Mesenbrink will face new competition in a higher weight class, he’s already shown he has the grit to take on any opponent he’s given, becoming one of the most dominant wrestlers in the sport.

After an early career win at nationals and undefeated season, Lilledahl has proven he has the capability to come out on top. While it was a close 2-1 decision against Princeton’s Marc-Anthony McGowan, Lilledahl went on to secure back-to-back U.S. national and senior open championship titles establishing himself as a dominant force.

The same could be said for Barr, who alongside Mesenbrink has shown to be a consistent and elite starter for the Nittany Lions. Barr’s already defeated the competition he’ll face this season, and enters the year with the confidence to pull off a repeat championship run.

Duke and Welsh are two potential new champions that Penn State could see in the nationals this year. With Duke capping off his freshman year with a 38-6 record and a third place podium finish, there’s no doubt a possibility he could mimic Lilledahl and come out a champion in his second season.

Welsh has already shown he’s capable of a gold medal after defeating reigning champ Max McNelly in the Big Ten tournament before falling just one point short against him in the finals. If Welsh enters the season with the determination to take back the title, I don’t think there’s a way you could count him out.

Elliott Inscho: 4 national champions

Penn State is returning three national champions from last season. I think they’ll all repeat at the 2027 NCAA Championships alongside a name that’ll be atop the podium for the first time.

Mesenbrink’s entering the season with back-to-back national titles and a Hodge Trophy on his resume, and he’s the No. 1 ranked wrestler at 174 pounds after moving up from 165. There’s still some competition around him, but after he posted an undefeated record en route to the title last year, I’m confident he’ll be able to complete the trifecta. I’d be remiss if I wasn’t.

At the lightest weight class, Lilledahl should probably be the national favorite to claim a 125-pound championship in the spring. He earned his first title with a tight win over McGowan last season and I expect him to be a major contender to do it again in 2027.

Barr wasn't far behind Mesenbrink last year, placing third in Hodge Trophy voting while mirroring the 174-pounder’s unblemished record. He’s the top dog at 197 ahead of Oklahoma State’s Cody Merrill and Little Rock’s Stephen Little, but was flat-out dominant last season and should wrestle for the title in a few months’ time.

Duke is the final Nittany Lion ranked atop his weight class, even after moving up to 165 to fill in for a moved-up Mesenbrink. He placed third in the country at 157 last season, and I think he’ll have a solid shot to push into a new class that seems less competitively crowded than his former division.

Gavin Leonard: 4 national champions

Lilledahl, Mesenbrink, and Barr are all well capable of repeating as individual champions this season. While they are near guarantees, Shayne Van Ness and PJ Duke are toss ups.

The Hodge Trophy winner is arguably the safest bet you could make, as Mesenbrink has given us every reason to believe that he should be the favorite. Although his move from 165 to 174 means he will face bigger competition, his previous dominance and current skillset can easily translate to the weight class.

Every wrestler that Lilledahl faced during the tournament will be returning this year. With Lilledahl going undefeated last season, he’s already shown his ability to defeat the talent that is standing in his way of back-to-back titles.

Barr’s career trajectory is the definition of an upward trend. From a 14-0 record as a freshman, to national runner-up, to Big Ten and NCAA champion, Barr has done nothing but continuously improve. Barr has also already beaten some of his main challengers for this year's title: Angelo Posada, Camden McDaniel, and Cody Merril.

Duke and Van Ness are close calls simply because of their performances against their competition, leading me to believe that only one of the two will reach the top of the podium at the end of the season.

Van Ness came up short against Stanford’s Aden Valencia in the NCAA final, giving him his only loss of the season. Not only can Valencia give him troubles, but so could Oklahoma State’s Sergio Vega and Virginia Tech’s Caleb Henson, who have all won individual national championships. Duke avenged his loss to Nebraska’s Antrell Taylor, but lost to Robideau in the NCAA tournament.

title: Column | ‘Pride and Prejudice’ teaches the limit of first impressions
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
How much do first impressions matter?

Everyone has a few minutes or even seconds of their lives they wish they could have back, like redoing a first meeting or having chosen to reserve judgment until finding out more information.

The same dance of miscommunication and social faux pas has been memorialized in literature since at least 1813, when the English novel “Pride and Prejudice” by literary icon Jane Austen was published. The tale follows the Bennet family and their five unmarried daughters searching through the social pools of England for beneficial courtship when the uber-rich Mr. Bingley and his brooding friend Mr. Darcy come to town.

The main character, Elizabeth Bennet, is clever, funny, judgmental and sometimes stubborn. Her wit allows her to transcend her family’s middle class stature in British society. She and her older sister, the lovely Jane, attend a ball with wealthy men, and Mr. Bingley quickly falls for Jane, despite her socioeconomic status falling beneath his.

Simultaneously, Mr. Darcy insults Elizabeth, saying she is “tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt [him]” — the catalyst for Elizabeth’s low opinion of Mr. Darcy as a rude, pompous man.

Most of the time, first impressions are incredibly telling. Our brains make judgments in the milliseconds after seeing a person’s face, and we continue to filter all following information through the data that we get from the initial meeting, also known as the anchoring bias. This evolutionary survival tactic keeps us safe from ill-intentioned people; it’s often our secondary thoughts about a person, whether it be making excuses for behavior or wanting to follow social harmony norms, that may push us into trusting a person that sets off alarm bells in our intuition.

However, there are times when the first impression is so overwhelmingly positive that your heart leaps, but the rules of society, your own anxiety or your upbringing make you push back on the urge to make the connection. Mr. Darcy’s rude comment was because he was using his own prejudices against Elizabeth’s social class and family’s impropriety to suppress his overwhelming attraction to her, which the society around him would condemn.

As Elizabeth Bennet has high standards for love and her pride is bruised, she refuses to give Mr. Darcy another chance to impress her, also passing judgment on Mr. Bingley’s snobbish sisters that Jane resists judging herself. Elizabeth, in a conversation with her close friend Charlotte Lucas, says, “I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.”

Throughout the novel, Elizabeth’s pride informs her opinions and treatment of Mr. Darcy, but both value true love and dedication beneath their stubborn facades, only letting Darcy fall deeper in love. After Elizabeth trudges through three miles of mud to Netherfield, Bingley and Darcy’s residence, to check on a sick Jane, Mr. Darcy recognizes her willingness to put love before propriety, something he does the same for his own sister, and his bias against her begins to soften.

Elizabeth, like many people today, does not let her intolerance for Mr. Darcy lift because of her perception of his stringent dedication to high society’s norms that put judgment of class over one’s character. However, her refusal to let this negative conclusion on his personality waver despite his care for her seeping through the brooding guise throughout the novel is a common mental pitfall, even today.

For Elizabeth and for us in reality, it’s all too common to experience the satirical article headline, “Heartbreaking: The Worst Person You Know Just Made A Great Point.” Being a hater of someone who makes rude comments or doesn’t put the shopping cart away is incredibly easy and almost cathartic, making us feel like we have the moral high ground by showing disdain for bad behavior.

The lesson may take an obnoxious form, but humans remain complex with myriad good and bad traits, leaving us the burden of parsing through our tolerance level before it becomes reprehensible or reflects our own flaws.

This doesn’t mean everyone is secretly good and meant to be trusted; even Jane’s consistent faith in Mr. Bingley’s sisters is broken because of their goal of breaking up the socially taboo couple throughout the novel. It does, however, reflect that people should be given the opportunity to change, like Mr. Darcy in his class prejudice and Elizabeth in her stubborn pride.

Following Mr. Darcy’s distaste for dancing and Elizabeth’s ridicule of such an opinion, he asks her to dance at the following ball, meeting her where she was. After scandal nearly grips the Bennet family with the elopement of Lydia, the youngest Bennet daughter, Mr. Darcy quietly changes the course of the marriage, leaving the family unscathed by reputational ruin in the end.

By realizing the erroneous judgment he made on Elizabeth for purely cosmetic reasons, he sought to change his ways for her, even if she didn’t approve or care. It was for the sake of love that he wanted to do better, which led to Elizabeth’s heart opening up to the possibility of accepting that Mr. Darcy was no longer the pompous, arrogant man she had met at the first ball.

First impressions matter. They’re the blueprint by which we interpret the people around us, but the blueprint doesn’t reflect the true nature of structure when it’s actually built. By letting our pride go and exploring who a person is beyond the facade, real assessment – and potential connection – can finally happen.

title: Column | Barney Ewell is an underappreciated Penn State legend. It’s time we appreciate him
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
A Heisman winner, Olympians across every sport, world record holders, mastermind coaches and trailblazers who pushed the boundary of what was possible both in and out of competition — Penn State has no shortage of athletic brilliance.

When it comes to idols to look up to, there’s no shortage of names, statues or memorials to glance at for inspiration, the university does a great job honoring its past. The blue and white loves to embrace its diverse backgrounds and its pioneers, from LGBTQ+ activist Sue Rankin to the honorable Wally Triplett story that stood in the face of racial tensions.

I honestly feel like the university does a great job of passing along these stories so they maintain imagery inspiring to younger folks, rather than relying on generational accounts that don’t wholly encapsulate them.

A few weeks back, I took a walk to the All Sports Museum for an assignment, hoping not only to get a good grade but to help build some better appreciation for those stories, yet instead I was shocked to find one that is sadly too quiet around University Park.

With a list of nine prefilled questions I had for Poorman’s ‘Career Profile’ assignment, I asked one of my own to the museum director, Lew Lazarow, about a story he wanted to share — he immediately took me over to the exhibit on Barney Ewell.

After a few minutes with Lew’s knowledge, my perspective changed: The university failed to properly remember one of its most honorable figures in history. And somehow, we’ve all forgotten.

Already dealing with the strain of growing up Black in the early 20th century, Ewell battled polio as a youth, became one of Pennsylvania’s greatest high school sprinters of his era and was dubbed the “world’s fastest man” during his time in Happy Valley.

Everyone dubbed the sprinter the next Jesse Owens when he arrived in college. When WWII came around, Ewell had to limit his dominance to the collegiate ranks due to Olympic cancellations.

What did Ewell do? He added another feather in his cap by joining the army in 1942, serving for five years before returning to Penn State to finish his degree in physical education. The 30-year-old was destined to get his Olympic glory.

However, he chose to compete in the 1948 games — a time he was considered to be past his prime. Again, the veteran proved the towering doubt wrong, winning the gold in the 4x100, the silver in the 200m and 100m. In the trials for those very games, Ewell tied the world record for the 100m dash.

All that remains to remember him is a plaza and statue in the city of Lancaster with his namesake, but it’s time to add some of that commemoration to the track here in Happy Valley. Now you know the story thanks to my lame history lesson, and I’m holding onto hope that someone who has the power to immortalize him on campus does now too.

It’s long overdue for Penn State to commemorate and celebrate him during Veterans Month. If we continue to pass over his story, we risk losing the story. Ewell’s journey is too essential to what Penn State is to simply be forgotten. Ewell passed 30 years ago, and with every year, we risk his memory being confined to the history books.

title: No. 10 Penn State women's volleyball sweeps Maryland, wins 8th straight match
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 10 Penn State continued its road stretch on Wednesday night, facing off against Maryland following a 3-2 win against Wisconsin on Sunday. Penn State had history on its side, as the last Maryland win between the two Big Ten squads dated back to 1983.

The blue and white continued its end-of-season surge, sweeping the Terrapins.

Whitney Lauenstein gave Penn State its first two points with a soft kill to the left side, and then a cross-court kill to the right side, both assisted by Alexis Stucky.

Maryland didn’t get on the board until the 5-0 mark, when Brooklynne Brass contributed a kill to center court. Following this play, Maryland went on a 4-1 run to bring the match to a single-point difference; however, a Stucky assist to a Gabrielle Nichols kill kept the separation.

For a while, each team traded two- and three-point leads; however, midway through the match, Penn State went on a three-point run, after a Sydney Bryant attack error, and a kill each by Lauenstein and Nichols. This led Maryland to call a timeout.

Bryant corrected her error and got the first point following the stoppage off of a kill. The two teams split four points in total, getting the set to the media timeout.

After the set stoppage, Penn State and Maryland traded single points for six consecutive points. With this, Bryant added to her pending kill total of four, yet Kennedy Martin topped, thanks to a consistent Stucky set, with five.

After Emmi Sellman’s service ace for Penn State brought the point differential to four, Maryland called its second timeout of the set. After the timeout, Penn State earned five of the following eight points, extending its lead to seven.

While Brass was able to extend Maryland’s play with a kill, Nichols and Martin paired for the 24th and 25th points, each contributing kills as the Nittany Lions took set one.

While Maryland started set two with the first point after an Ava Brown kill, Penn State controlled the majority of the first half of it.

Following Brown’s kill, the blue and white went on a four-point, unanswered run.. Maryland didn't experience its first multi-point run until Bryant and Sara Toth each contributed a kill paired with a ball-handling error by the Nittany Lions.

While this gave Maryland a three-point run and put them within one of an even score, Penn State responded with four points of its own, two of which were attack errors from Bryant.

Bryant, at this point in the match, had totaled seven kills, but the Nittany Lions’ defense seemed to have figured out a way to halt her momentum, and Maryland struggled to come up with alternate points of attack.

Nearing the media-timeout mark, Maryland put forth one more stretch of points, swinging the set away from a domination, and more towards a back-and-forth style of play. Ioabba Dimitriou added a kill, assisted by Toth and Brass, putting the Terrapins within three, yet a Launstein kill ultimately brought the match to the 15-point mark.

The Nittany Lions added to their 15th point, with a Stucky service ace and Launstein kill following the media halt, and forced Maryland into another timeout

This stoppage seemed to serve as a bit of a reset for the Terrapins, as Maryland went on a three-point unanswered run, two of which were Raina Chwialkowski service aces. The blue and white followed up with a momentum spark of their own, started by Martin’s 11th kill.

Four more points on the Nittany Lions' behalf followed, including a block assist and kill from Martin, and a kill from Sellman. Maryland’s Haley Melby added a kill of her own to separate what would be an eight-point run to close out the set.

Still, two Terrapin errors and a Martin kill ended set two in favor of the Nittany Lions.

In an effort to close out the match in three sets, Nichols came out swinging with a kill to center court. Haley Burgdorf replicated, that time, a kill to the right sideline.

The Terrapins evened the score after a Stucky service error and a Lauenstein attack error, yet Martin quickly brought the upper hand back in the blue and white’s favor with a kill.

After a speedy back-and-forth, Penn State proceeded to go on another multi-point run, this time earning six straight points, three of which were attack errors by the Terrapins. Sellman also added two kills and Kendall Northern ordered one of her own.

The two teams traded one- and two-point runs until right after the media timeout, in which Penn State earned five straight points again, two of which were Ava Fadulto service aces.

Following Fadulto’s aces, an Eva Rohrbach kill brought the Terrapins within eight, yet Sellman’s eighth kill shut down any momentum that could’ve formed and brought Penn State within four points of set and match point.

While Bryant’s 12th kill separated the Nittany Lions’ 23rd and 24th points, a one-time powerful swing by Nichols ultimately ended the match in three sets, and Penn State continued its away-game journey with another win under its belt.

Up Next

Penn State remains on the road for one more match, as they travel to Champaign, Illinois, taking on the Fighting Illini at 8 p.m. Saturday. Penn State is now 3-0 on its four-game away streak.

Following Saturday’s match, Penn State will stay at home to compete against Rutgers, and then travel to Fishers, Indiana, for the Big Ten Tournament.

title: WR Koby Howard out against Minnesota after Matt Campbell said his recovery is in 'a pause state'
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State released its first availability report ahead of Saturday night's game against Minnesota.

Koby Howard is listed as out, as Matt Campbell said Tuesday that his return is in a "pause state." He hasn't played since the nonconference slate, and although his return was initially "a post-bye week discussion," there's now no timetable.

The Nittany Lions only have two players who's statuses might change during the week. Offensive lineman Malachi Goodman and kicker Cristiano Rosa are both listed as probable.

This is the second straight week that Goodman is probable after he left Penn State's game against Purdue for a few snaps. He then started against Washington last week, but only played the first half.

"Malachi has been dinged up," Campbell said postgame. "We knew if we could play him early, that would be really positive. We just didn't know how long he could go."

Meanwhile, Rosa last saw the field against Wisconsin on Sept. 26 as kickoff duties have fallen to punter Lucas Tenbrock.

Howard is joined by defensive end Max Granville, linebacker Alex Tatsch, cornerback Tyler Armstead and defensive tackle Alijah Carnell, who are all listed as out. Granville and Tatsch are out for the season.

title: Big Ten roundup | Rutgers wins pair of duals, conference goes 6-2 in opening week
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
The college wrestling season is underway, and while Penn State hasn’t taken to the mat yet, some of its Big Ten rivals have gotten their season started.

The Nittany Lions' conference foes got out to a 6-2 start to the season, with three teams beginning undefeated.

Here’s how the conference has performed in the campaign’s opening week.

Illinois

It was smooth sailing for the Fighting Illini in their season-opening dual against Hofstra. Illinois cruised to a 45-0 win, scoring its most points in a single dual since it defeated Princeton 46-0 in 2012.

After a 4-2 decision from 125-pounder Ethan Perryman, Troy Hohman, Greyson Clark and Michael Gioffre delivered three consecutive technical falls to build a commanding 23-0 lead. 165-pounder Ryan Bennett earned a 4-2 decision before Colin Kelly and Chris Moore secured two more ensuing technical falls.

A 9-1 major decision from Payton Thomas preceded a dual-capping technical fall by Peter Marinopoulos to secure the shutout victory.

Indiana

The Hoosiers were active in the opening week of the 2026-27 campaign, wrestling twice and splitting a set of same-day duals on Nov. 7.

To open the week, Indiana battled to a 24-14 victory over Lock Haven. The Bald Eagles took the dual’s first match when Curtis Nelson scored a 7-3 decision over Gavin Jendreas, but the Hoosiers rattled off six consecutive wins to take an insurmountable 24-3 lead with three matches to go.

Even without a mathematical chance to win, the Bald Eagles swept the trio of remaining matches to cut the final score to 24-14 in favor of Indiana.

Later in the afternoon, it was time for the Hoosiers to take on No. 12 Lehigh, and it was far from the same result against the Mountain Hawks.

Lehigh quickly asserted its dominance with a pair of decisions, a technical fall and a fall to establish an 18-0 edge. Indiana got on the board with a decision by Kai Owen and a technical fall from Tyler Lillard before the Mountain Hawks earned three straight tech falls to close the match in convincing fashion.

Michigan

Michigan tied a program record in a blowout win over VMI, and it was never a close contest.

The Wolverines opened the dual with consecutive pins by 125-pounder Henry Aslikyan and 133-pounder Moses Mendoza. Kellen Wolbert delivered a major decision at 141 pounds before Sergio Lemley and Justin Gates turned in back-to-back technical falls.

Cameron Catrabone pinned his opponent and Josh Knudten scored a major decision to continue the run. Brock Mantanona and Hayden Walters each posted technical falls before heavyweight Niko Sahakian capped the 50-0 victory with a 12-1 major decision.

Rutgers

It was also an active weekend for Rutgers, which improved to 2-0 on the young season with a pair of dual victories. To open Sunday, the Scarlet Knights boatraced LIU to a 51-0 win.

The dual opened with two Rutgers technical falls by Anthony Knox and Brett Ungar, then a pair of major decisions from Tahir Parkins and Brandt Harer. Three consecutive technical falls followed by three consecutive pins made it an easy season opener for the Scarlet Knights.

Things got a bit harder in their second match of the day, though. Knox and Ungar earned a technical fall and decision, respectively, before Navy got on the board with a 4-2 decision by Caedyn Ricciardi.

Harer pinned his opponent before his brother Connor battled to a 2-1 decision. Andrew Barbosa won a 9-4 decision at 165 pounds, but Navy notched its second win of the dual when Danny Wask took a decision of his own.

Shane Cartagena-Walsh’s 14-6 major decision secured the dual for the Scarlet Knights, and the Midshipmen earned some garbage time points with two meet-closing decision wins.

Wisconsin

The Badgers opened their season against the same opponent that Penn State will face in its 2026-27 debut Thursday, earning a 32-7 win over Bloomsburg.

Wisconsin won the dual’s first four matches, all closely contested decisions, before Bloomsburg’s Michael Turi and Morgan Schwarz earned a 2-1 decision and 14-6 major decision, respectively.

A fall, forfeit and pair of major decisions to follow allowed the Badgers to cruise to a season-opening win. They faced harder competition a few days later, ultimately falling to Army in a 25-12 dual.

The Black Knights won the first five matches, including a technical fall and a pair of major decisions, before Cody Goebel got Wisconsin on the board with a 5-4 decision win. Army immediately made up for the slip with a decision win of its own.

Badger wrestlers Clayton Whiting and Clayton Ingham earned bonus points in each of their wins, but it was too little, too late. Brady Colbert won a 7-3 decision to finish the dual and hand Wisconsin its first loss.

title: ‘Something greater than ourselves’ | THON holds annual ‘100 Days ‘Til THON’ event
author: Jacob Godshall I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State held its annual ‘100 Days ‘Til THON’ event at the HUB-Robeson Center on Wednesday from 11 a.m to 3 p.m. The event boasted a packed schedule which included a DJ competition, line dancing, a silent disco and more.

The event marks 100 days until THON’s 48-hour dance marathon and fundraiser from Feb. 19 to 21. In addition to hosting events and competitions throughout the time period, THON committees also set up tables all around the HUB with information, merch and sweet treats.

According to the 100 Days ‘Til THON captain, Hailey Corey, 20, of Harveys Lake, Pennsylvania, much of the preparation for this event, and THON as a whole, occurred over the summer. She said THON is not just a one-weekend event, it is a year round effort.

The day kicked off in Alumni Hall with a DJ competition and silent disco. Inside, many students mingled with THON members while wearing bright headphones and participating in the silent disco. Others gathered around the snack table to grab cookies made by THON’s hospitality team.

Corey, a third-year studying biochemistry and molecular biology, said interim events like this remind people about the fundraising goal.

“As we lead up to THON weekend, it reminds people (to) keep pushing your donor drives. Keep trying to get people to put in just $5 to help the cause,” Corey said. “So it's really important to remind people of our mission and our goal as we go throughout the entire year.”

Corey said she strongly supports THON’s mission, and that working with the THON community has been “impactful and inspiring.” According to Corey, the THON environment on campus is very welcoming and enjoyable.

“It's just really a joyful environment and it really goes to show how Penn State creates that community,” Corey said. “Even though it is a really large school, we still have that community within.”

THON outreach captain, Ellie Werner, 20, of Lower Gwynedd, Pennsylvania, also said that THON brings the Penn State community together.

“I think it really shows that, if we have a goal and a shared mission, we can all come together for something greater than ourselves,” Werner, a second-year studying supply chain and information systems, said. “Just seeing the families at all these different THON events has shown me the true impact that we have, and I think it's so cool that college students can come together and do something.”

THON members weren’t the only ones participating in the event. President of the Whiplash dance team, Samantha Cormier, 21, of Chantilly, Virginia, was in attendance with her group as well. Cormier, a fourth-year studying broadcast journalism, attended with her group to dance alongside THON dancers inside Alumni Hall.

According to Cormier, Whiplash spends “months out of the year” fundraising for THON, and that, since the group is fairly small, each of their impacts feel more significant.

“It's really empowering to see that, with just 25 girls, we can make such a difference just amongst us,” Cormier said. “But it's super important to us because we love raising money for the kids and all of our events and fundraisers. It's just so fun for us.”

Cormier also said 100 Days ‘Til THON gets people excited and ready for THON, since students can just “pop in and out” as they please.

“It's just super fun and it's a great way to come together, especially to see the total of how much was raised during Dream Forward,” Cormier said.

Dream Forward is one of THON’s fundraisers, and it ran from October 25 up until the 100 Days event. According to THON’s website, the fundraising goal this year for Dream Forward was $1.5 million.

Nicole Grigoryev, 21, of Rockville, Maryland, said raising money for the kids and the Four Diamond families is what keeps her coming back to THON.

Four Diamonds is a pediatric cancer organization that supports families financially, and through research. Since 1977, THON has raised more than $254 million in support of Four Diamonds.

“I would say that I keep staying involved because every year we get to hear like Four Diamonds families speak at all the events, and their kids talk about their experiences, and I think that's what really keeps me motivated,” Grigoryev, a fourth-year studying psychology, said. “We all just help keep each other motivated because, at the end of the day, we're all in it for the same cause.”

At the conclusion of the event THON members announced they had surpassed their goal of $1.5 million, and raised a total of $2,353,873.76 through the Dream Forward fundraiser.

title: Annual Greek Sing brings creativity, fundraising together
author: Sophie Fried | For the Collegian
description:
It's time to face the music — on Tuesday, the Penn State Panhellenic Council (PHC) and Interfraternity Council (IFC) held their annual Greek Sing competition in Schwab Auditorium. The musical event featured 16 sorority and fraternity pairings, each with prepared costumes and choreography.

From Alpha Xi Delta and Alpha Epsilon Pi taking to the stage dressed as "Despicable Me" characters to Delta Zeta and Phi Kappa Tau putting on a "High School Musical" inspired number, there was no shortage of creative dances at the event.

The event sold out the auditorium and was livestreamed to those not in attendance. Over 2,000 people sent in votes for their favorite performance.

Maddie Smith, 22, of Center Valley, Pennsylvania, is the vice president of community development for Panhellenic and one of this year's Greek Sing lead organizers.

Smith said Greek Sing isn't only about comedy and entertainment, but it's also an opportunity to create a more fun and engaging way to fundraise.

“I think a lot of the time fundraising, people think you know it’s like a bake sale, things like that,” Smith, a fourth-year studying communication sciences and disorders, said. “But this is a really active way to care about the arts, musical, that sort of thing while also doing it for a good cause.”

Smith said the event has a deeper meaning and embraces what THON stands for.

“Greek Sing is important because it gets everyone excited for THON," Smith said. "We're all about cross-chapter collaboration, cross-council collaboration, so having people come together, hang out, make new connections is what THON is all about.”

Decked out in yellow minions costumes, winners Alpha Xi Delta and Alpha Epsilon Pi took home the $5,000 prize that gets donated to the philanthropy of their choice and an opportunity to perform during THON 2027's Greek Hour. The group’s performance even featured Gru himself and an amusing cameo from Vector.

As for other standouts, Kappa Alpha Theta and Phi Kappa Psi received a $500 donation to the philanthropy of their choice for winning best costume. They dressed to impress, wearing furry jackets, jerseys and chains in a classic ‘90s street style inspired by Macklemore. Alpha Phi and Alpha Tau Omega received the same donation amount for winning best choreography with their Bruno Mars routine, which featured plenty of splits and backflips.

Delta Gamma was awarded a donation of $1,000 to the philanthropy of their choice for raising the most money for the Centre County Donation Drive, while the "Fan Favorite" performance award was given to Pi Beta Phi, Delta Gamma and Alpha Gamma Rho for their witty “Fast and Furious”-themed dance.

Lauren Mellas, 21, of New Canaan, Connecticut, is the executive director for THON 2027 as well as a judge for Greek Sing. Mellas looked beyond the costumes and choreography, taking on a more heartwarming perspective in her judging decisions.

“I think the biggest thing for me as I was watching all the performances was, 'How would a kid feel watching this?'" Mellas, a graduate student studying strategic communications, said. "And I feel like minions was perfect because I just know all the kids are gonna love it THON weekend, and the weekend is all about them.”

Mellas said she appreciates Greek Sing for how it strengthens Greek organizations' role in THON fundraising and creates personal relationships between Greek organizations and THON families.

Coming away from this event, Mellas urges people to remember that Greek Sing, despite being a competition, is all for the kids and ensuring that THON weekend is as magical as possible for them.

While the "Despicable Me" performance was the grand prize winner, there were a few other dances that caught the judges attention.

“I think the ‘Rio’ group was awesome, and I feel like again the kids would love that," Mellas said. "And then the other one that I really enjoyed was the ‘High School Musical’ one. They had a lot of moving pieces like their blow-up basketballs."

Elise DeWan, 21, of Collegeville, Pennsylvania, was another judge who highlighted two other teams that stood out to her.

“I like the ‘Teen Beach Movie’ and the Bruno Mars ones a lot too," DeWan, a fourth-year studying business management, said. "Very good choreography.”

DeWan is a member of the Penn State field hockey team and the Student Athlete Advisory Committee. This is her first Greek Sing, and she was excited to have an opportunity to be on the panel with some of her fellow athletic staff.

“I think it's great because it gets everyone kind of thinking bigger than themselves and brings everyone together.” DeWan said.

title: Penn State OL has ‘all 5 working as 1,’ contributing to recent run game success
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
If there’s one thing about the offensive scheme Matt Campbell’s made abundantly clear, it’s the fact his offensive line consists of five starters who hadn’t played alongside each other until this season.

Malachi Goodman, Trevor Buhr, Brock Riker, Cooper Cousins and Anthony Donkoh have routinely been the starting five for the Nittany Lions all season long, and it took the group until the Purdue and Washington games to establish a firm, sustainable foothold in the run game.

“We’ve got five guys that are playing together on that offensive line for the first time,” Campbell said Wednesday. “That was trying to get the cohesion and unification of that group, and then you had guys playing injured for a while in that group, and we’re trying to make the right decisions on who are we? What gives us the consistency to have a great running game?”

Cousins credited how the offensive line correctly utilized the bye week after Penn State’s loss to Michigan to push even harder for the success of the running backs.

“We've been straining and grinding ever since that bye week came up, and you know we've gotten over that hump and we've worked through it,” Cousins said Tuesday. “Credit to our coaches for putting us in the best positions possible. Five have been working as one, and we've really started to see this offense come into fruition.”

The result was numerous breakout runs from running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace, who’ve each had a 100-yard performance in the past two weeks. The coaching staff put the fate of Saturday in the hands of the offensive line, and they delivered, aiding Hansen’s 36-yard rush deep in Washington territory to help seal the victory.

Cousins said the offensive line’s ability to play complementary to each other was one of the most important factors of the group’s success on Saturday. He also stressed how the team played with “physicality, grit and nastiness,” traits he noted the coaching staff drill into the offensive line as the standard.

“I wouldn't really say it's one person on our offensive line,” Cousins said. “It's all five working as one. It's not just an individual. It's Trevor pulling around, getting critical blocks for our running backs to free up lanes. It's Brock fitting certain combinations and getting good push. It's Donkoh, Malachi and Garrett (Sexton) holding their own on the island.”

Cousins said Sexton, who relieved Goodman in the second half as the starting left tackle had been banged up, particularly played with a “mean streak.” He was proud of how the redshirt sophomore held his own.

The performance wasn’t unforeseen, either, as Cousins knows Sexton as someone with a strong work ethic and dedication to improvement. Sexton is one of the team’s biggest “film junkies,” according to Cousins, and they're typically found in the offensive line room analyzing game film.

“Sexton's in there every morning, and late at night working on his craft,” Cousins said. “He's always working after practice and constantly grinding, and I think that's why when he went out there and it was his turn to go and hold it down on the left side, he held it down to the best of his ability. He did a phenomenal job.”

Sexton has been the next man up behind Goodman all season and has done his job right. After proving himself at practice and at Husky Stadium, Campbell said he wished he “would have talked more about Garrett after the game” because Hansen’s big run in the fourth quarter was due to Sexton’s block.

“He plays with his length and he plays with his abilities, and he's super smart,” Cousins said. “That's what you'll see on the tape with Sexton, like he'll know what the defense is doing before the snap even happens because he's that smart. He works at it, and he drives for it.”
