title: Penn State wrestling commit Grey Burnett named USA Wrestling Athlete of the Week
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State recruit Grey Burnett was just declared USA Wrestling Athlete of the Week after his dominant 57-kilogram win at the Bill Farrell Memorial International last weekend.

The Perrysburg, Ohio, native notched three tech falls in his four-win run at the tournament. Burnett came out on top against tough competition, defeating two-time world team member Irie Jackson of Jamaica 11-0.

He defeated former Iowa wrestler Dean Peterson, 6-2, to advance to the semifinals of the tournament.

The No. 7 seed took down Puerto Rico’s Jacob Moran in a 10-0 tech fall in just 1:26. Moran was a national semifinalist at Indiana in 2026. He concluded his run with a 13-3 tech fall over top-seed Zane Richards, who was a 2023 Senior World Team member at 57 kilograms for the USA.

Burnett will join fellow Perrysburg High School alum Marcus Blaze next year after announcing his commitment to Penn State last fall. He will be a key addition to the lightweight roster alongside Luke Lilledahl.

Burnett already has both national and international experience after clinching his third Division 1 State Championship in the 126-pound class last year, while also earning a spot on the U17 World Team at the U.S. Open to win the bronze medal last summer.

He will join the list of top-tier recruits Sanderson has been able to scout, being ranked No. 3 in the nation by FloWrestling in its latest rankings.

title: ‘A place that really cared’ | WR Chase Sowell, his parents find peace in final season at Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Penn State marched into Seattle and beat Washington, 28-25, last Saturday, wide receiver Chase Sowell was animated.

Sowell skipped off the field, pumping his arm in the air as he approached the Nittany Lion faithful in the stands. He high-fived dozens of fans on his way to the locker room, celebrating another elite performance that resulted in a win.

Sowell’s actions during and after the game showcased his passion for the program, a sentiment he echoed during a media availability Wednesday.

“Everybody around this place I feel like is just so in tune with this place and loves everybody around this place,” Sowell said. “I definitely couldn't imagine a better way to end my college career. So I'm definitely blessed and definitely thankful for sure.”

Before arriving at Penn State, Sowell had bounced around, spending one year at Colorado, two at East Carolina and one at Iowa State. When he first met with Matt Campbell before transferring to the Cyclones, he made his priorities clear, and NIL wasn’t among them.

“I told coach Campbell when I first went to Iowa State that I didn't need the money, I didn't need the NIL,” Sowell said. “I was just like, ‘Hey, I want my family to be able to come to the games, watch me.’ That was something that playing so far away, I never really got to experience.”

Sowell also wanted a car, having previously relied on a scooter for transportation at his former schools. But above all, he wanted “a place that really cared about me as a person,” through both success and adversity.

During his freshman year at Colorado, Sowell learned he wasn’t part of new coach Deion Sanders’ future plans, forcing him to find a new home. His stint at East Carolina was a step in the right direction, but joining Campbell at Iowa State and reuniting with him at Penn State ultimately gave him what he’d been searching for throughout his college career.

“Finding a place like this to match that with (was) just like a cherry on top finding such amazing people throughout history, (the media) and the fans,” Sowell said.

But Sowell isn’t the only one who’s benefited from his move to Happy Valley. His parents have found a sense of peace knowing their son is in a place where he feels valued.

Both of Sowell’s parents were collegiate athletes at Florida, with his mother, Keisha, later pursuing a professional soccer career. They understand the demands of college sports, making their comfort with his current situation all the more meaningful.

“I don't remember the last time I actually seen my mom genuinely happy and at peace,” Sowell said. “Just being mama bear, she's always had that stress over me, and making sure that I'm OK, making sure that I'm fine. But this is the first time I ever felt she's actually fully trusting me at a place, and fully trusted the people that I'm around, and just felt comfortable where I'm at.”

That peace of mind means the world to Sowell, whose parents helped guide him throughout his athletic journey. Now, he also has the opportunity to share his experience with his younger brother Hunter, a redshirt freshman on Penn State’s roster.

Sowell said his biggest goal is to make sure “my family was good.” Part of that has come with his mentorship role over Hunter this year.

“Just making sure that I lead him in the right direction and show him that it is possible, no matter where you come from,” Sowell said. “No matter what spot you're in right now, it doesn't matter. It's all about the ending to the race.”

Although his time at Penn State will last less than a year, Sowell has found something he spent much of his college career looking for — a place he can call home.

“(Penn State) will mean everything for the times and the years to come and go on,” Sowell said. “I always look back at this place as something that saved me and my family. So I'm definitely appreciative.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell talks RB Carson Hansen’s growth
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Matt Campbell met with the media on Wednesday ahead of Penn State’s matchup against Minnesota on Saturday night.

Campbell talked about the growth of running back Carson Hansen, his thoughts on the expanded 24-team College Football Playoff and the inevitable roster retention conversations.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Analyzing Carson Hansen

Running back Carson Hansen has found his footing in the run game over the past two weeks, running for 215 yards and two touchdowns since the bye as the Nittany Lions have added that dynamic to the offense.

“I think Carson is a guy that's proved over the course of his career that he's a really good running back, and I think as that group around him has started to mold, I think we've been able to kind of mold the running game kind of to our tailbacks,” Campbell said.

Hansen’s been a part of a duo that’s emerged as of late, with running back Cam Wallace being the other half. The one-two punch has benefited from the offensive line growing during the season.

The five starting offensive linemen have played in every game together, even with center Brock Riker and left tackle Malachi Goodman banged up. As a result, their chemistry has begun to flourish.

“I think both those guys are starting to settle in and feel confident because the five guys in front of them are really confident and starting to really play good football,” Campbell said.

College Football Playoff expansion

With the official expansion of the College Football Playoff to 24 teams starting next season, it has opened up additional opportunities to get into the playoffs.

It also went down the path of a tournament format, similar to that of March Madness. The feature of more teams gives more programs the national championship hope they otherwise wouldn’t have later in the season.

“I just feel like it always gives you an opportunity to unveil exactly who is the champion,” Campbell said. “I think there's so much more that we have to put together still in college football, with what's a regular season look like? How do we get the right amount of games? Do I feel like this is the right way to find the champion? Yes, a tournament is the right way to find the champion.”

However, it also has eliminated conference championship games, something that’s been a regular in college football for years. Campbell said that was a conversation in the summer during Big Ten meetings, as the college football world still needs to answer questions.

Despite the expansion, Campbell’s philosophy for future years still remains the same for rebuilding Penn State’s program.

“I think the reality is, how do you build a program that gives you the ability to do it not just once, but how do you build a program that's got sustainable success?” Campbell said. “And I think that in college football, as we're finding, can be a challenge, and the unique reality we have is we get to lay a foundation to that this year, and then have the opportunity to build ourselves forward as kind of the rules and regulations around us continue to change.”

Roster retention

The season has entered the final quarter, and questions are beginning to circulate about who will enter the transfer portal and who could stay, no matter what program it is.

It will be Campbell’s first full offseason as Penn State’s head coach, and he’ll have to battle through the transfer portal, both leaving and adding players. However, Campbell’s approach to that remains similar to everything else, keeping a focus on what’s upcoming rather than in the future.

“I think my belief has always been, focus on what's right in front of you,” Campbell said. “And I think the moments of getting your team better, getting players better and then you get to the end of the season, and I think no matter who you are, no matter what your situation is, you get to the end of the regular season, and there is that gap between whenever the regular season ends and whatever postseason football looks like that. I think you can really sit down and have those conversations.”

Campbell mentioned the tricks of having those conversations with 18 to 22 year olds, who are still figuring themselves out. He recognized those conversations will be happening and they have to happen with his players, but it’s not something that should be a true focal point right now, especially given Penn State is battling for bowl eligibility.

“We're going to have those conversations, but those conversations probably need to come at the end of the season,” Campbell said. “And what we need to focus on right now is us, you, we, getting to be the best we can be right now. And if you don't do that, you're going to miss out on an opportunity, no matter what that looks like for yourself, and certainly for us as a football program.”

MORE FOOTBALL CONTENT

title: Former Penn State player, Steelers legend Dick Hoak dies at 86
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Dick Hoak, a legendary Penn State letterman and former Pittsburgh Steelers player and coach, died Wednesday at 86-years-old, the Steelers announced.

A cause of death hasn't been made public.

A Jeanette, Pennsylvania, native, Hoak played running back, safety and quarterback at points of his collegiate career from 1958 to 1961. He was drafted as a running back in the seventh round of the 1961 NFL Draft by the Steelers.

During his 10 NFL seasons with Pittsburgh, he tallied 3,965 rushing yards with 25 touchdowns, retiring in 1970 as the No. 2 running back in franchise history.

He was named to the 1968 Pro Bowl and currently ranks seventh on Pittsburgh's top rushing charts.

Hoak was hired as the Steelers' running backs coach in 1972 and held the position until 2006, with the franchise winning five Super Bowl during that stretch.

Hoak was known for his unwavering loyalty to the Steelers, particularly to the Rooney family, turning down a head coaching offer from the USFL's Pittsburgh Maulers.

He was honored by the Pro Football Hall of Fame with the 2025 Award of Excellence. Hoak was also an inaugural member of the Steelers Hall of Honor, inducted in 2017.

MORE FOOTBALL COVERAGE

title: National Signing Day | Live updating Penn State Athletics' 2027 recruiting class
author: Collegian Sports Staff
description:
Editor's note: This list is being updated throughout the day as recruits sign to Penn State.

Nov. 11 officially served as National Signing Day for many of the blue and white's varsity athletic teams.

Below is the Nittany Lions' live, updated list of signees as they come in.

WRESTLING

As the Nittany Lions soon begin their National Championship defense season with ambitions of going back-to-back, Cael Sanderson unit also welcomes a fresh batch of athletes on the mat.

Here’s how another Sanderson recruiting class is starting to take shape for the blue and white.

Gavin Mangano

By Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian

Mangano committed to Penn State on September 28, 2025.

The Shoreham, New York, native amassed a 622-48 record and two state championships over his three years at Shoreham Wading River High School. Mangano ranks No. 10 in the country, according to FloWrestling.

Mangano will join PJ Duke, Rocco Welsh, Jayden James, and class of 2027 commit Will Soto as Penn State wrestlers who have trained at the KD Training Center.

Grey Burnett

By Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian

Burnett will join fellow Perrysburg High School alum Marcus Blaze next year after announcing his commitment last fall. Burnett will wrestle at the lightweight level next year.

The Ohio native won his third Division 1 State Championship in the 126-pound class last year after a 4-1 decision over No. 8 Tommy Wurster.

He finished out his junior year with a 43-1 record before clinching a spot on the U17 World Team at the U.S. Open to win the bronze medal last summer.

James Whitbred

By Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian

Penn State has signed James Whitbred for the 2027-28 season.

Whitbred competed at 133 pounds in s freshman, then at 152 pounds during his sophomore and junior years at State College High School. He finished those three years with an 89-25 record in those three years.

The junior finished sixth in the state and first in his region.

WOMEN'S VOLLEYBALL

The Nittany Lions season is almost done, and the inaugural Big Ten Tournament begins soon.

With all eyes on the court, Katie Schumacher-Cawley collected the No. 1 PrepDig recruiting class in this cycle. Here’s how that batch shapes up.

Kate Kalczynski

By Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian

Kalczynski, a six-foot outside hitter, announced her commitment to Penn State on April 19 via Instagram.

The Troy, Michigan native, ranked No. 14 overall in the Class of 2027, attended Mercy High School and played for Legacy Volleyball Club. Kalczynski averaged a .418 kill percentage throughout her high school career.

Over four varsity seasons, she accumulated 1,339 kills, averaging 3.9 per set. Kalczynski also hit .313 across her junior and senior seasons.

Kalczynski flipped her commitment to the Nittany Lions after previously committing to Ohio State.

Taylor Harrington

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

A six-foot-three middle blocker from Wakefield High School and Paramount Volleyball Club in North Carolina, Harrington announced her commitment to Penn State on June 16, 2025.

Harrington is the top-ranked player in Virginia and the second-ranked middle blocker in the nation, according to PrepDig. A threat on both ends of the court and a strong blocker and setter, Harrington is one of the most versatile players in her Class.

Harrington served on the girls’ U19 national team and won a gold medal at the 2025 NORCECA Girls U19 Pan American Cup.

Molly Robertson

By Sienna Pierce | For the Collegian

Robertson committed to Penn State on July 26, 2025, from North Allegheny High School in Wexford, Pennsylvania.

The 5-foot-10 setter was the 2024 Pittsburgh Post-Gazette Girls’ Volleyball Player of the Year. As a sophomore, she also won many accolades such as MaxPreps PA Volleyball Player of the Year, PIAA 4A all-state recognition, first-team all-section and first-team All-Big 56.

Despite being a setter, Robertson is also a skilled hitter, earning 391 kills and 250 digs in 2024. She plans to continue her family legacy, as both of her parents are Penn State alumni.

Nejari Crooks

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

Coming from Wesleyan Christian Academy and the Triad Elite Volleyball Club in North Carolina, Crooks committed on June 15, 2025.

The 6-foot right-side hitter combined for 419 kills, 340 assists, and 71 service aces in her senior season. In her career, she has 1,380 total kills and 1,306 assists.

Crooks is ranked the No. 10 recruit in the nation and was the 2026 Gatorade Player of the Year in North Carolina.

Olivia Henry

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

An outside hitter standing 6-foot-5, from IMG Academy, the Bayside, New York, native committed to Penn State on Jun 17, 2025.

Henry is currently the No. 3 prospect and the highest-ranked outside hitter in the nation.

BASEBALL

After Mike Gambino’s worst finish as coach of Penn State last season, its been a busy offseason for the Nittany Lions. Below is the newest batch of players to fill the ranks for Gambino’s team.

Cooper Hillen

By Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian

Hillen, from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, committed to Mike Gambino’s program back on Aug. 2, 2025.

The shortstop earned first-team all-league honors each of the past two seasons. As a sophomore, he slashed .321/.486/.593 and led Lampeter-Strasburg High School to the state semifinals.

Hillen stands at 5-foot-10 and 177 pounds.

Jon Saunders

By Gabriel Kovadlo | For the Collegian

Saunders, a Monroeville, PA, native, announced his commitment to Penn State on Sep. 7, 2025.

The soon-to-be Nittany Lion is a right-handed pitcher and first baseman at Gateway High School, where he has shown off his fast pitching, maxing out at 92 mph on fastballs, 78 mph on changeups and 75 mph on sliders. The 18-year-old also runs a 4.18-second 30-yd dash.

Saunders is listed at 6-foot-3 and 213 pounds.

Ben Sclafani

By Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian

Sclafani, coming from Bethesda, Maryland, announced his Penn State commitment on Sep. 14, 2025.

At Georgetown Prep, left-hander Sclafani was one of the team’s aces, leading them to IAC tournament championships in every season. Sclafani finished his sophomore season with a 4.30 ERA and 56 strikeouts in 48 innings.

Sclafani is 5-foot-9 and 170 pounds.

Freddy Corrado

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

Corrado, coming from Hazleton Area High School, announced his commitment to the Nittany Lions on Aug. 9, 2025.

The 6-foot-5 right-handed pitcher throws a fastball in the 91-94 mph range, along with an upper-70s curveball and upper-80s changeup.

Corrado is ranked as the 468th best in the nation and received Preseason Underclassman All-American honors in 2025 and 2026.

Brady Helms

By Dominic Megats | The Daily Collegian

Helms announced he committed to Penn State back on December 4, 2025

The Hartford, Wisconsin, native comes in at 6-foot-1 and brings a lightning-fast swing. Helms primarily spends his time in the infield at shortstop and third base, but can become versatile in the outfield with time. Helms has been ranked No. 9 in Wisconsin.

The righty is set to join the Nittany Lions in 2028.

Colton Manning

By Dominic Megats | The Daily Collegian

Manning, a West Chester, Pennsylvania, native, isn’t going too far as he committed to Penn State on Nov. 27, 2025.

Manning brings a heavy left-handed swing to the Nittany Lions. Additionally, the 17-year-old is capable of having his presence felt on the mound. Manning has a fastball that tops at 84 mph, a curveball that drops to the 68-72 mph range, a slider that reaches 75 mph and a changeup in the 72-72 mph range.

Manning is set to join the blue and white for the 2027-28 season.

Aiden Drotos

By Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian

Drotos, a soon-to-be Penn Trafford graduate, announced his commitment on May 9, 2026.

The Pennsylvania left-handed pitcher stands 6-foot and is a stout 180 pounds with a 90+ mph fastball that has an average spin rate of 2432 revolutions per minute, which sits above the MLB average.

Drotos was previously a dual-sport athlete before shifting his primary focus to at the end of his sophomore season after battling Crohn’s disease. In his senior season, he will be looking to continue his dominance on the mound for the Warriors, who have won 51 games across the last three seasons.

Drotos is ranked the third-best pitcher in the state and the 31st best prospect in his recruiting class.

Callen Miller

By Darius Harandi | For the Collegian

As a sophomore junior college transfer, Miller, from Somerset, Pennsylvania, committed to Penn State in October 2026.

The 6-foot-5, 240-pound catcher was named to the 2024 Pennsylvania State Coaches Association Class 3A All-State second team during his time at Somerset Area High School.

Briar Persing

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

Out of Montgomery High School, the Pennsylvania native announced his commitment on Aug. 9, 2025.

The right-handed pitcher clocks in at a 91mph fastball and showed a great breaking ball and changeup during his national showcase this year.

Standing at six-foot-one and 205 pounds, Persing received Preseason Underclassman All-American honors in 2025 and 2026, as well as a top 500 national ranking.

Curt Friedrich

By Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian

Hailing from Summit, New Jersey, Friedrich announced his commitment on Aug. 16, 2025.

Friedrich is an ambidextrous two-way player, batting right-handed but pitching left-handed. During his time at Delbarton, he held a batting average of .297 and an ERA of .92, giving up only four runs in a career 30.1 innings pitched.

Freidrich is currently listed at 5-foot-8, 165 pounds.

SOFTBALL

After a season boosted by young talent, coach Clarissa Crowell brings in another decorated recruiting class. Here's what Crowell's 35th-best Class in the nation looks like.

Addison Sabers

By Ashley Felsberg | The Daily Collegian

Sabers is part of the blue and white’s 2027 class and was originally committed in September of last year.

The 6-foot corner infielder is from Overland Park, Kansas and played for St. Thomas Aquinas. Sabers has a recruiting rating of 92 and is ranked the 12th-best player in her position in her recruiting class.

Nationally, Sabers is ranked No. 103 and ranked No. 2 in Kansas. She was also named Gatorade Player of the Year in the 2025-26 season.

Recruiters and coaches noted that Sabers’ patience and wide zone allow her to make consistent contact.

Addison Louderback

By Ashley Felsberg | The Daily Collegian

Louderback is another commit for Penn State’s Class of 2027, committed in October of last year. Louderback is an outfielder and Pennsylvania native; however, she went to high school in New Jersey, playing at Notre Dame High School.

Just last year, Louderback recorded 31 hits in 74 total at-bats, totaling 18 runs and 20 RBIs. The 5-foot-4 center fielder’s most notable 2026 season stats were her .826 slugging percentage and .420 batting average.

Lauderback is an offensive powerhouse, and her power hitting should drive in runs for Penn State.

Ryleigh Dooley

Riley Warner | For the Collegian

The Leesburg, Virginia native committed to Penn State in early Sep. 2025. Dooley is a catcher from Heritage High School and plays for VA Fury Platinum Bacci (club). She is 5-foot-8, with a 1.75-second pop time and an overhand throw velocity of 65mph.

Line Drive Softball ranked her No. 52 nationally in its 2027 Hot 100. In 2026, she was a first-team all-region and first-team all-state player. In 2026, she was also the first-team All-Dulles District Catcher for the 3rd year in a row.

Whitney Davis

By Riley Warner | For the Collegian

The Burton, Ohio native committed to Penn State in September 2025 and intends to major in broadcast journalism with a minor in Spanish. At Berkshire High School, she is an all-around athlete competing in volleyball and softball. For Berkshire softball, she has played various on-field positions: pitcher, catcher, first baseman, and shortstop. At Penn State, Davis will play first base and serve as a utility player.

She plays well on both sides of the ball, as during the 2025 season, Davis set the all-time stolen base record at Berkshire with over 100 stolen bases. At Berkshire, she has set other records too.

Davis currently holds the following records: season hits (60 in 2024), career hits (155), runs scored in a season (51 in both 2024 and 2026), career runs (128), stolen bases in a season (56 in 2026), and career stolen bases (136).

During the 2026 season, Davis made the conference First Team, becoming one of three players in Berkshire history to do so.

Julia Caruso

By Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian

Hailing from Derry, New Hampshire, three-star recruit Julia Caruso announced her commitment to the Nittany Lions in September 2025.

The right-handed pitcher was named New Hampshire Gatorade Player of the Year in New Hampshire for Pinkerton Academy this past Spring after a 10-1, 141-strikeout season. She also batted a .426 average and led the Astros to a 16-2 record.

Caruso also holds the program record for career strikeouts (410) and was a finalist for the PGF Futures All-American Game.

Grace Lombardi

By Daniel Almash | For the Collegian

Lombardi, a middle infielder from Red Bank Catholic High School in New Jersey, has signed to the Nittany Lions 2027 recruiting class. She had been committed since September of last year.

She was ranked nationally No. 31 in Line Drive’s 2027 HOT 100. Her 2025 season was impressive, to say the least; she tallied a batting average of .518, an on-base percentage of .529 and an OPS of 1.252.

Lombardi’s defensive versatility and offensive production helped Red Bank Catholic win its first Shore Conference championship in 15 years.

Madelyn Vogan

By Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian

Three-star pitcher Madelyn Vogan was Clarisa Crowell’s first pledge of the 2027 cycle. The Sharon, Pennsylvania, native committed on Sept. 1, 2025.

At Sharon High School, Vogan was named the 3A state player of the year. The Tigers went 24-1 in 2026 and finished as the state runners-up.

In August, the right-hander joined the Rhode Island Thunder for her final travel season. She is spending the fall playing alongside future Penn State teammates Ryleigh Dooley, Grace Lombardi and Julia Caruso.

WOMEN'S HOCKEY

In most rankings, coach Jeff Kampersal brought in another top-ten recruiting class to Penn State.

Here’s how that group shapes up for the Nittany Lions.

Aubryn Monter

Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian

Forward Aubryn Monter committed to Penn State on June 28, 2025.

The North Ridgeville, Ohio, native played for Lovell Academy’s 16U team. During the 2025-26 season, Monter scored 59 goals and added 47 assists in 66 games.

The Class of 2027 forward was Jeff Kampersal’s first commit of the recruiting cycle.

Kate Pasma

By Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian

Defenseman Kate Pasma committed to Penn State in July, 2025.

The Georgetown, Ontario, native played for the Mississauga Jr. Hurricanes in the OWHL U22 AA league, where she is currently captain for the 2026-2027 season. In three years with the Hurricanes, Pasma has registered 16 goals and 48 assists for 64 total points in 85 games played.

Sydney Stoughton

By Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian

Now signed, forward Stoughton committed to Penn State on April 14, 2026.

The Mason, Ohio Native plays for Lovell Academy 19U in the AAA and has been team captain for the past four years. She is one of only four players in Lovell Academy’s history to surpass 350 career points.

Over the past three seasons, she has scored 85 goals and added 68 assists in 124 games.

In that stretch, she was called to play in the U.S. World Juniors Classic U-18 squad in 2024-25, where she tallied two assists in six games.

MEN'S LACROSSE

Jeff Tambroni enters his 16th season leading Penn State. The Nittany Lions' leader has reached the Final Four in two of the last four seasons. Tambroni brings in a strong 2027 class and looks to continue his long-term success.

Danny Lucovich

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Penn State’s pipeline from Malvern Prep is well-established, and Lucovich is the next in a long line of Friars to don the blue and white.

The four-star recruit is tabbed as the No. 49 overall prospect in the class of 2027. Lucovich is an elusive, slick-shooting attackman who can facilitate well and make clean passes. He’s been committed to Penn State since Sept. 18, 2025.

Kellen Bladon

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Bladon, a 6-foot attackman, plays for Western Reserve Academy in Ohio. He’s a four-star attackman and Inside Lacrosse ranked him the No. 26 overall recruit in the class of 2027.

He plays for Evolve Elite on the club circuit and Inside Lacrosse praised him as an assertive dodger who can get inside and finish on the crease. The outlet also noted that Bladon is strong defensively for an attackman.

The four-star recruit committed to Penn State on Sept. 16, 2025.

Adam Dodia

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

The only defensive player in Jeff Tambroni’s 2027 class, Dodia is a 6-foot long pole out of Salesianum School in Delaware.

A four-star recruit, Inside Lacrosse describes Dodia as “confrontational.” Also a basketball player, he has footwork and athleticism that will translate well to the college game.

Inside Lacrosse didn’t rank Dodia in its 2027 class. He’s been committed to Penn State since Sept. 8, 2025.

Ayden Matthews

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Matthews is the crown jewel of Jeff Tambroni’s 2027 class. The five-star attackman has been ranked as the No. 9 overall player in the nation after standing out at The Lawrenceville School in New Jersey.

Inside Lacrosse praised his high-motor scoring ability and versatility to perform all over the field as skills that could translate to the next level with the Nittany Lions. He initially committed to Penn State on Sept. 22, 2025, and has previously been ranked as high as the No. 5 prospect in the class of 2027.

Nate Randles

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Randles is a smaller-statured attackman standing just 5-foot-7, but that didn’t stop Inside Lacrosse from naming him as the No. 28 prospect in the class of 2027.

Randles’ size has led the four-star recruit to draw comparisons to Rob Pannell. Both wear jersey No. 3 and share a similar compact build, but the most direct link is that Pannell played under Jeff Tambroni at Cornell.

Inside Lacrosse noted that Randles has been able to add strength to his smaller frame, something that will help at the next level. He committed to the Nittany Lions on Sept. 8, 2025.

Wyatt Douglas

By Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Douglas is big. Like, Hunter Aquino big.

Standing 6-foot-5, exactly the same height as the standout junior-to-be attackman, Douglas is an elusive midfielder and can shake free on dodges from the top of the box. He’s also an efficient scorer who can put the ball in the net from a variety of situations.

Douglas is a four-star prospect and the No. 59 overall recruit in the Class of 2027. He’s been committed to Penn State since Sept. 18, 2025.

WOMEN'S LACROSSE

After a successful first season in Happy Valley, coach Kayla Treanor added another decorated class to the program. Here's the young talent signed for the blue and white.

Riley Davis

By Joey Bolger | For the Collegian

Penn State lands the No. 1 overall recruit in the Class of 2027, midfielder Riley Davis.

The five-star from Academy-Notre Dame De Namur headlines a premier recruiting class for the Nittany Lions, who currently hold the number three recruiting class in the nation for the 2027 recruiting cycle.

Davis is known for playing aggressively with powerful shots, frequently catching defenders lacking.

Penn State is known for its aggressive nature and high-pressure tempo offense; Davis fits this system perfectly and will thrive under coach Kayla Treanor.

Mia DiBenedetto

By Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian

Defender DiBenedetto committed to Penn State on Sept. 8, 2025.

Hailing from the William Penn Charter School, DiBenedetto was named to the Inter-Ac league second team in both 2025 and 2026. The Lafayette Hill, Pennsylvania, native is a four-year starter for Penn Charter, the No. 4 team in the country at the close of the 2026 season. She began her varsity career in eighth grade, providing strong support for an elite high school team.

DiBenedetto played on the invitation-only Philadelphia highlight division roster for All-America Lacrosse in 2026. She also participated in Best in Class at the Women’s High School Nationals in both 2025 and 2026.

Lucy Bevilacqua

By Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian

Bevilacqua comes to Happy Valley as a star attacker from Mamaroneck High School, where she was named a US Lacrosse 2026 All-American.

Bevilacqua helped lead her team to a 12-9 record last season while also suiting up for Sound Lacrosse.

Brooke Schultz

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

Schultz, a four-star midfielder from Haddonfield Memorial High School in New Jersey, committed to the Nittany Lions on Sept. 20, 2025.

With 78 goals in her first three seasons and 43 forced turnovers, Schultz is a clear threat on both ends.

Kelsey Young

By Joey Bolger | For the Collegian

The No. 8 overall recruit in the Class of 2027, midfielder Young, has signed to Penn State.

Young is the second five-star in Penn State’s 2027 recruiting class, joining the top recruit in the nation, Riley Davis, in Happy Valley.

Elite speed and athleticism, paired with high intelligence, make Young one of the most intriguing prospects in this class. She creates many opportunities for her teammates to get open shots and works well when defenses collapse on her.

Young will fit perfectly in Penn State’s fast-paced offense and could make an early impact.

Carley Curry

By Lola Brand | For the Collegian

Curry, the midfielder from Notre Dame Prep High School in Maryland and a member of the Skywalkers 2027 Blue Team, announced her verbal commitment to Penn State on September 18th, 2025.

The star midfielder participated in American Select Lacrosse and Nike G8, two nationally recognized lacrosse events that showcase top talent from across the country.

Known for her speed and versatility, Curry is an aggressive offensive player who can attack the goal while also creating scoring opportunities for her teammates, making her a well-rounded midfielder.

Her ability to contribute as both a scorer and a facilitator makes her a promising addition to the Nittany Lions’ midfield.

Avery Acquaviva

By Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian

Acquaviva, an attacker and midfielder, committed to the Nittany Lions on Sept. 9, 2025.

The Sudbury, Massachusetts native earned USA Lacrosse All-American honors in 2026 as well as league honors while playing for Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School.

Acquaviva was selected for the Eastern Massachusetts Girls’ Lacrosse Coaches Association first team in 2026 and also participated in the highlight division under New England for All-America Lacrosse in 2026.

Emerson Acquaviva

By Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian

Versatile midfielder and defender Emerson Acquaviva joined her twin sister in committing to Penn State on Sept. 9, 2025.

Acquaviva has twice earned USA Lacrosse All-American honors while playing for Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School in 2025 and 2026. She earned league honors in the Dual County League in 2025 and 2026.

Acquaviva was named to the EMGLCA first team and the New England highlight division for All-America Lacrosse in 2026 alongside her sister.

Haley Washall

By Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian

Coming from Sacred Heart Greenwich in Connecticut, midfielder Haley Washall committed to the Nittany Lions on Sept. 20, 2025.

The Wappingers Falls, New York, native was an All-American selection and received conference honors from the New England Preparatory School Athletic Council in 2026. She was also invited to play on Connecticut’s highlight division team at All-America Lacrosse.

Washall began her varsity career in seventh grade with Wappingers Central School District, where she remained through her sophomore season. She received all-section honors as a freshman in 2024.

The New York State Sportswriters’ Association selected Washall as second-team all-state as a sophomore in 2025. Washall scored over 200 goals and totaled 300 points over four years at Wappingers, reaching those milestones as a sophomore. As a sophomore, she averaged 9.2 points and 7.2 goals per game.

Washall transitioned to Sacred Heart Greenwich for her junior season, where she helped the squad finish as the No. 7 team in the country.

Dalton Klaus

By Nick Myers | For the Collegian

The four-star attacker from Hunterdon Central Regional High School, as well as a member of Triple Threat Elite, the New Jersey native announced her commitment to Penn State on Sept. 1, 2025.

Klaus led the Red Devils in both scoring and assists as a junior, scoring 64 goals and assisting 45 times in their 16-6 season.

Her elite footwork and speed allow her to create space in transition, with her stellar finishing and accuracy creating a wealth of opportunities on both ends.

WOMEN'S SOCCER

Penn State is waiting to hear its NCAA Tournament draw, but Erica Dambach’s unit has still been busy. The long-time leader brought in the nation's No. 1 recruiting class.

Here’s the next generation signed with Dambach’s unit in her 20th season in Happy Valley.

Taylor Morrell

By Darius Harandi | For the Collegian

On Aug. 7, 2025, Morrell from Leesburg, Virginia, announced her commitment to Penn State. The 5-foot-6 midfielder and forward attends Paul VI Catholic High School in Chantilly, Virginia, and plays club soccer for Virginia Development Academy.

Morrell is the No. 4 recruit in the nation and has experience with the U.S. Under-17 Women’s National Team, where she scored four goals at the 2026 Concacaf Women’s U-17 Qualifiers in Costa Rica. The team also qualified for the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Throughout her junior season at Paul VI, Morrell scored 16 goals and recorded eight assists in 11 games as the Panthers reached the VISAA Division I state championship game. Due to her efforts that season, she was named the 2025-26 Gatorade Virginia Girls Soccer Player of the Year.

Morrell was also named the 2025 United Soccer Coaches Youth Girls National Player of the Year, a 2025-26 ECNL All-American, and the 2025-26 ECNL Mid-Atlantic Conference U17 Player of the Year.

Abbey Spalla

By Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian

Spalla, a South Fayette, Pennsylvania, native, decided to stay in her home state and announced her commitment to Penn State through Instagram and X on August 19, 2025.

Despite not starting her collegiate career yet, the defender from Beadling Soccer Club has already had national-level experience. Spalla was called up to the U-18 roster for the U.S. Youth National Team training camp in April, June and October of this year, bringing next-level talent to Jeffrey Field.

Spalla is not short on accolades, having been named an All-State player by the Pennsylvania Coaches Association and previously earning All-WPIAL honors.

Annie Fowler

By Gabriel Kovadlo | For the Collegian

Fowler, from Northfield, Illinois, is the No. 2 goalkeeper in the nation. She announced her commitment to Penn State on Instagram on Aug. 20, 2025.

Fowler plays for FC United (IL) as the team’s captain and for New Trier High School’s varsity team, where she was selected to the IHSSCA (Illinois High School Soccer Coaches Association) 2025 Girls’ All-State Goalkeeper honors as a sophomore.

She was also a part of a U-15 United States Youth National Team that earned gold in a CONCACAF (Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football) tournament. Additionally, she was invited to the Girls Academy National in 2023 and 2024, and won a national championship with her Girls Academy U-15 team.

Fowler looks to bring her experience to Penn State and contribute to the squad’s success.

Lexie Fragnito

By Gabriel Kovadlo | For the Collegian

Fragnito, a forward from Syracuse, New York, announced her commitment on Oct. 25, 2025.

Fragnito plays for Syracuse Development Academy and Marcellus High School, where she has found great success on and off the field. Fragnito earned the prestigious New York Girls Soccer Gatorade Player of the Year award for the 2025-2026 season.

She scored 44 goals and recorded 17 assists that year, finishing her junior season with 95 total goals and 38 total assists in her high school career. She has been described as a strong, fierce competitor, with the ability to read the game very well.

Fragnito ended her junior season with a state title win, in which she recorded one of the two goals scored in a 2- 0 final. Simultaneously with all the on-field success, she has been able to maintain an A average in the classroom.

Fragnito looks to join the Penn State squad this upcoming season, bringing her skills and success with her.

Anaiah Williams

By Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian

Williams, the nation's No. 2 defender from Glenbard North Area High School in Illinois, announced her commitment to Penn State on Instagram on Aug. 16, 2025.

The defender from Eclipse Select ECNL recently competed in the 2026 FIFA World Cup on the U-17 Women’s National Team after being named to the roster in late September. Williams started in four of five matches, tallying two assists and one shot across all games.

With plenty of ECNL accolades, including being named to the 2025-26 Midwest All-Conference First Team and U15 All-American, Williams brings plenty of top-level talent to the Nittany Lion roster.

Ava Pascarella

By Darius Harandi | For the Collegian

Pascarella, a West Chester, Pennsylvania, native, decided to stay close to home, committing to Penn State in July 2025. She attends Bayard Rustin High School and plays club soccer for Penn Fusion’s ECNL team.

Pascarella was named a Pennsylvania Soccer Coaches Association High School All-State selection.

Ellie Wiseman

By Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor

Wiseman, from Austin, Texas, announced her pledge to Penn State on Aug. 8, 2025.

The right-foot-dominant, 5-foot-4 defender comes from McCallum High School and spent her club time with Sting Austin 09 ECNL.

Ellie Mathews

By Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian

Penn State signed top-50 prospect Ellie Mathews, who will take the field as a midfielder for the Nittany Lions.

Mathews is the No. 46 player in her class and No. 16 midfielder.

The Macomb, Michigan, native has played club soccer at Nationals GA for 11 years, the same club that current Nittany Lions Kealey Titmuss and Layla Tomezak played at. She also has experience with the U.S. team, having been selected to the 2021 and 2022 Olympic Development Program Regional team and the 2022 National Team.

MEN'S SOCCER

After his first season in charge of Penn State, Rob Dow has begun filling his ranks for the future.

After a season in which the Nittany Lions finished 3-9-3 and winless in Big Ten play, here’s how Dow’s newest recruiting class shapes up.

Matheus De Paula

By Henry Bustin | For the Collegian

De Paula committed to YSC Academy in Wayne, Pennsylvania, on April 10, 2026.

The midfielder was recognized for his achievements playing in the Philadelphia Union Club, where he won a Dallas Cup and a GA Cup. He has also made several professional appearances throughout his career.

Standing at 5-foot-7, his awaited performance will be a sight to see as an official Nittany Lion.

Mateo Gallegos

By Ava Aguiar | For the Collegian

Dow secured the No. 1 recruit in Pennsylvania after Gallegos announced his commitment to Penn State via Instagram on Sept. 9.

Gallegos was recently promoted to the professional world as he began playing for the Philadelphia Union II this past season. Even in high school, he has already played internationally after being selected to compete on the Mexico U-16 Youth National Team.

With longtime assistant Colin McMillan soon to take over on the sidelines as head coach, here’s how the first recruiting class shapes up for the first-year boss.

Keaton Crosbie

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

A recent commitment is officially signed.

Timeo Domergue

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

The blue and white added a big hitter to its roster.

Domergue officially committed to Mark Pavlik’s Penn State on March 3 and remained pledged, adding a 6-foot-5 outside hitter to first-year coach Colin McMillan’s class. The Boca Raton, Florida, native played on the United States’ Men's U19 National Team and Tribe Volleyball Club.

Gavyn Harrison

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

The lone middle blocker of the Nittany Lions class officially signed.

Harrison is a 6-foot-6 native of Laguna Niguel, California and played at Santa Margarita Catholic. He also had a long time training stint at Balboa Bay Volleyball Club.

WOMEN'S GYMNASTICS

Jennifer Green has been at the helm in Happy Valley since Aug. 4, yet the new coach has already been busy building her first roster. Below are Green’s first-ever signings.

Kieley Restrepo

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

After committing on Sept. 8, 2025, Restrepo officially signed to the blue and white. The Farmington, New York, native is slated as a 3-star by College Gym News and competes on bars, beam and floor.

She competes at the club level with Infiniti Elite Gymnastics under coach Tammy Marshall, who is a member of the UMass Hall of Fame. Restrepo was also a three-time National Championship Qualifier.

Mary Claire Gillis

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

After pledging to join the Nittany Lions on Oct. 29 and visiting only two weeks before that, Gillis has officially signed with Penn State.

College Gym News tabs the Highland Park, Texas, native as a three-star recruit, as the all-around competes on the uneven bars and floor. She trains with Metroplex Gymnastics, which produced four other DI commits this cycle.

Gillis, who committed to Nebraska in October of last year, also took an official visit to UNC.

Leah Danielson

By Myles Hannak | Sports Editor

Danielson committed to the blue and white in May, pledging to coach Sarah Brown, but officially signed to join coach Green in her first year.

The Littleton, Colorado, native is an all-around gymnast who competes and trains with the Colorado Gymnastics Institute and Arapahoe High School. College Gym News tabs Danielson as a three-star athlete.

Pennsylvania native Aleah Morgante joins the Nittany Lions as a recent pole vault commit, having announced her commitment to Penn State on Nov. 9.

Morgante is the 2026 PIAA state champion in pole vault and is also a five-time state medalist. On the national stage, she was named a 2026 Nike Indoor Nationals All-American as well as a USATF Junior Olympic national champion.

Throws coach Darrell Hill signed another big-name prospect in his just second year at Penn State. Javelin thrower Hunter Pitcavage joins the Nittany Lions as the 2026 Nike Outdoor Nationals javelin champion.

title: Tate McRae’s single 'Housewife' has sparked debate online. Some students say it’s empowering
author: Hadley Louisa-mae Milhomme | For the Collegian
description:
Pop star Tate McRae recently dropped the lead of her forthcoming album, called “Housewife.” It’s a word laden with stereotypes, especially as traditionalism has found its own corner to call home on social media.

McRae, a Grammy-nominated artist, has done global tours and had songs hit the Billboard Hot 100. The lyrics on McRae’s “Housewife” — contrary to the apron-adorned mother that may come to mind when thinking of the word — advocate for personal autonomy and financial independence. Many listeners are debating if the song resonates as “the new dream” for women, an idealization separate from a domestic role, and Penn State students have weighed in too.

As a frequent concertgoer, including to McRae’s tour, Azelle Sumpter, 19, of East Dubuque, Illinois, views the song through a lens of empowerment, as McRae talks about relying on herself rather than relying on a husband. Those who don’t view it this way, she said, are “looking into it a little too much.”

“You know her stance on things, and her other music, she’s very much about women and power,” Sumpter, a first-year studying professional photography, said. "I don’t think we should bring down actual tradwives."

In January, 2026, in McRae’s cover story for People Magazine, McRae spoke of writing about the double standards women face when it comes to physical appearance and stage appearance. On her track “Purple lace bra,” a hit song off her album “So Close To What,” she sang of women getting scrutinized for things men never get questioned on.

In her Miss Possessive World Tour, a portion of merchandise proceeds were donated to the Global Fund for Women, an organization that grants long-term financial resources directly to grassroots gender justice organizations globally.

When addressing the causes she supports in an interview with Variety, McRae said, “I think it’s pretty obvious what kind of person I am and the things I support. And I hope that my fans can see that through the things that I’m putting my energy towards.”

Maya Cienfuegos, 20, of State College, Pennsylvania, feels differently.

“Because it uses the term housewife, more hypersexualized, I feel like being a housewife is sexualized within itself," Cienfuegos, a third-year studying systems neuroscience, said. "So then you have a woman talking about being a housewife, it is going to sound sexual and cater to a specific audience."

She continued, “I think it could turn a little controversial, similar to how tradwife culture has because you can’t dismantle a system while playing into it and using the same words that that system uses.”

Cienfuegos added that using the term in a different way has some potential to open the door for people to redefine it and give it empowerment.

Maddie Powell, 19, of State College, Pennsylvania, said she definitely saw it as empowering.

“She talks about her making the money and then having a man be there with her, not in a negative way necessarily, but more like she has the power in the situation," Powell, a second-year studying biobehavioral health, said. "She doesn't need the man to be happy or successful, that all comes from herself.”

Powell said it's important for artists to put out music like “Housewife,” and for women to give it a listen.

“When female artists have such a big platform, they should be using it to influence the younger generations and put positive messages out there,” Powell said.

title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball continues road stint with two conference matchups
author: Jimmy Blair | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions are one of the hottest teams in the country, snagging two ranked road wins against Minnesota and Wisconsin this past weekend. This puts the blue and white’s conference record up to 11-3, tied for second in the Big Ten standings with Oregon and Wisconsin, two sides they’ve beaten over the past month.

Looking ahead this week, the blue and white continue its run of road games with a matchup against Maryland in Xfinity Center on Wednesday at 7 p.m. ET, followed by a trip to Champaign to take on the Fighting Illini at 8 p.m ET.

In the broader scope of the season, only one home match against Rutgers follows this week and stands between the Nittany Lions and the Big Ten tournament. Penn State has gotten hot at the right time, and hopes to continue its run of form through the end of the regular season and into the conference tournament.

The blue and white will look to continue to play its style and lean on the All-Americans on Katie Schumacher-Cawley’s roster that have been dominating in this stretch, like Kennedy Martin and Alexis Stucky.

Maryland

The Terrapins have had a rollercoaster of a season. They started strong, posting a 10-1 record going into conference play with wins against Arkansas, Seton Hall and Georgetown.

However, the Terrapins’ season has since fallen off the rails, and they can’t get back on track. They’ve posted a 3-11 record in conference play, winning against Iowa, USC and Northwestern.

Many of their conference losses have been sweeps, and they have lost all of their matches against ranked teams.

While this may be a good sign for the blue and white going into this match, it could make the Terrapins unpredictable in what team Penn State gets. The team that started 10-1, or the team that has since gone 3-11.

Maryland will have to lean on the experience their squad has gained this season and take control early. Their home crowd will help, so the blue and white’s objective should be to shut down any chance of Maryland gaining control of the match. This’ll start by controlling the net and establishing a presence at net, neutralizing the Terrapins’ opportunities for kills.

Illinois

The Fighting Illini have been consistently strong all year, posting a 17-8 record and a 9-5 record in the Big Ten. A big week is coming up for the team, and they have an away match with No. 1 Nebraska Thursday before their matchup with Penn State.

Despite losses to Oregon and Wisconsin, the Fighting Illini impressed in ranked matchups this year: They won over Minnesota, Washington, Michigan State and Indiana.

Aside from a loss to the UCLA Bruins, Illinois has been hot as a team as it heads into the end of its conference schedule. This upcoming week is an opportunity for the team to make a statement with two top-ten wins to close out its regular season.

These final games before the conference tournament are so crucial, due to potentially having to rematch a team in the tournament that a school had faced weeks before. Therefore, this upcoming match against Illinois will be a huge matchup for the blue and white as well, and it will want to close out its road stretch with a win against a conference opponent.

title: If you're feeling the mid-semester slump, you can still get back on track
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
Fall and winter breaks are quickly approaching, and while that means holidays and excitement for many students, it can mean semester burnout for the larger student body.

It’s easy to fall out of your routine as the semester amps up and you become busy with midterms and club activities, but it’s also important to “lock in” as the university hurls itself towards the semester’s end. At the same time, the end-of-semester lock in can be difficult when you’re planting yourself within a schedule and simultaneously surviving the endless swirl of commitments you’ve already committed to.

Here are some tips to survive the end of the semester and maintain some semblance of a schedule.

Prioritize

One of the hardest realizations for many students to have is that you can’t do everything. No one can.

While you can have a Rolodex full of friend’s numbers and an endless list of parties and meetings and classes, that arrangement probably won’t leave you feeling fulfilled. The only thing it’s keeping full is your schedule, while your brain is frenzied and overwhelmed.

It’s okay to be busy, and it’s okay to say “yes” to the things you enjoy. But it’s also okay to say “no.” The first step of getting out of a slump is prioritizing the things you actually want to give your time and energy to. That’ll make it easier to both create and keep a schedule.

Keep a calendar

Once you have your list of what you want to participate in and what you find important and nourishing for your soul, write it all down. Create a calendar and a schedule for yourself, especially if you didn’t do so at the beginning of the semester.

There aren’t any rules for this either. It can be on paper, on Google, on Outlook or on whatever platform you’d like. It can be color coded or not.

Knowing when your activities are scheduled for is an easy way to help keep you on track.

Practice self-care

Once you create your schedule and calendar, find time to reserve for just you. Sundays can be reserved as relaxing me-days. The best time might be in the morning for some — waking up early can create more time for yourself.

Use this time you reserve for your self-care activities, whether that’s exercise or face masks or journaling or whatever it is that makes you happy. Taking care of yourself gives you more energy to be there for others and show up for all of your commitments.

Stop doomscrolling

When keeping a schedule and trying to take care of yourself to get back on track, it’s important to actually go to sleep. Not doomscrolling is one easy way to save some time in your evening and fall asleep.

It’s also a way to protect your mental health from the negativity of the internet.

You can hide the TikTok app on your phone’s homescreen, which can help you avoid the endless doomscroll and get to bed on time. I can’t recommend this lifestyle switch enough!

Have something to look forward to

If you're stuck in the mid-semester slumps, having a light at the end of the tunnel can help get you out of it. Giving yourself something to look forward to can help motivate you to keep being productive, even as the semester gets harder and final exams and projects begin popping up.

The motivation, which can be any you’d like, really — a gift, time with family, your favorite sweet treat – gives you an incentive to keep going and keep trying your best as you navigate all of the twists and turns a semester can bring.

Delayed gratification may not work for everyone, though. If you’re skeptical, try short-term goals to keep you going as you navigate the end of 2026.

Have a great end of your semester and, as the kids say, "lock in, twin."

title: It’s No-vember. Here’s what to say ‘no’ to this month
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
The winter months are a great time to remember that "no" is a complete sentence. You don’t have to overextend yourself or push yourself outside of your comfort zone for others this season. This part of the year can be an anxiety-filled time, so it's important to make sure you’re doing okay.

A great way to do that is to implement No-vember rules into your daily life. Here are some ideas of what to put on your list.

No prioritizing going out over school

As much as this can feel like a punishment, putting your schoolwork first at the end of the semester is crucial to ending the year on a strong note. Whether that means waiting for the weekend to go out with your friends and saving the weeknights for studying or simply cutting down a night or two, you will feel the positive impact quickly.

This can start by switching your study spot from Cafe 210 to the Biobehavioral Health Building. Just remember, a more sober and less hungover end of semester does have its benefits. As much fun as going out with your friends can be, getting an A on a test and getting a good job post-grad can be just as fun. (I think?)

There will always be another wine Wednesday, but there won’t always be another chance to pass your accounting exam.

No doing the entire group project

It's called a group project for a reason. You don’t have to be the team leader. Prioritizing friends in your classes is important but so is prioritizing your grades. Don’t be afraid to let your professor know if someone isn’t pulling their weight.

All you're required to do for the group project is your part. The second you start on someone else's slides is the same moment you give up your free time for your classmates, who probably wouldn’t do the same for you.

If you were able to get your slides done, they can do the same. You’re taking this class for your major, not to be an unpaid assistant to the rest of your group.

No letting the weather stop you from going to class

There are only so many 40-degree days you can say are “too cold” to make it to class. As unfortunate as the colder months can be, you did choose to go to school in a valley of ice and snow.

Take this month to go invest in a solid winter jacket and some snow boots. It's time to hunker down for the winter. If you can make it to the frats in a tank top and jeans, you can probably make it to Willard at noon. Your professors aren’t interested in hearing that you’re “too chilly” to make it, and I guarantee you’re not interested in seeing your GPA drop.

Now is the time to persevere in the face of weather adversity and say no to skipping class and no to excuses.

No allowing people to push your boundaries because “everyone is stressed”

Giving others grace is an important part of every friendship. It's necessary to treat those in your life with love and respect and understand that there is a lot going on in the later months. These are your friends, after all.

However, stress is only an excuse for so long. Just because the winter scaries are plaguing campus, it doesn’t give your friends the right to treat you poorly. The CHEM 110 final being right around the corner doesn't qualify as an excuse for your friends to treat you like a punching bag.

It's important this month, and every other month, to make sure you’re taking care of yourself.

No being the “cleaning fairy”

For an apartment or dorm with at least two people, it’s very convenient that somehow your roommate hasn’t had to take the trash out in two months. They’re benefiting from the perks of the “cleaning fairy,” and you've essentially picked up a second job.

It can feel easier to simply do the tasks needed around the apartment, as opposed to letting them sit, but you have to remember this is a shared space and it's their responsibility as much as it is yours. Don’t let the dishes sit in the sink for several business years, but also don’t just do them to avoid the conversation with your roommate.

As a grown-up, they’re sure to understand that the apartment tasks don’t just get magically done, and you can’t let them live in a world of delusion about it.

No picking up someone's shift out of guilt

Just because you don’t have anything going on (besides doom-scrolling for a couple of hours) doesn't mean your job or coworkers are entitled to your time. Taking a rest day is just as important as any big plans you might have that interfere with a shift.

You have to survive the winter months somehow, and R&R is needed to make that happen. Your job is important, but your schedule is your schedule, and this November is the time to stand on that.

title: Series history | Penn State, Minnesota series features success from both squads
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is set to host Minnesota this weekend in a series that dates back decades.

The Nittany Lions and Golden Gophers played their first game 33 years ago and have since played a total of 17 games for the Governor’s Victory Bell trophy.

Here's a look at the full series history between the two teams, which Penn State currently leads 11-6.

Early Penn State domination

The two teams first met in 1993, which was the first of four straight wins for Penn State, winning 38-20.

Quarterback John Sacca found wide receiver Bobby Engram for three first-quarter touchdowns, allowing the Nittany Lions to pull away early.

The following year, it was an even bigger beat down against the Golden Gophers, as Penn State emerged with a 56-3 win. Kerry Collins passed for three touchdowns while Ki-Jana Carter rushed for three more on the ground.

After two years of not playing Minnesota, the Nittany Lions won two more matchups in 1997 and 1998, where they won 16-15 and 27-17, respectively.

Minnesota’s four-game run

Minnesota flipped the switch in 1999 when it upset No. 2-ranked Penn State, 24-23, at Beaver Stadium.

While the Nittany Lions opened with a 7-0 lead, the Golden Gophers scored 17 points in the final 18 minutes of action to earn the upset in Happy Valley.

Minnesota won again in 2000 in a 25-16 contest behind four field goals from Dan Nystrom.

That stretch continued in 2003 and 2004 with 20-14 and 16-7 wins, respectively.

Early 2000s success

Penn State ended its four-game losing streak against Minnesota in 2005 and started another stretch of four straight wins, beginning with a 44-14 domination.

The Nittany Lions upended No. 18 Minnesota with five rushing touchdowns from running backs Tony Hunt, Derrick Williams and Rodney Kinlaw.

In 2006, Penn State escaped with a one-point overtime victory. Hunt scored the game-winner and kicker Kevin Kelly drilled the extra point to come out on top.

Penn State completed the first shut out in series history in 2009, as its defense shut down the Golden Gophers. The Nittany Lions had 464 yards of offense while Minnesota had just 138.

Penn State won its fourth straight game, 33-21, in 2010. Quarterback Rob Bolden threw for 130 yards and a touchdown as running back Silas Redd had 71 yards on the ground.

Recent-year moments

After both teams had their share of winning streaks in the series history, neither has won more than two consecutive games in 16 years.

In 2013, the Golden Gophers had their largest-ever win against Penn State, cruising to a 24-10 victory. Running back Zach Zwinak scored a first-quarter touchdown for the Nittany Lions, and kicker Sam Ficken split the uprights for a field goal in the second quarter.

Meanwhile, Minnesota found the end zone three times in the first half, while also converting a field goal. The defenses dominated the final 30 minutes as neither side added to the scoreboard.

Three years later, Penn State came out on top, as Saquon Barkley took the Nittany Lions’ opening handoff in overtime for a touchdown, winning the game 29-26.

Penn State entered the 2019 matchup undefeated as the No. 4 team in the country. However, Sean Clifford’s struggles earned the Nittany Lions their first loss.

Clifford threw three interceptions, with the first two resulting in touchdowns for No. 17 Minnesota. The Golden Gophers took a 24-13 lead into halftime and held onto Penn State’s attempted comeback behind a three-touchdown performance from quarterback Tanner Morgan.

Back in Beaver Stadium in 2022 for the White Out, Clifford had his way, as he dismantled Minnesota, 45-17. He found tight ends Tyler Warren and Theo Johnson for touchdowns in the second quarter and wide receivers Parker Washington and Mitchell Tinsley for scores in the third quarter. Nick Singleton added on with a rushing touchdown as well.

The Nittany Lions only outperformed Minnesota by 139 yards on offense, but were able to utilize strong field position to put things away.

The last time the two teams met in 2024 resulted in the fourth one-point game in series history.

The Golden Gophers took an early 10-0 lead before Drew Allar found wide receiver Omari Evans for a 45-yard touchdown. After a field goal from the Nittany Lions and another touchdown from Minnesota, Allar found the end zone with a four-yard rush, but couldn't tie it up as Ryan Barker’s extra point was blocked and returned for two points.

Penn State took a one-point lead in the third quarter courtesy of a 12-yard rushing touchdown from Singleton before both teams exchanged field goals. The Nittany Lions ultimately drained the clock with a fake punt and another fourth-down conversion, winning the nailbiter in Minneapolis.

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Will Penn State women’s volleyball’s win streak allow a deep postseason run?
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
Editor’s Note: Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

In the very first edition of Sports Editors Weekly nearly two months ago, we debated if Penn State was back in the title-contender conversation. Shortly after, the Nittany Lions went on a bit of a skid, losing three of their next four matches.

However, October was an exciting month for Katie Schumacher Cawley’s squad. It won eight of its 10 matches in the month, and Penn State is currently riding a seven-game win streak that includes five wins over ranked opponents. This week, the blue and white have found themselves in the top-10 of the AVCA rankings for the first time since September.

We’re revisiting the question: Does Penn State have what it takes to go on a national championship run?

Gianna Dowling: Closer than ever before

In September, I took the stance that Penn State was capable of making a deep postseason run. Despite some bumps in the road for the Nittany Lions, my opinion remains steady.

I believe that Penn State is a much better team now than they were two months ago. The blue and white have gone through the Big Ten gauntlet, defeating top teams like Wisconsin, Purdue, Oregon and Washington. With their strong back half of the season, they’re poised to carry momentum into the postseason, beginning at the inaugural Big Ten Tournament in two weeks.

The team has plenty of national champion-caliber talent on its side, led by back-to-back Big Ten Player of the Week Kennedy Martin. The senior right-side hitter has 20-plus kills in six of Penn State’s last eight games, including a season-high 34 against No. 19 Minnesota.

Alexis Stucky is one of the best setters in the country, and the Nittany Lions’ young core have been playing veteran volleyball. Sophomore Gabrielle Nichols has been dominant at the net, ranking third in the Big Ten with 111 blocks. And freshmen Haley Burgdorf and Kendall Northern are two of the team's top attackers.

The combination of late-season momentum and plenty of star power makes me confident that the possibilities are endless for Schumacher-Cawley’s team. It won’t be easy, but a deep run into December is certainly possible.

Myles Hannak: No

My main gripe earlier this year was the Nittany Lions’ inability to get over the hump against other top contenders. Penn State added some big wins under its belt, but there still isn’t enough to show me it can hang with the best of the best.

I’ll admit the result lingers from its match with Nebraska — a buzzsaw of a program that defeated anyone in front of it — but the Nittany Lions looked like they couldn’t even claim a set, let alone the match.

Penn State can beat some ranked teams, maybe even go on a deep run in the NCAA Tournament or the inaugural Big Ten postseason bracket, but the blue and white don’t have what it takes to defeat any of the national contenders. It’s a good team, not a great team.

Kennedy Martin is good; Ryla Jones returns from injury soon to anchor the defense; and Alexis Stucky is one of the best setters available. All this to say it may not be enough to match the pace of other teams’ rosters, which seem to have more depth of talent than this Penn State squad.

If no hardware returns to Happy Valley, that’s fine. It’ll come soon enough, with the pieces already here and those inbound soon.

title: Questions to ask potential roommates as house-hunting season begins
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s time to start thinking about the next academic year. If you haven’t made a plan for housing next year, you should start: State College’s peak off-campus signing window starts in November.

While finding housing is a big enough task in itself, you must also consider who you'll share your future space with. Here’s some things to consider when choosing your roommates.

Sleep schedules

The most basic question you can ask a potential roommate is: Are you a morning or night person?

You should also find out what both of your habits are during these times, to dig deeper instead of closing off the conversation on a surface-level question. If your roommate stays up longer, will they turn the lights off when you start counting sheep? Will they call their friends late at night?

It’s also important to consider if they’ll be mindful in the morning. If your roommate has a dreaded 8 a.m. class, will they be quiet as you finish your beauty sleep? Or will they be clanging the hangers in their closet, shuffling the items around in their backpack?

Another person’s habits in the morning and night speaks volumes as to whether they’re either a night owl or an early bird. Be sure to choose a roommate who has a similar sleep schedule.

Cleanliness

After discussing sleep schedules, another generic topic to discuss is cleanliness — although actions speak louder than words. Make sure to define the word “clean” when speaking to a potential roommate, as everyone has a different definition.

Specific habits may be more or less important to different people. Start by monitoring how you live and your own everyday behavior. If there's something you do that takes away from your idea of what clean is, make sure you're not getting upset at your roommate for doing the same thing.

For example, if you make your bed every day, you may also want your roommate to do the same thing. Alternatively, if you notice your desk is cluttered, then it should be fine if your roommates’ is as well.

Also, be sure to establish who will do the mundane cleaning tasks: Taking the trash out, doing the dishes, tidying the living room. Roommates typically rotate these tasks, or just do them on an as-needed basis.

The most basic rule of thumb is to take the trash out when you fill it or not let dishes pile up in the sink. (Be careful, though. That seems to be a bit more of a rare find these days).

Guests

Concerns with guests apply to both parties, not just your potential roommate. You may want to ask what kind of guests are allowed, how frequently they can come and how long they can stay.

An easy way to knock out all of these questions is by communicating with one another when you plan to have a guest over. A quick text to ask for permission will most likely result in the other party agreeing.

The topic of significant others is an important one to discuss too, specifically if slumber parties are allowed. If your roommate has a significant other, do you care if they spend the night with you there? Or would you only allow a sleepover if you’re away for the weekend?

Remember, these are also questions for your roommate to consider if you have a significant other. It’s all about reciprocity!

Friendship expectations

Are you looking for the ultimate BFF in a roommate, or would you rather co-exist with each other? Make sure to establish those expectations with one another before living together.

If you’re looking for a built-in best friend, talk about your interests to see if you’re compatible. It may help if you both have a favorite artist or the same hobby, creating a bond from the start.

It’s also worth discussing weekend plans with one another to understand each others' priorities. Some may want to go to football games and tailgate all day, while others prefer staying in and watching the game on the TV. You may want to consider going-out habits too. It can be difficult if one of you wants to stay out for half the night while the other wants to get some beauty sleep.

However, if you just want to co-exist with your roommate, then you may want to ask questions that focus more on how they live in a space, rather than their interests. Habits and hobbies are both equally important to consider when choosing a roommate to ensure the most compatibility with each other.

At the end of the day, if you’re a considerate human being, you should have no problems with your roommate.
