title: 21 Penn State professors are testing Meta’s AI smart glasses. What can they do for education?
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
For months, several Penn State professors have been working to understand the strengths and limitations of Meta’s artificial intelligence (AI) smart glasses.

The glasses are the second generation of Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer smart glasses, according to a Sept. 17 Penn State University Libraries press release. They’re currently being used as part of the 2026-2027 Faculty Engagement Award, which is held annually by the University Libraries’s Teaching and Learning with Technology (TLT) department. Some see potential for them to become a powerful tool for educators, but there remains concerns on how to ensure their use doesn’t breach the privacy of those around the wearer.

TLT seeks to research their potential to “enhance experiential learning, improve accessibility and extend instruction beyond traditional classroom boundaries,” according to a press release announcing applications for faculty to use the glasses. Amy Kuntz, TLT’s faculty engagement and learning design supervisor, said the glasses were delivered in June to 21 Penn State professors across University Park and several Commonwealth campuses.

She said the glasses were paid for primarily with Penn State Education and General Budget (E&G) funds. Penn State recently announced in a press release that it’s addressing a $124 million shortfall in its budget. Steps outlined by the university included reducing the budget for E&G units; the president’s strategic funds; and the Office of the Vice President for Commonwealth campuses.

A single pair of Gen 2 Wayfarer glasses has a base cost of $379, with additional costs depending on if a user requires prescription lenses for them, according to Meta’s website.

“As with previous years’ technology used by Faculty Engagement Award participants, the purchase is an investment in improving instruction to benefit student success through the exploration of innovative uses of technology in teaching and learning,” Kuntz said.

Meta’s smart glasses, which have the ability to take photos and video using a pair of cameras located at either end of the glasses, have been in circulation since 2021. The second generation of these glasses, first released in 2023, integrated voice-activated AI features capable of using the cameras to view and interpret the world.

Use of Meta’s smart glasses, however, has become a source of concern both globally, and they’ve been banned in specific locations, such as courtrooms.

Critics say the glasses recording audio and video violate the privacy of people around the user being recorded — especially when they’ve been tampered with to remove any indicators that the glasses are recording. The indicator, a blinking white light, used to be removable without interfering with the cameras, but the camera is now disabled if the user obstructs the indicator.

Kuntz said the glasses were reviewed and approved “through university approval channels” prior to the purchase. She also said participating faculty received an orientation and training on the glasses for teaching and learning purposes; and there was an expectation to follow “all applicable university policies.”

Despite her concerns about the potential privacy breaches from the glasses, Michelle Kaschak said she applied for the award because she wanted to use the glasses to create video tutorials for her online classes; her tutorial ideas included library searches and navigating the American Psychological Association’s website for citation help.

Kaschak, an associate teaching professor of English at Penn State Lehigh Valley, also wanted to use the glasses to read text files and test if accessibility applications were as capable as Meta had advertised them to be.

She said her experience with the glasses has “solidified” her privacy concerns. She added that she’s discovered limitations when testing the glasses for accessibility: The glasses are only able to record up to two minutes of video, and the AI hallucinates when reading text.

“I wouldn't have known that had I not been able to play with them a little bit,” Kaschak, 50, of Fogelsville, Pennsylvania, said.

While she hasn’t found the glasses ideal for teaching, Kaschak said they still have potential accessibility applications for students with vision or hearing loss, or those who are “more auditory learners.”

“I do think at some point in time they could have a good educational use,” Kaschak said. “They're just not there yet which is partly, I think, why it was good to have this program to see how they could be useful.”

Cecil Shelton, an assistant teaching professor of statistics in the Eberly College of Science, said he’s using his glasses to create “point-of-view” videos for teaching assistants in his STAT 200 classes.

He said he takes steps to make sure no one is around him when he’s using the glasses, like reserving spaces on campus. Penn State administrative policies, including AD40, provide guidance on how Meta’s and other smart glasses can be used by both students and faculty to record in classes.

Shelton, 39, of Kentucky, said he understands why there are privacy concerns about the recording capabilities of Meta’s smart glasses. But these concerns, he added, are also present in cell phone proliferation, the cameras of which can record unknowing people without displaying any recording indicators.

“Anytime you're embracing a new technology, there's always concerns related to that technology,” Shelton said.

Tiffany Petricini, an associate teaching professor of communication at Penn State Behrend, said she wanted the glasses to assist in making minor changes to course material while teaching; and to expand her research into effective, responsible use of AI in education.

Petricini, 40, of Pittsburgh, said the functionality of the Gen 2 Wayfarer glasses have not lent themselves to being an effective tool to use in her teaching. However, she’s been able to converse with students about the ethics of using the glasses and potential privacy breaches among similar AI technology, she said.

She said Penn State should offer the glasses for students to use, similar to how the university offers other technological resources. She also said Penn State can include prerequisites to renting out the glasses, like its AI Essentials course, and a code of conduct to ensure they’re used with “respect.”

“It's not fair for me ever to say what's right and what's wrong in class, because there is understanding the ways in which these technologies are being used in the world, which cause harm and which also bring benefits. And then talking about how, as a society, we navigate those costs and those benefits,” Petricini said. “Now that I see them, now that I've worked with them, now that I see their limitations — a cell phone can violate someone's privacy so much more and so the AI glasses, maybe, are finally bringing to the table some of the concerns that have been off of our radar for so long that existed pre-AI wearables.”

title: Transfer portal roundup | How former Lady Lions perform in new homes
author: Nick Myers | For the Collegian
description:
A fresh era of Lady Lions basketball is beginning under a new coach, Tanisha Wright, and an almost entirely new group.

Here’s a recap of how some former Lady Lions have been performing in their new schools and roles.

Kiyomi McMiller

Joining the Lady Lions as a sophomore, after her freshman season at Rutgers, guard Kiyomi McMiller was the clear standout on both ends of the court during the 2025-26 season.

In her single year with Penn State, McMiller led the team in scoring with 21.6 points per game, as well as in assists with 4.5 and steals with 1.8. McMiller improved in every major statistic from her freshman year, despite the team finishing only 11-18.

During the offseason, McMiller chose to leave Penn State and join her third organization as a junior. McMiller, coming off an 18-15 season, landed with the Florida Gators.

Through her first three games as a Gator, McMiller has been outstanding. Now averaging 29.7 points a game, she is the second-highest scorer in the nation. She is also averaging career highs in both rebounds and steals, as she emerges as the team’s focal point.

In just her second game in Florida, McMiller already etched her name in the history books. She scored 42 points against UCF, breaking the record for most points in a home game. She also holds the fourth-largest scoring performance in program history.

Gracie Merkle

As a redshirt sophomore, Merkle began her Penn State tenure in the 2024-25 season. She’s known for her stellar defensive ability and paint scoring and quickly emerged as one of the Lady Lions' key players.

Merkle led the team in scoring during her sophomore season with 15.5 points per game, before improving to a career-high 19.2 in her junior year. She also led the team in both rebounds and steals for her entire career as a Lady Lion, averaging a combined 8.4 rebounds and 1.3 steals per game.

Merkle was coming off a strong 24-9 season and a Sweet 16 appearance in the NCAA Tournament when she chose to transfer to Minnesota for her final eligible season. Now the tallest player on the roster, Merkle is likely hoping to make an impact on both ends of the court for the Golden Gophers.

Throughout her first two games, it’s clear Merkle may not have the same role as in previous years, now that she is on a contending team. She is currently averaging around 15 minutes a game, the lowest in her career by far, as well as career lows in both scoring and rebounds, with 14 points per game and just 3.5 rebounds a game.

Minnesota is currently ranked No. 18 in the country, as it remains undefeated across its first two games.

Maggie Mendelson

Starting her collegiate career in Nebraska, Maggie Mendelson joined Penn State as a dual-sport athlete, also serving as a member of the 2024 NCAA Championship-winning volleyball team in her junior year.

During her junior and senior years, her role on the team wasn’t as prominent. She only touched the floor in 15 of the team’s 29 games, averaging just two points and three rebounds.

This season, however, as a member of the Pepperdine Waves, she has exploded in almost every way statistically. She leads the Waves in four of five major stat lines, with 12.5 points and three blocks. Most notably, however, she is averaging 15.5 rebounds per game, tying her for the top figure in the nation.

The Waves are now 1-1 this season and in first place in the WCC. Mendelson is one of the key pieces of their team, on both sides of the court.

Talayah Walker

Junior guard Talayah Walker is one of the most prominent scorers in the NCAA.

As a freshman at Penn State, Walker had a somewhat silent season. She only started in two of the team's 29 games, averaging 5.6 points and 3.3 rebounds per game.

After a 2024-25 season filled with struggle, the Lady Lions finished 10-19, going 1-17 in the conference. Walker decided to transfer during the offseason and joined the Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets. She’s now in her second year with the team.

Walker had immediate improvement as a sophomore, now leading the team and averaging 17.5 points per game and 6.1 rebounds. And she’s also had even more improvement from last year: Across three games, Walker averages 25.7 points, placing her as a top 10 scorer in the nation; and spearheaded by her 40-point, season-opening performance against the Hofstra Pride, she set an ACC record for the most points scored in a season opener.

The Yellow Jackets are 2-1 to start the season in a historically competitive ACC, largely due to Walker’s contributions on offense.

title: Penn State notebook | Cael Sanderson talks numerous roster updates ahead of first dual
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Cael Sanderson met with the media ahead of Penn State’s season opening match against Bloomsburg at Rec Hall on Thursday.

Sanderson addressed lineup changes, Haines’ future with Penn State and Masanosuke Ono’s adjustment to folkstyle wrestling.

Here’s what Sanderson had to say on Tuesday.

Roster Updates

While the roster has yet to be officially released, Sanderson clarified many questions surrounding the lineup. In Sanderson’s opening statement, he confirmed that Marcus Blaze will be making the move up to 141.

“It felt like it was a good move for him personally, and obviously was a strong move for our team as well,” Sanderson said.

Sanderson made clear that the jump was a good fit in multiple ways. He added an outlook on the freestyle impact of his jump, especially given that the Olympic Games are a little under two years away.

“In the long term move, as a guy that's planning on wrestling 65 kilograms with this upcoming Olympic year,” Sanderson said. “The move-up makes a lot of sense for him.”

Sanderson also confirmed the speculation that Mitchell Mesenbrink and PJ Duke will move up a weight class, especially given the absence of Haines now with the latest court ruling.

Additionally, he announced that both William Henckel and Cole Mirasola are taking religious mission years and will not be on the roster this season. Sanderson did not add many details, noting that “it’s a year they can grow and go share their faith.”

Cole Mirasola’s absence will leave Connor Mirasola as the projected starter at 285 pounds. Sanderson credited Connor’s transition to heavyweight as he’s ready for the upcoming season.

“There’s a difference between trying and doing, he’s just doing,” Sanderson said. “I’m actually really excited, probably like everyone else, to see him compete at heavyweight.”

Levi Haines’ next steps

After the appeals court ruled in favor of the NCAA, reversing the lower court's grant of an extra year of eligibility for Haines on Nov. 6, Sanderson opened up about the logistics of the whole situation.

“I don’t really understand the whole process,” Sanderson said. “I don't get how some kids in some states and some teams in some sports are getting that year and some aren’t. Obviously that’s something you would hope the NCAA would have the ability to enforce, right?”

The next step for Haines may be pursuing an individual case, which Sanderson found disappointing, saying it’s “just a sad thing that every individual around the country has to pursue.”

He noted that they are still deciding what they will do from there, as he heard the news at the same time as the public. However, if Haines becomes eligible again, Sanderson recognized that it actually “makes things more complicated,” given the plans to jump in weight by Duke and Mesenbrink.

Masanosuke Ono’s transitional challenges

Blaze’s move to 141 pounds opens the spot at 133 pounds for Nate Desmond and Masanosuke Ono. Sanderson has yet to decide who he’ll give the nod to, stating that “we’re getting close, so we’re going to have to make those decisions.”

While Ono is competing for a spot in the starting lineup, he’s also navigating the difficult transition of freestyle to folkstyle wrestling.

Yet, Sanderson praised Ono’s talent and attitude, highlighting that "he's a very humble guy and very coachable, just very grateful.” He also recognized that he doesn’t “see him get taken down too much,” since he’s been training in folkstyle in the wrestling room.

Sanderson mentioned some of the challenges he’s had away from the mat as well, including the language barrier and academics; however, his work ethic has allowed him to transition more easily with those.

“Part of the work for him has been going to class and doing well…he’s gotten A’s and he’s worked really hard,” Sanderson said. “I think the biggest challenge for him to start was the language barrier and being able to pass his classes.”

title: ‘Ibn’s story is great’ | Penn State CB Ibn McDaniels’ interception a culmination of considerable growth
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s second half collapse was only three points away from total disaster, and an unlikely hero saved the game with a crucial interception in the fourth quarter.

Cornerback Ibn McDaniels, a redshirt sophomore transfer from Syracuse whose seen increased playing time in recent weeks, was a half-step behind his matched wide receiver in man coverage.

But when quarterback Demond Williams Jr. threw the ball to his target’s back shoulder, McDaniels leapt in the air and caught the ball to bring Penn State’s offense back on the field. It came as a surprise to fans, as McDaniels has only tallied three tackles and a pass breakup on the season.

“To be honest with you, I think the guy that's been the surprise of our whole team on defense has been Ibn,” Matt Campbell said Tuesday. “That guy has played as good as anybody the last two weeks, and the play he made in a critical moment in the football game on Saturday is unbelievable and it's awesome.”

Rocco Becht said McDaniels has made a huge impact on the practice field in the bye week, and he was ready for his opportunity to translate it to a game. Becht praised McDaniels’ length and speed in pass defense, particularly because it challenges the quarterback's ability to air out the deep ball.

“He was able to go out and make great plays for the defense (in the bye week), and it showed,” Becht said. “The coaches saw it, and they decided to put him in the game, and he's been able to go out there and make great plays. For him, just his ability to have so much length and speed at that position is huge.”

Over the course of two seasons with the Orange, McDaniels played in 15 games and logged only four tackles, a tackle for loss and a pass breakup before hitting the transfer portal. Since arriving in Happy Valley, his playing time has slowly increased over the course of the season.

Campbell added due to the team’s troubles with injury this season, he’s going to continue relying on McDaniels’ ability to make an impact off the bench.

“Ibn’s story is great,” Campbell said. “Especially as injuries mount up, you're going to need some of those guys to step into bigger roles and the confidence that they build when they have some success. I think those are big wins for everybody.”

And it wasn’t just McDaniels who impressed the coaching staff off the bench, as Campbell said cornerback Jahmir Joseph, offensive linemen Garrett Sexton, defensive tackle Ty Blanding and running back Cam Wallace have all come off the bench in critical moments in recent weeks, contributing to the back-to-back wins.

Defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn stressed the importance of having strong depth at the cornerback position, especially in conference play.

He said the team “needs to have multiple guys at that position,” and McDaniels and Joseph were the two standout depth cornerbacks who are trusted to hold down the fort when Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson need rest.

“We just trust them in games,” Lynn said. “Now they have to keep on doing it every single day, but I think that they've been doing an outstanding job, and it helps keep those other guys fresh.”

title: ‘It’s a real problem’ | Penn State looks to address 2nd half mishaps to prevent future collapses
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
When running back Cam Wallace broke free for a 46-yard rushing touchdown in the second quarter, it looked as if Penn State was going to run away with its game against Washington, holding a 28-6 lead.

Add onto the fact it got the ball back before the half and was getting the ball to start the second half with the score still the same, and the Nittany Lions could’ve put the game away without having to worry about the second half.

Instead, Penn State was subject to a near collapse in the second half, allowing the Huskies to get back into the game.

“It's a real problem,” Matt Campbell said Tuesday. “I'll be honest with you, and my concern is, I think there's times where it's a mental maturity piece of it, in my opinion, that you're up in some of those games and kind of like it's a mental relapse.”

Penn State got the ball back with 1:49 left on the clock in the second quarter and a chance to add onto a four-touchdown first half. Instead, Campbell opted to be more cautious, with the big lead and the fact the Nittany Lions were getting the second half kickoff.

The caution came from multiple factors according to Campbell. First, Washington had three timeouts and could’ve used them to try to get the ball back itself. Also, the offense went backwards with a sack of Rocco Becht, making the decision even easier to let the time run out and take the 28-6 lead into the half.

“If you don't take the negative play there, then I probably don't put ourselves in that situation,” Campbell said. “But with the negative play, I just felt like it was risky with the lead that we had and us getting the ball back.”

While the Nittany Lions had momentum, the drive after the half started to flip the game the other way, as they went three-and-out with a total of two yards gained on a rush by running back Carson Hansen on third-and-10.

That started the comeback for Washington, which eventually spiraled into a three-point game with just under eight minutes left on the clock.

“We just got to be able to play the play, not overthink things, come out with a sense of urgency like we do in the first quarter, and just be able to lock in and stay calm and stay poised,” Becht said. “ Not just everyone, just including myself as well, we just got to go out there and play the play, and not make it overly complicated for ourselves. And it's easy fixes. We just got to be better detailed.”

It wasn’t just the offense that began to unravel in the third quarter, and into the fourth, as the defense also started giving up bigger plays and allowing the Huskies’ offense to start to roll.

D’Anton Lynn referenced that “leverage and missed tackles” allowed Washington back into the game, letting the Huskies gain a rhythm on offense that they couldn’t find in the first half.

“You look at the second half, there's five plays, whether it's run game or pass game, we lose leverage, and guys don't make each other right, and we give up big plays,” Lynn said. It’s frustrating, but we have to not get bored doing the same thing over and over again.”

Penn State has been outscored 42-9 in the third quarter during the Big Ten slate so far. It’s something that Campbell, the coaching staff and the players know needs to be fixed.

It didn’t ultimately come back to bite Penn State on Saturday, as it still came out with a victory. If the Nittany Lions clean it up in the third quarter, that may not be the case in the final weeks of the season as they battle for bowl eligibility.

“92% of those games, you go back and you study it, and we had this study because we lived in this world for my entire career in the last 10 years, that if you win the third quarter, you're going to win the game in a one-score game, and that is probably my biggest frustration,” Campbell said.

title: Penn State wrestling's Cole Mirasola, William Henckel taking year off for mission trip
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State will be without two of its top young wrestlers for the 2026-27 season.

Cole Mirasola and William Henckel will take a religious mission trip and pause their eligibility clock for the upcoming season, Cael Sanderson confirmed Tuesday.

"We have two wrestlers this year that are going to take religious mission years," Sanderson said. "Will Henckel and Cole Mirasola both just strong men of faith, and felt like it'd be a good opportunity for them to go out there and, their personal decisions, obviously, go out there and share that with the world this year. Mirasola was Penn State's starter at heavyweight last season, going 19-8 and failing to make the podium at the National Championships. His twin brother, Connor Mirasola, will be the heavyweight for this upcoming year.

Henckel was the Nittany Lions' backup at 174 pounds. He was expected to be the backup again this year in his redshirt freshman year, behind Mitchell Mesenbrink, who's planning to make the jump from 165 pounds.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says Koby Howard's return is in a 'pause state'
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Fresh off Penn State’s second straight win against Washington, Matt Campbell met with the media in Beaver Stadium for his weekly press conference.

Campbell discussed Koby Howard’s delayed return, Jack Ham’s medical emergency and more.

Here’s a look at what Campbell had to say on Tuesday.

Koby Howard’s availability

Ahead of Penn State’s trip to Michigan on Oct. 17, Campbell said Koby Howard’s return was going to be discussed after the bye week. After Howard missed the last two games against Purdue and Washington, Campbell said Howard’s absence is “in a pause state.”

“We were trying to beat a timeline coming back, and I think the reality is, I've continued to say I refuse to put Koby on the field until he's 100% ready to go back on the football field,” Campbell said. “Whether that pause means the end of the season, whether it's postseason play, I can promise you, I will let you guys know. But right now, I think we're in a pause state to make sure we get him fully 100% back to health.”

Howard has been out since the start of Big Ten play, with Campbell first announcing his injury on Sept. 22. Despite missing more time than some first expected, Howard has continued to be a vocal leader in the program.

“I've been really appreciative of our guys buying in on what it means to be a great teammate, what it means to be a future leader, because everybody's going to see how you led when it wasn't going well for you,” Campbell said. “It gives you the tools and that firepower when you do come back, and you got the ability to use your voice in a powerful way. And Koby's doing a great job.”

Players stepping up

Multiple players saw their biggest on-field contributions against Washington, including offensive lineman Garrett Sexton filling in for Malachi Goodman in the second half and safety-turned-linebacker Marcus Neal Jr. seeing the field for the first time since his position change.

Campbell had good things to say for Sexton postgame, but continued the praise for the backup lineman on Tuesday.

“To watch Garrett go in and honestly, the big block that happens on Carson (Hansen’s) run at the end of the game is because of Garrett Sexton,” Campbell said. “I thought (Sexton and Goodman) really showed a lot for Garrett being a young player that's growing.”

After Neal’s time was limited at the beginning of the Big Ten slate due to his struggles in coverage, he made the switch to linebacker during the bye week. He didn’t play against Purdue, but emerged on third down against Washington on Saturday.

“I think Marcus is only going to continue to grow at WILL linebacker,” Campbell said. “I think he is a guy that you go to practice every day, and you notice just the growth he makes on a daily basis.”

Campbell spoke about a number of other players who’ve also stepped up, including defensive tackle Ty Blanding and cornerback Ibn McDaniels.

“There's just guys that are showing up in some different moments,” Campbell said. “If we're going to be a great team, you need all those young guys to be growing forward.”

Jack Ham update

After Ham suffered a medical emergency before the game against Washington on Saturday, Campbell delivered positive news in an opening statement on Tuesday.

“Talked to him a little bit yesterday. Talked to him a little bit today,” Campbell said. “No. 1, he is talking. He's in stable condition. He's still out in Washington.”

Campbell, Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft and Ham’s announcing partner Steve Jones visited Ham at the hospital following the game, which Campbell said “was awesome.”

“I want to just say from my end a sincere thank you to so many people that have reached out,” Campbell said. “Obviously, what Jack and his family mean to Penn State football, and on behalf of our program and obviously the athletic department, the love, the care that we have gotten on behalf of Jack, we really appreciate it greatly.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn says defense needs to improve on 'leverage and missed tackles'
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn State’s 28-25 victory over Washington on Saturday, defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn met with the media at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday for his biweekly press conference.

Lynn discussed Marcus Neal Jr.'s growth at linebacker, the importance of having strong depth at cornerback and his thoughts on the Nittany Lions’ second half collapse on Saturday.

Here’s more on what Lynn said.

Evaluating Marcus Neal Jr. at linebacker

Marcus Neal Jr. got his first snaps as a Penn State linebacker against Washington after making the switch from safety. He finished the game with a solo tackle, primarily playing on third down, a decision made as he continues to develop into a true linebacker.

Lynn said “a certain level of it has to come natural” for the switch to be a success, and he’s seen flashes of it from Neal, who’s been practicing at the WILL spot the last two-to-three weeks.

“That was a way to get him on the field, just because we still feel like he just needs a little bit more time at the position before he goes out there on first and second down,” Lynn said. “But he's doing well.”

He also evaluated what Neal’s strengths are as a defender, highlighting his athleticism and adaptability. Lynn said he offers a lot of versatility, and he’s been able to showcase a natural linebacker’s toolset.

“There's a lot of stuff that he does naturally well down there, like he gets off blocks, he can blitz, he tackles, he plays downhill,” Lynn said. “There is some stuff that's different from a fit standpoint. It happens a lot quicker and down there. The more reps he's gotten, the better he's gotten.”

Depth cornerbacks

When asked about the growth of cornerbacks Ibn McDaniels and Jahmir Joseph, two defenders who’ve played well off the bench, Lynn said their performances haven’t come out of nowhere. He said both players showed good things in camp, but specifically took it “up a notch as far as their consistency” in the past few weeks. McDaniels showed that with his first career interception on Saturday.

“We just trust them in games,” Lynn said. “Now they have to keep on doing it every single day, but I think that they've been doing an outstanding job, and it helps keep other guys fresh.”

Lynn added having depth in the defensive secondary is pivotal to succeeding on defense in the Big Ten, particularly to take some of the workload off Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson.

“In the Big Ten, just from my experience, you need to play multiple guys at that position,” Lynn said. “Collins and Daryus have been doing an outstanding job, but there's definitely some games early in the year where like, man, you wish you could take some snaps off their plate, and it really starts in practice.”

Finishing games, the Washington collapse

Lynn has had time to go back and watch the game film from Saturday, and he identified two key mechanical areas the Nittany Lions need to improve on, particularly in the second half — “leverage and missed tackles.”

“I thought we did a really good job of it the first two quarters,” Lynn said. “You look at the second half, there's five plays, whether it's run game or pass game, we lose leverage, and guys don't make each other right, and we give up big plays. It's frustrating, but we have to not get bored doing the same thing over and over again. As the game goes on, and we start getting into the 40s, 50s and 60s as far as snaps, we can't lose that focus when we get tired.”

Despite how Washington scored 19 unanswered points in a second half surge to keep the game within a field goal, Lynn said winning was what truly mattered. However, that doesn’t mean he was happy with how Penn State got to the final score.

He said the reason for Penn State’s poor second half performances vary between weeks, but generally stem from self-inflicted errors. Lynn noted how “there were too many plays in that second half that we did not make them earn.”

“It was a win, but it wasn't a win that you felt good about at the end of the day,” Lynn said. “You go back, you watch the tape, and we try to be as process-oriented as we can. So, we're happy with the result. You go back and you watch the tape, and when you look at that second half, we didn't play like we deserved to win, and we all felt like that.”

title: Report: Bengals back out of trade with Eagles for former Penn State DE Arnold Ebiketie
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect the Bengals backing out of the initial trade agreement for Arnold Ebiketie.

The Cincinnati Bengals have backed out of a trade agreement for former Penn State defensive end Arnold Ebiketie, who was initially traded from the Philadelphia Eagles to the Bengals in exchange for a sixth-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, according to Ian Rapoport.

The trade was then called off, as the Bengals would've been forced to give up a compensatory draft pick because Ebiketie signed with the Eagles as a compensatory free agent, forcing the Bengals to give up a pick if the trade went through.

Ebiketie spent the first half of the NFL season with the Eagles, recording 25 tackles. He didn't record a sack or tackle for loss in nine games.

He joined the Eagles after spending his first four years in the NFL with the Atlanta Falcons, who selected Ebiketie with the 38th pick in the 2022 NFL Draft. In his four years with the Falcons, he totaled 16.5 sacks, including back-to-back years with six sacks in 2023 and 2024.

Ebiketie spent his final year of college in Happy Valley, where he notched 17.5 tackles for loss and 9.5 sacks. He joins a Bengals team that's searching for pass rush depth, as they sit inside the top 10 in sacks this season with 23.

title: ‘There is such a culture of invitation’ | Away from home, students find community in religious groups
author: Lily Chacko | For the Collegian
description:
Every day at sunrise, members of Penn State’s Muslim Students’ Association (MSA) gather in the HUB-Robeson Center or outside of Old Main for the first of the day’s five prayers.

It’s one of the many events MSA hosts, and its members are among many students across campus who have found community in religious organizations. Students in several of those groups said the organizations give them friendships and a way to keep up their faith, or make it their own.

Samihah Saleem, MSA’s Sisters representative, said Penn State does its best to accommodate her religious practices, but MSA provides her with a stable community. On the executive board, she advocates for the needs of the women in the organization; she also works behind the scenes to help organize events, special prayers and community work.

“MSA has just reminded me to be true to my faith. It helps me engage with other Muslims and create a community here,” Saleem, 19, of Pittsburgh, said.

She said MSA is intentional in ensuring everyone has an opportunity to go to an event each week, and she regularly attends events and goes to the Pasquerilla Spiritual Center for prayers. She also helps with setup for Jumu’ah, which is usually crowded, overflowing into the center’s lobby.

“Being away from home... it just makes everything a little bit harder,” Saleem, a second-year studying neurobiology, said.

Alyssa Maugeri was looking to join a religious organization on campus where she could feel at home when she was invited to attend Cru meetings by friends. From there, she said, she found the family and community she was looking for.

“It can be hard, like, being a Christian, especially at a school where there's a lot of like parties and things like that,” Maugeri said. “There's so many people [in Cru] that I want to stay in contact with for the rest of my life.”

Maugeri, 20, of King of Prussia, regularly attends Cru’s events, such as Bible studies, various weekend activities, and large group meetings. Cru also arranges rides for students to attend Sunday services at State College Alliance Church. She said she spends time with Cru around three times a week.

Cru offers summer missions for students, and this past summer Maugeri went to Thailand. She said she was grateful for the unique opportunity to build friendships and step outside her comfort zone.

Maugeri said students may come to college and find themselves with the opportunity to either make their faith their own or “leave it back home with your family.” Cru helped her personalize her faith outside of the context of her family, she said.

Similarly, Charlie Novick found a community through campus-affiliated religious groups. Novick, 20, of Lower Merion, Pennsylvania, is involved with Penn State Hillel and Chabad of Penn State, two Jewish campus organizations. Both organizations have downtown locations and offer resources for Jewish students on campus. The Hillel location downtown has interactive spaces where students can study, grab a bite and mingle with others — something Novick said makes the organization welcoming to the community.

Novick also said it encourages members to get to know new people. He’s equally involved in both groups, through which he has been able to attend weekly events, classes on different aspects of Judaism, he added.

“It’s definitely let me keep up with my faith. Without them, I probably would not have gone to any Jewish events. They also let me expand my faith because they offer so many opportunities to learn and grow within Judaism,” Novick, a second-year studying accounting and supply chain and information systems, said.

Novick said Penn State has been good at accommodating his dietary needs, as he keeps a kosher diet. North Halls opened Nosh, which serves all kosher food, last year.

This year, Penn State’s Catholic group, Nittany Catholic, partnered with FOCUS, a national Catholic ministry program that sends full-time missionaries to college campuses, for the first time.

Taylor Gandolfo, one of three FOCUS missionaries on campus, said there has been a consistent turnout for events like Bible studies, and students are making a deliberate commitment to their faith.

She said the resources on campus, such as three Sunday Mass times, make people more likely to take part.

“Penn State is founded on culture, whether it’s sports or school, I’ve learned,” Gandolfo said. “But the Catholic center has that same culture of, ‘If I have something good, I want the person next to me to also have it.’ There is such a culture of invitation.”

Gandolfo said she loves her job because she gets to connect with students on a personal level and accompany them on their journey with faith.

“Meeting people where they are does so much for them than feeling like they need to come to the church. The church is also able to come to them,” Gandolfo said.

title: On weekends, students tend to wander. Here’s some of their favorite whereabouts
author: Noah Spitzen | For the Collegian
description:
Weekends in State College are always eventful, especially around this time of year — the cool, autumn temperatures don’t keep Penn State students inside.

Students engage in a variety of activities on their days off, ranging from tailgating football games to spending time with friends and practicing different hobbies. With all there is to do, students shared some of the best things to do when the weekend comes around.

A very common weekend tradition for Penn State students in the fall is tailgating. Many alumni, families and fans travel to State College for every game day to celebrate Penn State football.

Like many of those fans, Jordan Plans, 19, of West Chester, Pennsylvania, said his top priority most weekends is going to the game and tailgating.

“All of us usually pitch in for a spot, and we all show up to that one location," Plans, a second-year studying mechanical engineering, said. "If I was jumping around them, it would mainly be if I'm getting to my tailgate, so I'll stop at this person's, stop at that person's, but ultimately end up at the one I'm supposed to be at.”

James Haggerty, 20, of Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, uses the football games as a way to kick back after a long week of studying.

“I really like the social aspect,” Haggerty, a third-year studying mechanical engineering, said.

“You know, meeting up with guys that I don't normally get to see during the week because we have different majors.”

When Haggerty isn’t attending football games, he enjoys meeting with Penn State’s Car Club, of which he’s a member, on weekends.

Siddharth Adiraju, 18, of Royersford, Pennsylvania, keeps busy on the weekend by enjoying his hobbies. Adiraju also visits his friends at their dorms, usually near South Halls.

“I like to do music," Adiraju, a first-year studying cybersecurity analytics and operations, said. "Either just playing my guitar or via software, like FL Studio.”

Haley Polaneczky, 19, of Bucks County, Pennsylvania, said browsing the shopping scene in downtown State College makes for a fun activity on the weekends. She said she likes going to Connections and Pitaya.

"I love Snap, Sora and Big Chicken," Polaneczky, a second-year studying biobehavioral health, said.

Liz Siemsen, 19, of Baltimore, Maryland, said she prefers getting outside and exploring nature on the weekends.

“I like to hang out with my friends and go on walks in all the pretty neighborhoods," Siemsen, a second-year studying biobehavioral health, said. "I know of a trail behind State College Area High School that's really pretty, but it's hard to find.”

Emi Gerveni, 19, of Philadelphia, also loves to get outside and exercise in her free time. As a member of Club Ultimate Frisbee, she regularly attends games. This weekend, she has a tournament with the club.

“We throw the frisbee on the HUB-Robeson Center lawn and in the Intramural (IM) turf,” Gerveni, a second-year studying biology, said. “I also like going on hikes, like a Mount Nittany hike is always fun with my friends.”

Nick Brown, 21, of Long Island, New York, likes to go home on the weekends in the fall. However, his spring weekends look a little different.

“I do a lot of studying,” Brown, a second-year studying graphic design, said. “I know very minimal people, so I don't really go out as much as most people.”

Brown tries his best to explore areas of town that he’s never been to before by trying new food spots. He’s a DoorDasher, so he said he takes note of different spots he wants to try.

From the places he’s already tried, Brown, a self-proclaimed “big chicken wing fan,” recommended Buffalo Wild Wings. He also recommended Tokyo Sushi and Hibachi.

Surya Suryavanshi, 22, of India, enjoys heading to the Arboretum on nice days to enjoy the sunset.

There's also the State College night life and bar scene, which is active all throughout the school year. Suryavanshi, a fourth-year studying computer science, mathematics and economics, said his favorite places to go out for a drink with friends are Bill Pickle’s Tap Room and Cafe 210 West.

If it’s later in the night, he said he hangs out with friends downtown or at restaurants like Tadashi, Honeygrow and Teadori. He and his friends also enjoy going to local bowling alleys.

A recent favorite memory from his weekend plans was his costume inspired by “The Odyssey.”

“I was Agamemnon for Halloween,” Suryavanshi said. “I spent an entire week making my costume from scratch, went around with my friends to some house parties and just tried to walk around and scare people.”

title: Blue in the Face ‘more than just another club,’ members say. ‘It’s community’
author: Katrina Carter | For the Collegian
description:
Television and films capture a capella groups as a niche hobby for theatre majors and choir singers, but Blue in the Face just wants to create a community using the oldest instrument in the world.

Blue in the Face, a co-ed a capella group at Penn State was founded in 2008 to serve as a creative musical outlet to students. Members have the chance to create musical arrangements, perform and even record their own work. It’s open to students of all majors and backgrounds, whether that comes with experience in music or not.

President Lilly Davis, 21, of Mercer, Pennsylvania, said Blue in the Face prides itself on the diversity of its members from engineering to theatre majors, and the group deeply encourages anyone to audition.

“I’ve got to meet a lot of influential people through this group,” Davis, a fourth-year studying theatre and telecommunications and media industries, said. “Everyone who joins this group is really dedicated and passionate about whatever they do. There's a really wide, diverse group of people in Blue in the Face, which has led me to meet some really interesting and cool people.”

Secretary Nova Figurelle, 20, of Glen Mills, Pennsylvania, enjoys being surrounded by such a positive environment and taking a break from the stress of college. He said after high school, it can become harder to balance extracurriculars and passions with college academics and pressures.

Figurelle said the group is like a tight-knit family, and many members end up joining because they’re eager to find a community that shares their same passions and allows them to continue doing something they love.

“It’s a fantastic way to make friends early on and just keep music in your life, because it’s tough,” Figurelle, a third-year studying information technology ethics and compliance, said.

Member Liam Schwarcz, 20, of Princeton, New Jersey, also emphasized the diversity of the group. While many assume a cappella groups consist only of theatre majors, Schwarcz said that the group includes various disciplines.

“There are people from all sorts of different backgrounds coming together, learning about one another, all sharing the common connection, the common language of music and sound that transcends every form of communication,” Schwarcz, a third-year studying mechanical engineering and engineering science and mechanics, said.

Schwarcz said the origin of its name stems from a musical joke of the treble notes found on a staff — F-A-C-E — being colored blue to represent Penn State.

He said there’s a “hands in” ritual at the end of rehearsal where members have the chance to share personal updates and highs and lows to foster a sense of togetherness.

“(It’s) more than just singing, it's more than just another club,” Schwarcz said. “It's more than just a concert and rehearsal. It's community.”

Justin Lee, 22, of South Korea, had no prior musical experience before attending Penn State, but he decided to audition after feeling inspired by the movie “Pitch Perfect.”

Lee, a third-year studying human-centered design and development, described the group as a second family that provided essential social support during his transition as an international student.

“I really think I couldn't have made it to this place if it weren't for my friends backing me up,” Lee said.

When not performing on stage, the group acts as a social outlet, with members bonding not only over rehearsals but also game nights, including playing a group favorite “Werewolf,” a mystery game.

Landon Keffer said the group's infectious energy makes it special to him, and he loves when they’re able to feed off of each other’s energy.

“If you’re having a bad day or week, you’re going to walk out of rehearsal feeling better,” Keffer, a third-year student studying electrical engineering, said. “I hosted a game night for Blue in the Face where a bunch of the members just came together after we finished our Halloween rehearsal. We played ‘Werewolf’ for probably three hours and it really brightened my mood.”

Unlike many a cappella groups, Blue in the Face creates all musical arrangements in house. Members participate in a two-round song selection process and arranging is entirely voluntary.

The group is currently preparing for several upcoming milestones, including an EP consisting of three songs performed this semester for release on platforms like Apple Music and Spotify. Many members expressed a desire for more formal recognition of a capella groups, as many students are unaware they exist.

“I feel like a lot of people when they think about a capella they think of ‘Pitch Perfect’ — which by all means, we have aspects of ‘Pitch Perfect.’ But it’s not that huge, dramatic fest that is the movie,” Keffer said. “It really is just a fun time of enjoying singing and that part of the Penn State community that most people don't really ever see.”

title: Column | The 24-team College Football Playoff is unnecessary. But they don’t care about fans' opinion
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The expected has been made official — the College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams.

Conference championships are no more. ESPN will carry every game until at least 2031-32, with a deal worth about $1.7 billion in place, per multiple reports. The season will begin in what’s been known as Week 0. Army vs. Navy will be played on Dec. 4.

The 24-team field gives each Power Four conference an autobid for its regular season champion, and the highest-ranked Group of Six receives one as well. The other 19 spots will be chosen by the selection committee.

I wrote a few weeks back when a “handshake deal” was in place about the pros, cons and unknowns of this new era. Now that it’s official, the fan outrage that has dimmed is back. And those who oppose this are absolutely correct in their reasoning.

It’s even worse when you hear what CFP executive director Rich Clark told reporters today via a teleconference.

“We're aware of the fan sentiment and that many fans aren't in favor of expansion, but that was certainly weighed into the decision,” Clark said. “It was considered, but ultimately, we just need to make a spectacular playoff. The CFP has a responsibility to our fans. They're the lifeblood of college football, and we owe it to them to make this great, and that really is our intent. But we appreciate our fans. We did take into account their sentiment, and that was rolled into this decision, but we decided to move forward with it.”

So basically, they heard that fans don’t like it. They did it anyway. Even though fans are the driving force of college football. They’re the ones who pay to go to the games. They’re the ones who turn their TVs on every Saturday to watch this sport.

The Athletic did a poll of 6,318 fans, and 81.7% of them voted against expanding the CFP. Fans are outraged on social media, saying the people making these decisions only care about money — which, at this point, is 100% true. The ratings for college football this year are down across the board with a 12-team playoff, even after a complete boom in viewership in 2025.

The Big Ten’s viewership dropped 10.4% in Weeks 0-8 compared to last year. The ACC’s is down 44.5%. Overall, the Power Four conferences and Notre Dame, which has its own TV rights deal, have a 5.4% decrease in viewership.

So what makes ESPN and the CFP think that people will want to watch these games? Based on the final rankings for last year’s CFP, some first round matchups would’ve been Georgia Tech at Notre Dame; Tulane at Texas; and James Madison at Alabama. All three of those would’ve been blowouts.

If college football isn’t getting incredible viewership for regular season games this year, they certainly won’t get it next year when regular season games mean practically nothing.

Yes, Power Four teams now have to schedule 10 games against fellow Power Four teams, which includes conference contests. But those better nonconference contests won’t matter for so many teams.

If the rosters stay healthy, Ohio State, Alabama, Texas, Notre Dame and Georgia are making it every year. Miami and Indiana can be in that conversation as well. It only matters for teams that are consistently good but not great — like Iowa. But if a team isn’t ever great, what makes people think those programs can win a national championship?

And then there’s the lack of conference championships. I always think back to 2023, the last year of the four-team playoff, when 12-0 Washington played 11-1 Oregon in the Pac-12 championship. They literally played for a spot in the playoff, and it was electric.

Those kinds of stakes will never happen again. It’s sad to think about how college football has gone so far downhill. But here we are.

At least for Penn State fans, you now have more chances to see your team competing for a national title.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | Parker Washington scores again, Kaytron Allen contributes on special teams
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Former Penn Staters continued their NFL seasons last week, adding to successful 2026 campaigns.

Parker Washington, Saquon Barkley and Juwan Johnson all found the end zone, while Dani Dennis-Sutton continued his standout rookie season.

Here’s a look at former Nittany Lion stars in Week 9 of the NFL season.

Parker Washington, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

Against the Baltimore Ravens on Thursday, Washington continued to position himself as one of the better receivers in the league. He reeled in two catches for 61 yards and a touchdown.

Quarterback Trevor Lawrence found Washington on a 50-yard reception, with 36 yards coming after the catch. Washington had a lane to the end zone and separated from two Ravens defenders.

Washington’s fourth year in the NFL has been nothing short of remarkable. Through eight games, he’s tied for ninth in the league in receiving touchdowns with five and third in average yards per catch.

Saquon Barkley, running back, Philadelphia Eagles

After coming back from injury on Oct. 26, Barkley has consistently found the end zone. That continued against the New York Giants on Sunday, as Barkley scored for the third straight week.

Barkley’s performance was overall underwhelming, recording just 22 yards on 13 attempts. His longest run went for just five yards.

However, he found the end zone with a three-yard run up the middle, marking the Eagles’ only touchdown on Sunday.

Dani Dennis-Sutton, defensive end, Green Bay Packers

Dennis-Sutton has shown out during the Green Bay Packers’ last two wins, showcasing his potential as a young defender.

Against the New England Patriots on Sunday, Dennis-Sutton recorded four tackles, half a sack and a quarterback hit.

Midway through the third quarter, the former Nittany Lion converged on quarterback Drake Maye alongside defensive end Brenton Cox Jr., bringing Maye down for a loss of two yards.

Dennis-Sutton now has a sack in back-to-back weeks, bringing his season total to three sacks.

Fellow Nittany Lion Micah Parsons returned to the practice field last Wednesday, so Dennis Sutton’s role could decrease soon if Parsons returns. But the two will likely take the field together at some point.

Kaytron Allen, running back, Miami Dolphins

Kaytron Allen saw the field earlier in the season for the Washington Commanders, but has been relatively silent since he was traded to the Miami Dolphins.

Against the Detroit Lions on Sunday, Allen recorded his first stat on his new team, lining up on special teams during a fake punt. He ran down the field uncovered and reeled in a pass from punter Bradley Pinion, making a defender miss and picking up 46 yards for first down.

This is the second straight week Allen has had a good special teams play for the Dolphins, as he had a tackle last Sunday.

The former Penn Stater also recorded his first rush since Oct. 4, although it went for a loss of one yard.

Juwan Johnson, tight end, New Orleans Saints

Johnson had just two catches against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday, but made the most of his time on the field.

Johnson’s two receptions went for 34 yards and a crucial touchdown in overtime, marking his fourth time finding the end zone this year.

During New Orleans’ first drive of the game, quarterback Tyler Shough connected with Johnson for a 19-yard pickup, and the Saints took the lead with a field goal.

After the Browns tied the game with a last-minute field goal, New Orleans marched down the field in overtime to take the lead. Johnson ran a 15-yard corner route into the back right of the end zone and reeled in a pass from Shough to take the lead and eventually win the game.

title: Which bowls does national media predict Penn State will play in? MLB stadiums, southern travel possible
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s knocking on the doorstep of bowl eligibility after the Nittany Lions won their fifth game of the season, defeating Washington, 28-25, on Saturday.

With only Minnesota, Rutgers and Maryland left to play, the odds of a sixth victory are in Penn State’s favor, so national media outlets are considering where the Nittany Lions might play this postseason if they win one more game.

Here are the current bowl projections after Penn State beat Washington in Week 10.

CBS: Fenway Bowl

CBS Sports has the Nittany Lions shipping up to Boston to play against East Carolina at the historic Fenway Park, home of the Boston Red Sox, at 2 p.m. on Dec. 26.

Although Fenway Park has been a football destination dating back to 1912, the Fenway Bowl was first played in 2022 when Louisville beat Cincinnati, 24-7.

Penn State hasn’t yet appeared in the Fenway Bowl, as it’s typically played between teams in the ACC and American conferences. However, because there will likely be too many Big Ten teams to qualify for a bowl, Penn State may have to fill one of the slots.

East Carolina mirrors Penn State’s 5-4 overall record while being 3-2 in the American conference, including back-to-back overtime losses to UAB and Memphis.

The Pirates have a clear path to bowl eligibility, as they play a 1-8 Charlotte on Saturday and later face Army and FAU to close the season.

It would be a full-circle moment for wide receiver Chase Sowell, who played two seasons as a Pirate before transferring to Iowa State in 2025.

Rotowire: Pinstripe Bowl

Penn State may be going back to a different baseball stadium, as Rotowire has the Nittany Lions returning to the Pinstripe Bowl at Yankee Stadium on Dec. 26. The game is played between opponents from the Big Ten and the ACC and will be at noon on ABC.

Rotowire projects the Nittany Lions will face North Carolina. The Tarheels have improved in Bill Belichick’s second season as head coach, currently 5-4 with a victory over a ranked Pitt and a three-point loss to then-No. 1 Miami.

North Carolina plays Louisville, Virginia and NC State to finish the regular season.

Penn State played in the Pinstripe Bowl last season and beat Clemson, 22-10, behind breakout performances by former Nittany Lion quarterback Ethan Grunkemeyer and running back Quinton Martin Jr.

ESPN, Athlon Sports: Duke’s Mayo Bowl

ESPN and Athlon Sports both have Penn State traveling to Charlotte, North Carolina, for the Duke’s Mayo Bowl, but ESPN’s two writers aren’t quite sure who to project as the Nittany Lions’ opponent. Kyle Bonagura and Mark Schlabach have Penn State facing Clemson and Duke, respectively.

Meanwhile, Athlon Sports projects Louisville as the opponent.

Regardless of the opponent, the Duke’s Mayo Bowl is set to take place at 3:30 p.m. Dec. 26 on ABC.

If Bonagura is correct, it would be the second consecutive year Penn State meets Clemson in a bowl, and the Tigers became bowl eligible after beating Syracuse, 18-13, on Saturday. The all-time series is tied 1-1 after the Nittany Lions’ victory in the Pinstripe Bowl last season.

On the other hand, Penn State has never played Duke, so a new series could be on the horizon if Schlabach’s prediction comes true. That would also mean Blue Devils’ head coach Manny Diaz would face his former team, as he was the Nittany Lions defensive coordinator from 2022-23.

Duke is 7-2 overall and got their sixth win by beating Boston College two weeks ago.

The Cardinals, meanwhile, are 6-3 including an upset victory over then-No. 16 SMU in Week 3. Riding the high of a four-game winning streak, Louisville only has North Carolina, Pitt and No. 6 Kentucky left on its schedule.

Penn State and Louisville met in 1996 and 1997 in a home-and-home series. The Nittany Lions took both games.

College Football News: First Responder Bowl

College Football News projects Penn State to head down south to University Park, Texas, to face North Texas in the First Responder Bowl on Jan. 2, 2027. The game would be played at 3:30 p.m. CT on ESPN at Gerald R. Ford Stadium.

The Nittany Lions have only appeared once in this bowl’s lineage, and it was in 2011 when it was called the TicketCity Bowl. Penn State lost to Houston 30-14 in the final game before the name was changed to the Heart of Dallas Bowl. In 2018, it was again changed to what it is now.

North Texas has already qualified for a bowl with a 7-2 overall record and is undefeated in the American conference. The Mean Green’s only losses came at the hands of Indiana and Texas State, and they’re now on a six-game winning streak before they play UTSA, Tulane and UAB to finish their schedule.

title: Column | Fentanyl’s destructive impact on college populations
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
The dangers of drugs have been prevalent since people decided they liked being high. But today, some drugs on the market kill thousands per year — a problem all over the United States. College, for many young people, is the starting point.

Drugs like fentanyl are becoming more common because of the iron law of prohibition. The concept, coined by Richard Cowan in a 1986 article titled “How the Narcs Created Crack,” posits that the more law enforcement cracks down on illegal substances, the more potent they become. In the States’ prohibition era, moonshine was invented and gained popularity — it was much more potent than beer, and it got people drunk off of much smaller quantities of alcohol.

In today’s era, it's still much easier to smuggle smaller amounts of drugs. Tiny amounts of fentanyl can get someone high, making it cost-effective and less likely to be seized. It’s also a huge part of why taking drugs today is such a gamble. In August, 14 people were arrested in connection with an alleged fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring. If there had been a laced batch, the distribution could have killed people all over State College.

Even though the percentages are relatively low for the whole student body, they are still significant at a large school like Penn State, which has a population of over 40,000 students at University Park. With fentanyl being much more common in illicit drugs and continuing to do so, students are at risk and vulnerable to accidental overdose and death.

“Nonmedical use of prescription drugs was more prevalent during college than in the later years of the study. Although the prevalence of cocaine and ecstasy use was low (cumulative prevalence estimates of 17% and 13% respectively), incidence for these drugs were particularly high in the later years of the study,” according to the National Health Institute.

Pennsylvania's Medical Amnesty and Good Samaritan Law protect students who are under the influence from legal consequences if they are the first person to call emergency services; give their name; and stay with the individual, according to Penn State’s student affairs.

But there are more preventative measures Penn State can take. The university could provide students with easier access to free Naloxone — Narcan — and fentanyl testing strips. Narcan, a drug sprayed into the nose or injected to reverse the effects of opioids during an overdose, would help students in an emergency: It can save someone from heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine and morphine overdoses. The university could also give students training on how to use the drug.

(University police carry Narcan, and certain resources will mail you Narcan for free.)

Now, even though drugs are portrayed as an issue at an individual level, there are numerous other factors contributing to this decadeslong epidemic. Drugs and drug use are painted as a problem at a personal level, a narrow-minded view that’s detrimental to any reform. Drugs are a much larger systemic issue, with irrelevant or obsolete policies blocking the way for any major positive change.

These policies cover a wide range of legal areas, but one particularly relevant here is possession of user amounts of narcotics. Under 21 U.S. Code § 844, punishment can, depending on the number of offenses, vary from around 90 days to three years in jail with fines up to $5,000. First offenses sometimes don’t carry any jail time and will result in diversion or rehabilitative programs. This is federal law, so it varies by state, but states tend to fall within these parameters.

I think these laws surrounding user possession of controlled substances should focus on rehabilitation rather than punishment. Paying a fine won’t stop someone from getting more drugs and prison is not a conducive environment to get clean. While they confiscate small amounts of narcotics off the streets, it's a short-term solution to a long-term problem.

Rehabilitation is a step in the right direction. It might not work for everyone, but helping people get clean is a net positive all around. Fewer people supporting the drug trade means less crime associated with drugs, as well as fewer deaths from overdose.

Drug policy reform is an issue on its own that can be talked about at length. It will take time and dedication to these policies to create long-term change, as well as strategic investments into communities around the United States. Drugs have injected themselves into every socioeconomic level of society but impoverished areas are more prone to the negative effects of drug use. There are ways to have monumental impacts on smaller scales as an individual and as an organization like Penn State.

Penn State can — and should — take measures to mitigate damages, though students will always take drugs. I would never suggest to anyone to do drugs anyway, but we’re past the era where you could experiment with something and not have serious health consequences. Now, you could take a pill or snort some powder one time, and it’ll be the end of you. It's not worth it.

However, if you decide to do drugs or if your friends partake in drug use, there are things you can do to be safer. First off, always having Narcan readily available is important and potentially the difference between life and death. Always test your drugs; fentanyl strips are available at the AppleGate Recovery location in State College and through the Overdose Prevention Program in Pennsylvania.

Since fentanyl is a powder, it doesn’t mix evenly. And never take anyone's word on what the drug actually entails.

Always call 911 if something goes wrong or someone overdoses; it’s better to be safe than sorry.

You can have fun without hard drugs and their subsequent looming threat of death. Drugs and the problems that come with them have a much more extensive scope that will take an international effort to reform. In the meantime, informing and protecting yourself and the ones around you is the best thing you can do.

title: Flu season is upon the States. Here’s what students, professors suggest to avoid getting sick
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
Many people have likely walked home from their friend’s house on a cold, November night. The wind can bite in the valley, and so too can the snow that’s soon to fall. And you might wake the next morning to find your throat is sore, your head hurts, or there’s a fever-driven blush reddening your face.

That walk home — even if it’s only a few minutes of you scuffling your feet — can make or break your health. There are many things students can do to protect themselves, experts say. Wearing layers and keeping your hands clean can really affect how you feel, even if those feel like trivial actions.

Isabella Cattadori, a professor of biology, said there are a handful of important steps to staying healthy. Preventive actions, like flu shots, can help offset more serious symptoms. Though you may still become infected, she said, you’ll recover in a “less dramatic way.”

Cattadori said washing your hands helps reduce exposure to germs, especially when going to highly populated places like the HUB-Robeson Center, gym, or even dorms.

“In the dorms, don't share things,” Cattadori, 61, of Italy, said. “Even if you are in those sort of common spaces after using things, just wash everything, just wash your hands.”

Cattadori said the flu isn’t the only thing to worry about during this winter season, especially for students who are already immunocompromised.

“You may be able to clear the flu eventually, but you may get a secondary bacterial infection, and those are really nasty to get rid of,” Cattadori said.

Some Penn State students have similar routines and tricks to stay healthy during flu season. Michael Ferrick, 20, of Mount Olive, New Jersey, has a set routine for how to stay healthy but also has a process for when he starts feeling sick. He said he takes multivitamins every day, tries to get a good amount of rest and drinks tea.

“I also just take preventative measures by knowing that If I'm starting to feel not well, I try to stay away from others for the day or try to stay off campus,” Ferrick, a third-year studying political science and history, said.

Ferrick is a busy student, so staying healthy is a must to keep up with his classes and other activities. He said when someone is first entering college, it can be hard to keep up with habits that prevent sickness. His advice to new students is to keep your dorm clean.

Ferrick said students should consider staying out of the cold to avoid getting sick. Taking the bus is one option, he added. CATA’s blue loop circles all throughout campus.

“If you don't have an air purifier, get one. Those dorms are kind of musty,” Ferrick said. “Definitely dress appropriately for weather. Never underdress. It will get to you very quickly with how much you're walking to class.”

Amanda Johnson, 21, of Yardley, Pennsylvania, said isolation is an important factor if you’re already under the weather. When she starts to feel sick, she said she tries to stay in her room for things that aren’t mandatory. Her main focus becomes making sure she gets better.

“On campus, I make sure that if I'm going to touch something like the desk or the handle, that I'm making sure I'm not touching my face or things that would go near my face, anything like that,” Johnson, a fourth-year studying accounting, said.

Johnson has experienced winter at three different Penn State campuses — Abington, Altoona and University Park — giving her a full scope of what Pennsylvania winters have in store.

One of her main pieces of advice is to keep your space clean, especially if it’s a shared space. Those living in dorms tend to have roommates, or at the very least share bathrooms with their entire floor. Even bathrooms on dorm floors can become a cesspool for germs, she said, and being vigilant helps promote cleanliness.

“You're around so many people in a dorm and like sharing a lot of communal spaces,” Johnson said. “I would make sure that I wash my hands a ton. And I would make sure that if you know somebody is sick that you're not around them a ton — even if they're a close friend of yours and you want to hang out with them.”

title: Penn State women’s basketball stays winless with loss to Dayton
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State led by as many as seven in the first half, but a late second-quarter run gave Dayton a lead they never relinquished.

The Flyers soared in the second half to pick up their first victory of the season, 77-71.

First half

For the first time this season, Tanisha Wright rolled out a different starting lineup. Skylar Durley and Cristen Carter joined Devyn Quigley, Petra Božan and Enjulina Gonzalez in the starting lineup, replacing Ava Black and Savannah White.

Penn State fell behind early, but Quigley took the Lady Lions’ first lead of the game with a banked three-pointer in the midst of a 7-0 run.

Unlike the previous two games, the blue and white didn’t pick up their first foul until the 3:46 mark of the first quarter, when it led 15-9.

After the media timeout, Dayton slipped inside for two easy layups, but Božan countered with her second triple of the game. Quigley was also hot from outside the arc; she made three of her first four attempts, including the final points of the first quarter.

The Lady Lions held a 21-16 lead after their highest-scoring quarter of the young season. It was also their first time leading at a quarter break since the first quarter against Cleveland State.

Quigley exited for the first time with 8:25 left in the second quarter, and the Penn State offense went into a lull. Wright called her first timeout with 6:46 remaining in the half, but the blue and white squandered the following set piece with their sixth turnover.

Dayton tied it up at 23 with a Sophie Swanson jumper, but Quigley came right back with one of her own to jump right back in front.

Penn State started to fumble opportunities with four turnovers in under five minutes, but Carter locked down Fatima Ibrahim on the other end to keep the deficit between three and six. Ibrahim racked up 23 points and 18 rebounds in Dayton’s season-opening loss to Illinois State, but Carter held her to just one basket in the first half.

Dayton got hot late and made five of its last seven field goals as Penn State went scoreless in the final 2:40 to take a 37-29 lead into halftime.

Second half

It was an ominous start to the second half for the Lady Lions. They got caught by the shot clock on their opening possession, then Ibrahim drove right down the middle on the other end.

Božan kept Penn State in it with three more quick three-pointers, surrounded by Dayton fouls and turnovers, and the Flyers called a timeout up 44-40 with seven minutes left in the quarter.

The Lady Lions made nine of their first 14 long-range attempts, and Božan’s five were just one fewer than her 2025-26 season total.

Penn State’s shooting kept it in the game as the defense crumbled. Durley knocked down a mid-range jumper after briefly stepping out with an injury to cut the Dayton lead to 49-45.

With 2:10 left in the third quarter, Božan picked up her third foul, and the Flyers went up 52-46 at the line. Penn State hung in through the end of the quarter and took just a three-point deficit to the final break.

Early in the fourth, Dayton lost Jayda Johnson to an injury. The senior from West Haven, Connecticut, scored 15 points in 14 minutes, which led the Flyers at the time of her injury.

Božan continued her huge night through the final buzzer. The junior finished with a career-high 27 points, but it was never enough to overcome the Flyers. She and Quigley, who amassed 23 points, combined for 11 three-pointers.

Dayton’s Molly O'Riordan netted the dagger with 55 seconds left. The forward drilled a contested three-pointer from the left wing to extend the lead to 72-65.

The Lady Lions never gave up. Wright’s sets provided a layup for Božan and a three-pointer for Quigley to cut the lead to three with 44 seconds left. Wright used her final timeout to set up another look as the clock ticked under 30 seconds.

For the second time this season, the Lady Lions fell victim to a crucial five-second violation. Durley couldn’t get a pass off, and Penn State turned it over, allowing Dayton to ice the contest.

Up next

Penn State is back on the road Sunday at 4 p.m. to take on Arizona State.

title: Borough council passes amendment to allow CATA bus service expansion amid proposed service adjustments
author: Jacob Godshall I The Daily Collegian
description:
The State College Borough Council adopted a resolution approving an amendment to the Centre Area Transportation Authority (CATA) Joint Articles of Agreement, allowing CATA to expand its services beyond its five member municipalities, after a unanimous vote on Monday night.

The resolution was approved by State College’s council, but the amendment won’t be formally approved until the State College Borough, Patton, Ferguson, Harris and College townships agree on the resolution. Then, CATA must submit the resolution to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania for certification.

The CATA Board of Directors approved the amendment on Sept. 28 and the five member counties participated in the approval process throughout October and November.

CATA’s Executive Director Todd Horsley spoke in front of the council on behalf of CATA and answered any questions that were posed.

According to Horsley, the main goal of the amendment is to expand CATA’s contracting ability by allowing them to transport outside of its member counties, as well as expanding their services.

“When I was here last fall, as the incoming CEO of CATA, I mentioned that we had planned to start looking at some potential on-demand services,” Horsley said. “Perhaps to places like the airport, local Amtrak or regional Amtrak stations.”

Through this amendment, CATA will be able to extend its transportation services outside of its member municipalities on a contract basis to non-member counties, the public sector and government entities.

This amendment passes in the wake of CATA’s proposed bus service cuts in State College due to the national driver shortage. Despite questioning from council member Susan Venegoni, Horsley assured the council that the extensions discussed in the amendment would not be affected by the proposed service cuts, and would be entirely separate.

According to CATA’s website, eight service adjustments are being proposed across five lines, with a complete suspension of services on the University/Parkway (UP) Circulator.

On the Atherton Street (AC) route, there is a proposed reduction in service frequency from Monday to Thursday, from 30 minutes to every 45 minutes. In addition, services will end at 8 p.m. on the AC route Monday through Saturday.

There are three proposed changes to the College Ave. (CC) route: a reduction of service on Sunday from every 30 minutes to every 60 minutes, an end to Sunday services at 10 p.m. and an end to Lemont, Havershire and Science Park services at 8 p.m.

For the Havershire, Martin, Vairo and Toftrees route (NV), Sunday routes will now end at 10 p.m., and the Waupelani Dr. and Downtown route (RP) will end at the same time.
