title: Penn State announces steps to address $124 million budget shortfall
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State announced steps to address a $124 million budget shortfall within its $2.2 billion Education and General (E&G) budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year (FY) in a press release on Monday. The shortfall was attributed to national trends of declining enrollment and tuition and rising health insurance costs.

The university plans to cut spending to deal with the budget shortfall. Any tuition and fees that were previously approved by the Board of Trustees for future fiscal years will not be affected.

The steps shared by the university include reducing the budget for the president’s strategic funds, the Office of the Vice President for Commonwealth Campuses and the E&G units.

Additionally, the university plans to centralize empty salary and fringe benefit savings that began on July 1, exchange a portion of Office of Physical Plant E&G funds for major maintenance or capital funding from the 2026-27 fiscal year and require capital projects using E&G funds to be preapproved by the provost and chief financial officer.

All budget surpluses at the end of the year will be returned to the central budget, while transfers to capital projects at the end of the year will not be approved. The release also notes that it is not “unusual” for E&G units to have unused funds at the end of the year, which can be used to reduce their budgets.

While enrollment increased at some Penn State campuses, enrollment did decrease overall by more than 3,000 students between fall 2025 and fall 2026, with significant declines expected at the Commonwealth Campuses slated to close in the spring. The enrollment impacts from the Commonwealth Campus closure were not included in the original modeling for the 2026-27 FY due to the university’s budgeting process, resulting in an estimated $87 million reduction in anticipated tuition and fee revenues.

The university's employee health insurance costs had a "significant impact” on the shortfall, according to the release. From Aug. 2025 to 2026, claims increased 15.7%, leading to a $37 million increase beyond original projections.

Together, the reduction in revenue and rise in insurance costs combined for the $124 million shortfall, according to the release.

title: Penn State women’s gymnastics announces schedule for 2026-27

description:

New head coach for the Nittany Lions, Jennifer Green, begins her inaugural season with a quad-meet at Rec Hall on Sunday, Jan. 10, against Pitt, George Washington University and Urisnus College.

The team has six dual meets before their next quad-meet. The blue and white face Rutgers at Rec Hall on January 16, before traveling to face former 2026 No. 2 in the Big Ten, Minnesota, on Jan. 23.

After the double dual, the blue and white remain at Rec Hall to face the former No. 1 in the Big Ten, UCLA, on Feb. 12. Shortly thereafter, the Nittany Lions are back on the road for a dual meet against another Big Ten opponent, the Ohio State Buckeyes. The Nittany Lions and the Buckeyes will compete in a dual meet on Feb. 21.

After this series of duals, Penn State faces another quad-meet this time against all Big Ten opponents. On Feb. 26, the team heads to Seattle for a meet against Michigan, Nebraska, and Washington.

title: Penn State men’s hockey notebook | Guy Gadowsky talks pressure, slow start
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State coach Guy Gadowsky met with the media Monday evening, two days removed from being swept by a Notre Dame team that was four games under .500 heading into the weekend.

Here’s what he said, as his club officially has the worst 10-game start (2-7-1) in program history. There was some interesting stuff.

Gadowsky ‘not shocked’ of his team’s record

When asked if he’s surprised that this year’s team is off to the worst start in program history, Gadowsky chuckled and said, “No.” He quickly said of his 24 active players, 12 are new.

He also mentioned that the team is into its Big Ten slate earlier than usual (seven games into the season), and the non-conference opponents haven’t been easy.

Penn State played its first conference opponent in its ninth game last year, while facing Minnesota for its sixth matchup in its Frozen Four season (2024-25), when it went winless in Big Ten games through December.

Not to mention, the Nittany Lions lost to Robert Morris (0-4 at the time) at home.

“I think in the last six games we've only had one win that hasn't gone into overtime,” Gadowsky said Monday evening. “Anytime you have half a new team, you absolutely have to work on things, and we do. And you never know how long it's going to take, but that's where we're at. So results-wise, yeah, we'd like to get absolutely better results. But as I said at the end of Saturday night and doing all the analytics and video, I'm telling you that was our best team performance. It was. So we're taking steps.”

Past success doesn’t lead to added pressure

Penn State is one of three teams to make the NCAA Tournament in the past two years and get to at least one Frozen Four (Denver, Western Michigan). Gadowsky and company are 43-28-6 in those seasons combined.

But for Gadowsky and his staff, his program’s past success doesn’t add any pressure for results. He said it might for the players, though.

“The coaching staff, we have the luxury of looking at things and what we control and when we are playing well, and when we're not,” Gadowsky said. “And so we put pressure on ourselves to improve every day. We don't necessarily put pressure on ourselves to have the results, especially when we've had so much turnover.”

Penn State played its best game all year Saturday, per Gadowsky

The result aside, Gadowsky said his team played the best it has all season in Saturday’s 4-2 defeat to Notre Dame. He said he and his staff have a formula they use that shows if they do things a certain way, they have a high probability of winning.

Gadowsky said when the team accomplishes these things — he wouldn’t specify what — Penn State wins over 87% of those games. He said that the formula uses contests from the last four to five seasons.

“There's only been a handful of times where we've accomplished those things and lost,” Gadowsky said. “Hockey is still hockey. There's goaltenders. There's penalties. It happens. Like, hockey is really weird. You see, sometimes you play great, and you can lose, and other times people seem to be happy when we win when we do terrible things and, like, hockey's weird that way. So we know throughout our history that when we accomplish these things, what percent of the time we win. And this was one of those nights.”

title: Stock up, stock down | WR Chase Sowell returns, LBs struggle in Penn State’s win over Washington
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State made the cross-country trip to Seattle and took down Washington in a tale of two halves.

The game featured an onslaught in the first half behind the return of Chase Sowell, while two defensive depth pieces stepped up in majors ways to help Penn State come out with a victory.

Here’s who’s trending up and down after Week 10.

Stock up: Chase Sowell

Wide receiver Chase Sowell returned to the field after missing last week’s game against Purdue with an injury.

He seemingly didn’t miss a step, leading the Nittany Lions in receiving yards and proving once again he can bring down just about anything thrown to him. Sowell made the most of his six targets, catching four of them for 125 yards and a touchdown.

Three of his four catches were highlight-reel plays, including a catch along the sideline that was perfectly placed by Rocco Becht and two catches with defenders on him. His one-handed catch down the field was the cherry on top for his performance.

Sowell’s performance provided a consistent spark in Penn State’s passing game. When he was out, no receiver truly stepped up in his absence. He showed that for the Nittany Lions’ pass offense to be in full rhythm, he needs to be on the field, even to just have that threat of a go-to receiver out there.

Stock down: Linebackers

The linebacker play was some of the worst of the season all around. Tony Rojas had an up-and-down game, not playing consistently throughout, as Washington players made him miss.

Linebacker Kooper Ebel also missed some tackles despite leading Penn State with eight, matching Rojas’ mark on Saturday. The duo has been on the field together for an overwhelming majority of the game as the depth has thinned out.

A key aspect of Washington’s comeback efforts were due to the lack of tackling from the two linebackers, forcing the implementation of linebacker Cael Brezina in Ebel’s spot down the stretch. The Nittany Lions also added Marcus Neal Jr. into the mix at linebacker on Saturday in third-down situations, but it was mainly Ebel and Rojas on the field throughout the game.

Penn State’s two-linebacker system that it has deployed in the last two games isn’t sustainable, and Matt Campbell knows it. However, there really hasn’t been anything done to try to fix it.

Stock up: Ibn McDaniels

One of Penn State’s depth pieces had himself the best game of his career. Syracuse transfer Ibn McDaniels recorded the first interception of his career on Saturday when the Nittany Lions needed a big play on defense.

McDaniels has slowly worked himself into the rotation at cornerback despite being the fifth corner on the depth chart. He played more against Washington than he has in any other game this season.

Penn State’s top cornerback, Audavion Collins, wasn’t on the field much during Washington’s comeback, but McDaniels made his presence known throughout it. He fended off Washington running back Jayden Limar’s stiff arm in the second quarter to add to his day.

If the Nittany Lions have to rely on depth at cornerback, McDaniels showed he could be a player to step up as another young defender in Penn State’s relatively youthful defensive unit.

Stock down: Andrew Rappleyea

One of the players whose production was limited was tight end Andrew Rappleyea. Over the past couple of weeks, Rappleyea has proven to be Becht’s most reliable receiving target outside of Sowell.

That changed on Saturday as Rappleyea had just two catches for 16 yards on three targets. Rappleyea’s lone drop would’ve likely been a touchdown had he caught the pass that was right in his hands. Ultimately, it didn’t factor into Penn State’s score as it reached the end zone two plays later.

Rappleyea’s numbers were his lowest since Sept. 26 when he didn’t record a catch against Wisconsin. Although his workload went down in the passing game, he still was key to some big runs. But his receiving numbers taking a dip like they did is why his stock has taken a bit of a drop after multiple strong showings prior to Week 10.

Stock up: Ty Blanding

The final player who’s stock took a big jump was defensive tackle Ty Blanding. The redshirt junior has quietly been a big piece of the rotation on the defensive line recently, a group that has noticeably been more physical throughout the past two weeks.

Blanding has lined up all over the line, sometimes on the edge as a third defensive tackle, while also providing size on the interior.

He was rewarded on Saturday, recording a tackle for loss and half a sack alongside defensive end Yvan Kemajou. Blanding also came up with a tackle on Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. that was called back for a holding. He’s won at the point of attack and has proven to be a reliable defensive tackle in the rotation.

title: Penn State PhD student gives lecture on potential for machine learning to improve winter storm forecasts
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Friday, over a dozen students and faculty members took their seats in room 117 of the Earth and Engineering Sciences Building or logged in over Zoom to hear how one graduate student is integrating machine learning and specialized radar systems to improve winter storm predictions and other weather forecasts.

The lecture, which is part of this semester’s lineup of the College of Earth & Mineral Sciences’s TRAnscendIng Natural hazards forecasting (TRAIN) seminar series, featured Song Zhang, a graduate student working in the Department of Meteorology and Atmospheric Science currently studying for her PhD in meteorology and atmospheric science.

Beginning at 2 p.m., Zhang presented her current research into using machine learning to produce improved forecasts by analyzing data received by polarimetric radar systems — which are capable of offering a 3D readout of their surroundings by sending and receiving horizontal and vertical pings — to create and retrieve models for estimating snowfall, and relating it to realtime observations of winter weather, such as changes in temperature based on altitude, in a process called data assimilation.

Ethan Schaefer, who has researched creating weather models for winter storms, said he saw “untapped potential” in how machine learning can be used to improve the analysis of snowfall data by polarimetric radar systems.

Having spoken with Zhang about the similarities in their respective work, he said he hopes to one day apply Zhang’s research into actual predictive winter forecasts to see if it improves hazard predictions both for larger storms and smaller snow squalls, which Schaefer said can reduce visibility down to up to half a mile.

“Whether it's a winter storm, a snow squall or anything in between involving snow or freezing rain, it is important that we continue researching these and understanding how we can put our new insights into weather models and give our communities a better heads up for these events,” Schaefer, a graduate student studying meteorology and atmospheric science, said.

Steven Greybush, a professor of meteorology and one of Zhang’s two PhD advisors, said he found it great to see Penn State graduate students “advancing our knowledge” of winter storms and other weather.

He said winter storms, such as the one that occurred in January, are “one of the most challenging forecast problems,” which Zhang’s research stands to help solve by allowing meteorologists to “see what’s going on” inside a winter storm. He also said machine learning has the potential to infer relationships between a storm’s characteristics that go beyond what data the “classical methods” of meteorology can provide.

Greybush said having this additional information will allow authorities to have more time to to issue warnings ahead of an impending winter storm and better inform people of its potential impacts, such as increased travel accident rates and airport delays.

“The more lead time we have, the better we can prepare for these events,” Greybush said.

Zhang, who has had several research papers published as part of her work on winter weather either at Penn State or as part of NASA’s Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) project to improve winter weather forecasts, said her research is meant to determine the limitations of machine learning, as well as expand on previous work while studying at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign using polarimetric radar and cloud microphysics probes on research aircraft to map out the structure of winter storms.

She said the methods she has used in her studies, particularly the use of data assimilation, have the potential to assist in other weather forecasts, such as for tropical cyclones and flooding, and the study of other phenomena such as aircraft icing.

“I've talked to experts in aircraft icing and they're very interested in temperature and the particle size retrieval using polarimetric radar because these are the finest scale resolution instruments that they can find compared to satellites or other instruments,” Zhang said. “The methods, the approach and even when the model retrieval is constructed, the retrieval itself can be used for other studies through data assimilation, so either the result or the method can be used in other people's studies to further improve snow intensity forecasts and also maybe other fields, too.”

title: ‘We got to grow from this’ | Improved Penn State men’s basketball focused on progress
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
PHILADELPHIA — Two rivalry games for Mike Rhoades with Penn State, and two losses.

Pittsburgh has had the Nittany Lions number in these last few meetings under the most recent boss in Happy Valley. After the embarrassment of an 80-46 defeat for the blue and white at the GIANT Center in Hershey Park last season, Rhoades brought in a new squad, this time built on veteran energy.

Even with the new-look Nittany Lions, Penn State mustered only an 82-76 defeat in another neutral-site clash at the Palestra. Even though the result was the same, the performance differed.

“I was really proud of our guys. The effort (and) the fight was there. I thought down the stretch, coming out of some timeouts and some free throws, we executed some calls,” Rhoades said. “Really proud of them that way. I thought there was some good stuff there. For a third game in a year to have a game like this, we need it.”

A group of Nittany Lions still fresh in their period to gel held in with the Panthers for all 40 minutes, giving a Pitt team a real challenge that had even more investment this offseason.

“They're older, they're bigger, (and) their bodies are more mature,” Pitt coach Jeff Capel said. “I think they play the right way. They really move the basketball (and) they have three guys inside that are good players that are leading them. They're very physical, and they're really good on the glass.”

One of the main catalysts to Penn State’s competitive night, despite the loss, was its physicality, along with age, as the Nittany Lions continued to match Pitt’s intensity. The blue and white also capitalized on that edge, taking 14 more trips to the charity stripe in an incredibly physical game.

This wasn’t a surprise, though. From local media day, to open practice availability or to postgame press conferences — Rhoades has said he wants his team to be aggressive.

“The greatest warriors in the history of the world. Right? They were savages, they were warriors, (and) they had a level of discipline that people still talk about them to this day,” Rhoades said. “We want to be an aggressive physical team, and we want to play to a great pace. We want to attack people, but you always have to have a level of discipline in the moment that it's needed, and we just didn't have that enough today.”

As it’s said, ‘complacency kills,’ yet even for a Nittany Lions group which earned two high-scoring nonconference wins to open its season and drew a steady eye on the program around Happy Valley, there was no risk of the results or positive nodes getting to them.

“There's some good things today, but we got to improve (and) we got to get better,” Rhoades said. “This was a disappointing loss.”

7-footer Ivan Jurić led Penn State in the loss, clocking in and out with another double-double. The Zagreb, Croatia, native has been in the midst of a sophomore jump, as it was noted all offseason for his need to add muscle and toughness.

“Anytime you challenge (Jurić), he responds the right way, it's not the other way,” Rhoades said. “He's not going to get on the bus and complain and make excuses. He'll take ownership, and I think that's one of the reasons why he's improved since the day he got here.”

They say you can’t teach an old dog new tricks, but with the situation Penn State is in, Rhoades may have no other choice.

“We're not the most athletic team; we sure aren't going to be in the Big Ten — That's okay,” Rhoades said. “We got to be the toughest and the most disciplined — We got to get better at that.”

It wasn’t just discipline that hurt Penn State’s chances, as it turned the ball over 16 times to the Panthers’ nine. The Nittany Lions’ loss came primarily from a crumble down the stretch in which it allowed some big Pitt scores and fumbled possession of the ball.

“We just got to get better (and) we got to grow from this,” Rhoades said. “We beat ourselves today, and then it beat us — Now we got to learn not to beat ourselves.”

title: Which wrestlers could pose as threats to Penn State's individual national title contenders?
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State wrestling earned its fifth consecutive national title last year, with three wrestlers being crowned national champions. Luke Lilledahl at 125 pounds, Mitchell Mesenbrink achieving his second win at 165, and Josh Barr at 197 pounds.

The three will return to defend their titles, along with many other Nittany Lions like Marcus Blaze and Tyler Kasak who have the potential to stack on to the team’s individual winners.

Here are the names across the country that could compete against the blue and white for a national victory.

125

While Lilledahl will return to the mat as the No. 1-ranked wrestler in the country and is projected as the season winner, he will once again meet up with his competitors from last year, who will no doubt be out for redemption after falling to Lilledahl last season.

Princeton’s Marc-Anthony McGowan lost to Lilledahl in the finals, placing second in the tournament. He still earned his second Ivy League championship and finished the season 17-6. His strong defense limited Lilledahl in the finals, and it could play a factor in future matches.

Stanford’s Nico Provo is also out for the trophy after losing in the Round of 16 to McGowan last season. Provo placed third overall after winning all six of his consolation matches, and defeating Vincent Robinson of NC State for third place. Provo helped Stanford earn its sixth-place finish at the championships, the Cardinal’s highest in program history.

133

Blaze is one of Penn State’s top promising contenders for a national championship and is a projected starter after finishing out his first collegiate season with a national fourth-place finish.

Only a second-year athlete, Blaze is ranked No. 4, but has tough competition from his fellow sophomore class. Blaze fell 5-0 against Aaron Seidel of Virginia Tech, who placed third last year after losing to Ohio State’s Ben Davino.

All three of the wrestlers fell to Jax Forrest of Oklahoma State, who took the national title as a freshman, after his undefeated run last year, joining the Cowboys for the second half of the season.

Forrest will be a force to be reckoned with at such an early point in his career, becoming one of Oklahoma State’s three true freshman national champions, and contributed an overall 26 points to the team standings.

141

While the starter for the Nittany Lions is unknown, there is potential for wrestlers like Braeden Davis to earn his way on to the podium. Davis went 14-7 in the regular season and 2-2 in the National Championships. Penn State could put out Nate Desmond, Masanosuke Ono or even a jump in weight by Blaze at the spot.

Nevertheless, it will be a hard climb as third-place finisher Luke Stanich of Lehigh will return as one of the favorites to win the title. Virginia Tech true freshman Bo Bassett is also a major threat. Bassett defeated Stanich 13-9 in the opening week, just days after winning a Senior World Championship.

149

Shayne Van Ness will be a starter for the Nittany Lions after a second-place finish at nationals last year, proving that he can handle himself on the big stage.

Van Ness will start the season ranked No. 4 as redshirt Caleb Henson returns to the mat as the projected champion.

Henson won the championship as a sophomore before returning and losing in the finals in 2025. He will compete against the No. 2-ranked Sergio Vega of Oklahoma State after he took the championship last year.

Vega made the jump to 149 pounds this season after winning at 141 last year, joining Forrest again on the strong Oklahoma State roster. He went 24-0 last season while never surrendering a takedown.

Stanford’s Aden Valencia beat out Van Ness in the finals last year to win it all. He returns for his sophomore season on a strong Cardinal squad and could be a threat to win it all again.

157

After a redshirt season last year left him off the mat, Kasak will come back as the No. 2 seed behind reigning champion Landon Robideau. He’s just ahead of 2026 runner-up Antrell Taylor of Nebraska.

Kasak earned third in the championships during the 2024 season, after clinching the Big Ten title and earning first-team All-Big Ten honors. He will come back hungry to climb the podium and finish at the top.

However, Robideau won’t make it easy. The third true freshman Oklahoma State Cowboy is gritty, being able to avenge both his losses from the regular season to come out on top and earn the title.

He made up one of the three true freshman national champions, and brought home the win from the U20 World Team Trials, and finished third at the U20 World Championships.

165

PJ Duke is another star athlete for Penn State, after a first-place finish in the Big Ten Championships and a third-place podium finish on the national stage at 157 pounds as a first-year.

Duke will move up in weight classes this year to replace standing national champion Mitchell Mesenbrink, as he likely moves up to 174 pounds.

The Slate Hill, New York, native is ranked No. 1 as a sophomore and was a key starter for Penn State last season. However, No. 2 Arizona State junior Nicco Ruiz is no stranger to winning at 165, taking both the Big Twelve and 2026 U23 Freestyle National Championships.

Purdue’s Joey Blaze will be another name to watch, as he finished sixth in the country last year after going 25-4 on the season. Blaze was Purdue’s fourth undefeated regular-season athlete, going 18-0 without surrendering a takedown. Now in his second year at the weight, he could pose another threat to Penn State’s 165-pound title hopes.

174

With the graduation of two-time champion Levi Haines from Penn State last season, teammate and two-time 165-pound champion Mitchell Mesenbrink will step up to take his place.

Mesenbrink has been one of Penn State’s most decorated athletes, having won back-to-back National Championships and Big Ten tournament titles since transferring in his sophomore year.

Mesenbrink will no doubt bring the same grit he’s carried with him into the class. However, new faces and a heavier weight could pose a challenge to the 165 veteran.

Nebraska’s Christopher Minto was no stranger to Haines, with the two being rivals throughout their collegiate careers. Minto fell short to Haines last season in both the Big Ten Championships and in the National Championships, losing by a close 2-1.

With Haines gone, Minto will have the chance to come back stronger and will be hungry to finally claim a championship for his own.

184

Rocco Welsh has been a big name for Penn State since transferring from Ohio State. Welsh boasted a second-place finish against Minnesota’s Max McEnelly in the national finals, after a close 4-3 decision.

Welsh won the Big Ten Tournament last year over McEnelly and dominated the field with a 24-1 record on the season and a 59-6 career record.

The two will face off again this season, as McEnelly will look to repeat his time as a national champion and continue to lead his program at Minnesota. He was the school’s first-ever champion at 184, and national title holder since 2022.

197

Josh Barr is no stranger to victory, and is the favorite at 197 pounds after winning the Big Ten National Championships last season.

Barr finished his junior season at 24-0, with six being major decision wins. The points he earned at nationals were a large contribution and factor in Penn State earning their 14th national team title.

Oklahoma State sophomore Cody Merrill could pose a threat to Barr, after a hard-fought 6-3 decision loss left him as runner-up. Merrill still finished his freshman season as an All-American and with a 21-5 record.

With Merrill already performing this well against a top competitor in his first year at the collegiate level, there is a high chance the two could battle it out this season, with Merrill coming out on top as a sophomore.

285

After the graduation of heavyweight champions Issac Trumble and Wyatt Hendrickson, the floor is now open for new competition to land their spot on the podium.

Oklahoma State’s Konner Doucet joins his teammates as the No. 1 seed, after being a starter last season. He dominated his competition in duals, going 14-2, and earning more bonus-point wins in the season than in his last four years combined.

Doucet will be a force to reckon with for either of the twins, Cole or Connor Mirasola, with Cole failing to reach the podium in his first year as a starter.

If Doucet is the starter — given that heavyweight freshman Dreshaun Ross could also start — he’d be in contention for the title alongside some returning Big Ten heavyweights. Iowa’s Ben Kueter, Ohio State’s Nick Feldman and Wisconsin’s Braxton Amos could also push to be at the top of the podium.

title: Big Ten roundup | Ohio State loses again, Maryland earns 1st Big Ten victory
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Week 9 featured lots of chaos and late-game heroics, the same was to be said in Week 10 across the Big Ten.

Ohio State lost its second straight top-25 matchup without quarterback Julian Sayin, while Maryland earned its first conference victory. The Buckeyes, Michigan and Nebraska’s losses resulted in coordinators being fired.

Here’s what happened to kick off Big Ten play in November.

Ohio State loses second straight

Things haven’t looked good for Ohio State since it lost Sayin against Indiana on Oct. 17. While the Buckeyes pulled out a win then, they’ve now lost two straight including a loss against Oregon on Saturday.

True freshman quarterback Luke Fahey was given the reins of the offense again and threw the ball 50 times against the Ducks. He finished the day with 36 completions for 360 yards, two touchdowns and an interception.

The Buckeyes were up 14-0 at the end of the first quarter. A fake punt by Oregon linebacker Teitum Tuioti extended a crucial drive for the Ducks, which then led to a touchdown and a momentum shift in the game.

The following drive, Fahey threw his only interception of the game. Oregon capitalized on the shorter field and found the end zone again before the half, taking a 17-14 lead into the locker room. Coming out of the break, the Ducks continued to drive down the field, as running back Dierre Hill Jr. had a 48-yard rushing touchdown on the first drive of the half.

The Buckeyes scored two touchdowns late in the fourth quarter to trim into the lead, but it was too little, too late as Oregon earned its fourth top-25 win of the season, 41-28, and Ohio State fell to 6-3 for the first time since 2011.

Ohio State fired its special teams coordinator, Robby Discher, on Monday.

Losses result in fired coordinators

For the first time in five years, Michigan State brought home the Paul Bunyan Trophy after defeating Michigan, 15-6, at the Big House.

It was a game of field goals for the Spartans, who scored through the uprights five times, resulting in all their points. The Wolverines’ first offensive success came with 1:55 to play, as Savion Hiter found the end zone before Michigan failed to convert its two-point conversion.

While Tommy Carr was given the nod at quarterback again for the Wolverines, he failed to produce positive results, throwing 14-for-26 for 136 yards and a pair of interceptions. Michigan’s offense generated just 192 total yards.

The Wolverines ultimately fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck, who came to Michigan with Kyle Whittingham. As a result, offensive line coach and assistant head coach Jim Harding was named the interim offensive coordinator.

A day before in Illinois, Nebraska lost its fourth straight game in a 24-13 contest against the Fighting Illini.

Illinois scored three straight touchdowns in a span of 18:10, while the Cornhuskers couldn’t find any answers. Quarterback Katin Houser had his first three-touchdown outing in Big Ten play and his first interception-free game since September.

The following morning, Nebraska fired its defensive coordinator Dana Holgorsen.

Maryland wins post-Locksley

For the first time since Week 4 of the 2025 season, Maryland came out victorious in a Big Ten matchup, but did so under interim head coach Aazaar Abdul-Rahim after Mike Locksley was fired on Oct. 21.

The Terrapins defeated Purdue, 34-29, one week after their closest conference game of the year against Illinois.

Four field goals from the Boilermakers created a 12-7 lead at halftime. However, Maryland scored three field goals in the third quarter to take the lead and never looked back.

It was a trio of big plays that categorized the Terrapins’ scoring against one of the worst defenses in the Big Ten. Quarterback Malik Washington found wide receiver Na’eem Abdul-Brush Gladding for a 44-yard touchdown early in the second half, followed by a 75-yard rushing touchdown from DeJuan Williams on the first play of the drive.

Maryland reached 34 points on the day as Washington connected with wide receiver Chris Durr Jr. for an 84-yard touchdown grab midway through the final period.

title: Big Ten announces 2026 Big Ten Championship will be the last after College Football Playoff expansion
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten has officially announced the 2026 Big Ten Football Championship game will be the last.

This year's championship game will be the 16th, as the contest dates back to 2011, and will take place on Dec. 5 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis.

"The Big Ten Conference is deeply grateful to the city of Indianapolis the Indiana Sports Corp, Lucas Oil Stadium and the hundreds of thousands of fans who helped make the Big Ten Football Championship Game a marquee event each season," commissioner Tony Petitti wrote in a statement.

With the finalization of the 24-team College Football Playoff starting 2027, the first round will take place during when conference championships are usually played. The SEC has also announced the elimination of its conference title game.

The Big Ten expressed its excitement for the expanded bracket because there will be "more meaningful games throughout the season for more teams," Petitti said.

Penn State has made the Big Ten championship twice since the game's inception, winning a thriller over Wisconsin in 2016. It lost to Oregon, 45-37, in its second appearance in 2024.

The Nittany Lions' 2016 Big Ten Championship win is one of the program's most iconic moments in the past decade.

title: Penn State men’s basketball honors 100 years of the Palestra with rivalry clash
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
PHILADELPHIA — 100 years of college basketball.

The Palestra has stood in the City of Brotherly Love for exactly a century come this January, and its season so far has commemorated the milestone of the ground being broken for the venue. In its concrete walls and heaven-touching rafters, the cathedral of college basketball, as it's been dubbed, has been home to many memories and historical moments throughout its tenure.

The sports icon’s venue saw yet another thrilling game when it hosted the 150th edition of the Pittsburgh-Penn State series on the hardwood, a matchup in itself that dated the very building it was played in this year.

“It was an honor to play in this building. This is one of the most historic venues in all of sports, especially in basketball,” Panthers’ coach Jeff Capel said. “It's my first time ever here, and so just the experience of being a shootaround today, walking around, feeling the legends that have been in here in the history throughout this building.”

Pitt fought off the Nittany Lions for a strong 82-76 win in a game that was narrow for all 40 minutes of action. The result pulled the infamous rivalry series to an almost even 76-74 Penn State advantage.

The rivalry clash was just another blip in the Palestra’s decorated past, one felt with every dribble and cheer. Charles Klaude, the same architect who designed Penn State’s own iconic arena, Rec Hall, drew up the plans for the Palestra, and history has been added to it ever since.

“Older people seeing Wilt (Chamberlin) in here, seeing Kobe (Bryant), seeing the Big Five games, and all the historic players that have played here,” Capel said. “It was an honor for us.”

For both squads, the player and coaching ties run deep to the commonwealth, but even for those who don’t, the power of the Palestra was still felt. Mike Rhoades took time postgame to share his affinity for his grandfather, who once played at the Palestra with Villanova, and his memories of going to the games or reading about them in the Philadelphia Inquirer.

But it wasn’t just those on the sidelines or with prior connections.

“I was explaining to these guys the history of the Palestra,” Rhoades said. “We had a lot of international guys, and some of them said this reminds them of places they played in Europe.”

Penn State and Pitt most recently met last year in a much different venue, appearing in Hershey Park’s GIANT Center in a late December game. The Panthers claimed that one decisively, but despite a different result, the fanfare and support were similar.

“When we talked to Penn State about playing, we wanted to try to take it to different places in Pennsylvania,” Capel said. “This is one that I think I'm pretty sure Mike (Rhoades) felt the same way: We really wanted to play here (at the Palestra). And the fact that it's celebrating 100 years was even more special.”

Both Capel and Rhoades continued their respect toward each other in their respective press conferences, despite no clear indication of when the two sides may see each other again. For the Penn State boss, Rhoades was adamant that his team would be back at the Palestra someday, as his squad has routinely made the trek out east.

“It's an old school rivalry. I remember being a kid, and my dad took me to a Pitt-Penn State football game, and the things I heard in the stands was an education for me," Rhoades said. "A lot of these people are probably going to work together tomorrow. That's what it should be, and it was good, good fanfare and good for college athletics, college sports, especially with all the craziness in the world.”

The Nittany Lions have played 65 games total at the Palestra, going 25-40 over that stretch.

title: Penn State men’s basketball loses to Pittsburgh at Palestra, suffers first defeat of season
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
PHILADELPHIA — 120 years of hoops between two programs and the 150th all-time meeting of rivals — the iconic Palestra hosted yet another classic game within its confines.

In the cathedral of college basketball, Penn State lost to in-state rival Pittsburgh 82-76 in front of a Panthers-favored crowd. Jeff Capel’s unit now has back-to-back wins over the Nittany Lions, both of which were under Mike Rhoades. The Nittany Lions still lead the series 76-74 all time.

"I thought we had some really good moments of basketball," Rhoades said. "Couldn't guard consistently enough, and we had some turnovers that really hurt us ... I thought there was times we just beat ourselves today — Pitt took advantage of it."

Blue and white 7-footer Ivan Jurić won the tipoff, but the ball bounced out of bounds to allow Pitt the first possession. In a foul-heavy opening few minutes, the Panthers took a quick five-point lead.

Rhoades continued to tinker with various lineup combinations due to the calls, as both of his big men picked up two fouls before the midpoint of the half. The Nittany Lions clawed back, as guard Jay Rodgers splashed his first 3-pointer with Penn State to tie it at 17-17, yet the ref’s whistle persisted.

At the 10-minute mark of the first frame, there were 17 total fouls, and Penn State logged nine of those calls. By the time the Nittany Lions had taken its first lead, the charity stripe was a major vessel for getting them there.

"I think (Penn State is) better than they were last year. First of all, they're bigger, they're older, (and) their bodies are more mature," Capel said. "I think they play the right way, they really move the basketball ... I'm rooting for them for the rest of the season, rooting for Mike."

At 7:55 in the first half, Penn State led 27-26 but had gone 12-of-15 from the foul line, while the Panthers had made only four trips. Both squads had fouled 10 times each to then.

The Nittany Lions made a push at momentum, as wing Brant Byers swished a pair of threes to guide them to a 35-30 advantage.

Pitt subdued that approach and went on a run to tie it off sloppy Penn State turnovers. The Panthers slammed down an alley-oop in the process to send the Palestra crowd, which was Pitt-friendly, into chants.

"It's an old school rivalry. I remember being a kid, and my dad took me to a Pitt-Penn State football game, and the things I heard in the stands was an education for me," Rhoades said. "A lot of these people are probably going to work together tomorrow. That's what it should be, and it was good, good fanfare, and good for college athletics, college sports, especially with all the craziness in the world."

Ultimately, with both sides trading buckets before the break, Pitt held a 42-38 lead.

The opening minutes of the second half resembled much of the first, as neither side was able to seize momentum up to the first media stoppage. Pitt senior guard A'lahn Sumler continued to be a scoring threat to the Penn State defense with 13 of the Panthers’ 15 points to start the half.

The Panthers soon navigated to a 63-56 lead, with momentum on their side as the blue and white offense began to falter with Dasonte Bowen’s playmaking stalling.

Pitt’s budding star freshman forward Chase Foster started slow but picked up his first scores of the game down the wire, giving the Panthers a six-point lead with five minutes to play.

That momentum stayed with the Panthers’ offense, as the blue and white couldn’t match the scoring pace in the final minutes. Costly fouls and empty possessions led to Penn State’s demise, with too little time to fix those mistakes.

A late full-court press and fast offensive pace couldn’t stop Pitt from winding the clock down for the win.

"We want to be an aggressive physical team, and we want to play to a great pace," Rhoades said. "We want to attack people, but you always have to have a level of discipline in the moment that it's needed and we just didn't have that enough today. We got a lot of new faces; we just got to get better (and) we got to grow from this. But we beat ourselves today, and then Pitt beat us."

Pitt’s Sumler led total scoring with 26 points, as Bowen’s 17 points led Penn State on 5-of-8 attempts from the field. Jurić logged 16 points and 13 rebounds, as the Zagreb, Croatia, native posted a double-double in every game so far this season. Penn State forwards Josh Reed and Roko Prkacin also both scored 11 points as the final blue and white scorers to reach double digits.

With the result, the blue and white drop to 2-1 on the young season.

Up next

The Nittany Lions continue their season back in Happy Valley with the Hoops for Troops match at the Bryce Jordan Center against Mercyhurst. Tip-off with the Lakers is set for Thursday at 6:30 p.m.

title: Week 10 report card | Balanced offense shines, missed tackles hurt LBs in win over Washington
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s on a winning streak for the first time since the nonconference schedule. The Nittany Lions survived a second half comeback bid to beat Washington, 28-25, at Husky Stadium in Seattle on Saturday.

It was a tale of two halves, much like the Wisconsin game in Week 4. But this time, the Nittany Lions pulled through in the end and are knocking on the door of bowl eligibility.

Here’s how I’d grade each aspect of Penn State’s performance in the win over Washington.

Overall: B

Penn State started the game red-hot with a 28-6 lead at the end of the first half, showcasing early dominance on both sides of the ball. However, the Nittany Lions came out flat in the second half, and the game came down the wire as the Huskies scored 19 unanswered points to bring the game within three points.

Coaching staff: C+

Matt Campbell ignited a fire in Penn State by telling his players about College and Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker and radio color analyst Jack Ham’s sudden medical emergency, leaving him hospitalized. The Nittany Lions flew out of the gates, rallying behind the legendary alumnus.

With that said, Campbell was once again out-coached in the middle eight. Penn State had the ball with two minutes remaining in the first half, and Campbell decided to play conservative, bleeding the clock.

Washington made all the necessary corrections at halftime and the Nittany Lions didn’t find an answer until a series of first downs in the fourth quarter, sealing Penn State’s victory.

Offense: B+

Four touchdowns within the first five drives were enough to outpace the Huskies on the West Coast, as both the pass game and run game were effective, equally finding the end zone.

Pass game: B+

Rocco Becht had 193 passing yards and two touchdowns at the end of the first half and finished the game 16-for-27 with 240 yards without another score.

Sowell’s return to the lineup offered Becht a clear No. 1 receiver, despite the fact he was only targeted six times. Penn State’s ace closed the game with 125 receiving yards and a touchdown on four catches, making the most of his limited opportunities.

Zay Robinson was the other wide receiver to find the end zone, finishing the game with two catches for 30 yards.

Run game: A-

Running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace each broke long runs and found the end zone, capitalizing on holes created by the offensive line and displaying improved patience.

Hansen’s 32-yard rush in the fourth quarter afforded Penn State the necessary breathing room to win the game with the ball. He finished the game as the Nittany Lions’ No. 1 running back, tallying 119 rushing yards and a touchdown.

This grade would’ve been an “A” if Wallace saw more success outside of his 46-yard rushing touchdown, as his six other rushes combined for only 10 yards.

Offensive line: B+

Penn State’s offensive line paved the way for Hansen and Wallace to rush north of eight yards per carry while giving Becht ample time to showcase his deep ball. However, three sacks, one of which was after a bad snap, leave a lot of room for improvement.

Defense: B

After only giving up a pair of field goals in the first half, the Nittany Lions allowed 19 unanswered points in the second half in a game that could’ve been a blowout.

Pass rush: B-

While the pass rush wasn’t as effective compared to when Penn State played Purdue, the Nittany Lions got significant pressure on Williams, contributing to his poor passing in the first half when he went 6-for-15 with only 39 passing yards.

Tony Rojas and cornerback Daryus Dixson hurried the quarterback while defensive end Yvan Kemajou and defensive tackle Ty Blanding combined for Penn State’s only sack in the second quarter.

Linebackers: C

The linebackers had an unusually quiet outing in Seattle, unable to contain the pass game in the second half due to many missed tackles, particularly from Kooper Ebel, who was still tied for first on the team with eight tackles.

Rojas had eight tackles with a tackle for loss and quarterback hurry, and Marcus Neal Jr. had one tackle.

It was a passable performance against a team like Washington, especially having such a big lead at halftime, but the room can’t slack if the Nittany Lions want to continue building on their momentum.

Secondary: B+

Safety Ibn McDaniels’ interception in the fourth quarter added the plus to this grade. It was a critical moment of defensive success amid Penn State’s disastrous second half, and it may have saved the game.

Dixson, safety Jamison Patton and cornerback Audavion Collins all registered pass breakups. Additionally, cornerback Josiah Zayas linked up with Ebel for a tackle for loss.

However, Williams finished 19-33 with 172 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Williams threw 136 of those yards in the second half as Penn State wasn’t able to maintain consistency through all four quarters.

Special teams: C

Kicker Ryan Barker made good on all of his extra-point attempts, but Campbell elected to keep the offense on the field on fourth down in the third quarter instead of trusting Barker with an over 50-yard field goal, a distance he’s struggled from this season.

title: No. 11 Penn State women’s volleyball defeats No. 7 Wisconsin, earns 7th straight victory
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming off a 3-1 win against No. 19 Minnesota on Friday night, Penn State continued its road trip with a meeting against No. 7 Wisconsin.

The blue and white earned its seventh straight win, defeating the Badgers in five sets.

Set one saw a quick back-and-forth between both squads. Whitney Lauenstein added two kills early on to keep the Nittany Lions neck and neck with Wisconsin’s attacks from Audrey Flanagan and Lynney Tarnow.

Wisconsin opted to use an early challenge on a Penn State attack and won, taking both a 4-2 lead and one of Lauenstein’s kills away. Following the challenge, the Badgers gained a multi-point lead off of a three-point run.

Penn State earned back possession after a Gabrielle Nichols kill, bringing the blue and white within two. A Badger attack error put them within one, but Wisconsin's Jaela Auguste extended their lead to 7-5.

Kennedy Martin added five more kills to the scoreboard; however, Penn State failed to block Auguste, which made the Badger lead even longer. Auguste totaled four kills of her own, and her pairing with Tarnow gave Wisconsin a six-point lead at the 18-12 mark.

Martin continued to answer back against a difficult Badger defense, with another cross kill and her ninth kill of the match to bring Penn State within four points.

Penn State called a late-set timeout with the score 21-17 after Wisconsin errors and an Alexis Stucky kill brought the Nittany Lions within four.

The blue and white failed to go down without a fight as Nichols added two more kills of her own, creeping within three points of the Wisconsin lead. However, an overpass kill from Flanagan brought things to set point, and a Martin attack error officially gave the Badgers the first set.

Wisconsin took the first point of set two off of a Champion kill assisted by Charlie Fuerbringer. The Nittany Lions, however, answered back with two kills of their own.

A fight for the one-point upper hand lasted for nine consecutive points until Penn State went on a five-point run topped by a Northern-Martin paired block.

Wisconsin ended the five-point run following a media timeout as Decelise Champion added her third kill. Northern replied with a kill, but possession was quickly flipped after Auguste added her fifth kill.

After the Nittany Lions added two more points, making their lead six. Following a Wisconsin timeout, Penn State earned four of five points, leading Wisconsin to call for another stoppage at the 22-13 mark.

With Penn State two points away from set point, Wisconsin went on a three-point run in hopes of carrying some momentum into the third set.

Penn State reached set point after a Fuerbringer service error; however, Wisconsin added two more points, following a Wardlow kill and Martin attack error. The Nittany Lions officially captured set two after Stucky assisted Martin for a kill to a hole in the center of the court.

Penn State continued its lead in the third set after a Fuerbringer block error; however, a service error by Stucky evened out the score at one.

The Badgers earned their second lead of the set after an attack error by Northern and a paired block from Travis and Tarnow brought the score to 7-5. While Penn State continued to creep back in, the Badgers remained ahead for the next ten points, and Penn State called a timeout.

After the stoppage, a paired block from Martin and Nichols brought the blue and white within three. After two Wisconsin kills and one service error, the match went to a media timeout, with Wisconsin leading 15-11.

After the pause, Penn State tied the set behind a four-point run thanks to kills by Emmi Sellman, Northern and Lauenstein, paired with an attack error by Wisconsin’s Travis.

Following a Wisconsin timeout, roles completely reversed, and the Badgers went on a three-point run, forcing Katie Schumacher-Cawley to call a timeout.

Despite being down three points and creeping closer to a Wisconsin set point, Lauenstein reopened play with three consecutive kills to even the score at 18-18.

The three-point run was ended by Champion, after she added her tenth kill of the match; however, Schumacher-Cawley successfully challenged the call, and Penn State was rewarded a point, giving it a one-point lead.

Following the challenge, Wisconsin earned six points, only separated by a single Lauenstein kill, bringing the set to 24-19. While at match point, Martin added another kill to give Penn State a last-minute extension; however, Champion finished the set with a kill assisted by Fuerbringer.

The first multi-point run for Penn State took place at the 4-3 mark when Martin and Sellman contributed a kill each and Wisconsin contributed two attack errors. Penn State added four more points to double their lead, only interrupted by a single Auguste kill.

Following the nearly perfect eight-point run, the Badgers and Nittany Lions traded short runs until Wisconsin broke away for a five-point run, bringing themselves within two of the blue and white lead. Penn State quickly replicated the momentum with five points of its own, only separated by a single Badger kill.

Penn State had a momentous end to the set, winning 25-19 and extending the match to a winner-take-all set.

The Badgers opened up set five with a Tarnow kill assisted by Fuerbringer, but the blue and white responded efficiently with a kill by Martin — her 24th of the night. Penn State continued its explosive offense, going on a three-point run after a kill each by Nichols, Martin and Northern.

Auguste continuously tried to break away with a run for Wisconsin; however, a relentless front line in Martin and Sellman made it difficult, and Wisconsin continued to sit three points behind for a majority of the match.

At the 13-11 point, Wisconsin called a timeout, as Penn State was only two away from taking the match. After the stoppage, Sellman contributed a seventh kill assisted by Ava Fadulto, bringing Penn State to match point.

The Nittany Lions officially took the match after Martin’s 28th kill assisted by Stucky.

Up Next

Penn State remains on the road, facing off against Maryland at 7 p.m. Wednesday.

title: The Rivet Winter Market brings holiday spirit, supports small businesses
author: Isabella Gearhart | For the Collegian
description:
As the holiday season approaches, local markets offer community members an opportunity to support small businesses while still shopping for unique gifts.

The Rivet Winter Market, held Nov. 7 to 8 from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. at Discovery Space and The Rivet, brought together a variety of local vendors who offered handmade goods and seasonal items, along with food stands serving homemade meals and treats. The event provided shoppers with an opportunity to explore local businesses, meet vendors and experience the creativity of the State College community.

Among the vendors was Chelsea Aukerman, a Penn State alumna and owner of The Bent Fender Jewelry LLC.

“I started in 2023, and I have a friend who makes cremation jewelry, and I’ve always wanted to do spoon rings,” Aukerman, 37, of Woodward, Pennsylvania, said. “I ended up buying a vendor. I bought a couple spoons and just tried it.”

Aukerman said the process involved trial and error, figuring out what worked and what didn’t. After making her first pieces, she began selling them at work, which helped her business grow.

Today, the company offers a wide variety of handmade products.

“I have earrings, necklaces, purse hooks and I started to do Christmas ornaments,” Aukerman said. “My purse hooks are really popular on Etsy because they make really great gifts.”

Participating in vendor events, such as The Rivet Winter Market, provides Aukerman with an opportunity to promote her business and reach new customers.

“No matter what vendor event you go to, you’re putting yourself out there,” Aukerman said. “It’s spreading your name out, getting yourself out there and talking to people. That’s what really helps boost your business.”

Beyond creating unique jewelry, Aukerman hopes customers find sentimental value in the pieces they purchase. Through repurposing silverware, she transforms family heirlooms into jewelry that can be kept for years.

“I hear stories all the time from people like, ‘My mom had a spoon ring’ or ‘My grandma had a spoon ring,’ so these things are definitely transferable through generations,” Aukerman said.

Eric Tobert, the owner of Phoenix Woodcraft, said his business originally began as a hobby when he was searching for materials for his personal projects.

“I was looking for a way to find cheaper wood for my own personal use and then discovered all this beautiful wood at low prices and decided to try and keep it out of the landfill,” Tobert, 51, of Greensburg, Pennsylvania, said.

Today, Phoenix Woodcraft repurposes used and recycled furniture into a variety of handmade kitchen and household products. The company offers cutting boards, magnetic knife blocks, trivets and picture frames.

At the market, Tobert said Phoenix Woodcraft can connect with potential customers and introduce people to its products.

“It gets you a lot of contacts that you’re not going to see otherwise,” Tobert said. “A lot of people take a business card and think about products that they might be interested in when they get home and then either contact us later or show up at another show.”

Beyond selling handmade products, Tobert hopes customers understand the importance of reusing materials and reducing waste. By turning old wood into new items, Phoenix Woodcraft gives discarded materials another purpose.

“Everything we do is an attempt to keep this old wood and all these useful products out of the landfill and give them a new life where they can be used again for 10, 20, 30 years or more,” Tobert said.

Katie Molinengo, the owner of Rooted in the Forest, draws inspiration from nature to create handmade products for the home.

Molinengo specializes in items inspired by a cabin lifestyle, offering pottery and pottery candles with a forest-inspired aesthetic.

Her interest in creating candles began as a personal hobby, eventually developing into a business that combines her love for art and nature.

“I have an MFA in painting, so it was starting with landscape painting,” Molinengo, 36, of Huntingdon, Pennsylvania, said. “I just love making candles, so I just wanted to make them for myself, but then it fused together to make a whole matching aesthetic.”

Like other vendors at the market, Molinengo said participating in the market helps build brand recognition through social media and word of mouth.

“I’ve run into people that said they’ve heard about Rooted in the Forest before, and I don’t remember actually meeting them,” Molinengo said. “That’s great, it sells out, and I’m always like, ‘This is good.’”

Molinengo hopes her creations bring a sense of comfort into people’s homes.

“It’s an experience for the home,” Molinengo said. “I think it makes the setting cozy, having a connection to nature.”
